#WATCH | New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced the disbanding of the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group (SRG), a specialised unit that faced years of criticism over its handling of protests, allegations of excessive force and mass arrests.

The decision, announced on November 16 alongside Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, fulfils a key campaign promise to separate counterterrorism operations from protest policing.

Under the new arrangement:
- A civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division will coordinate protest responses. Its members will be unarmed and have no arrest powers.
- A 30-officer First Amendment Support Team will focus on communication and de-escalation.
- A new Patrol Support Division will take on crowd-management duties.
- Police will be barred from using kettling, tear gas and long guns during demonstrations. Pepper spray will no longer be used as a general crowd-management tool.

The SRG's counterterrorism responsibilities will move to the NYPD's Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau. Its approximately 500 officers will be reassigned within the department.

The move has drawn support from civil liberties groups, though some have called for close oversight of the new structure. Police unions, meanwhile, have criticised the decision, arguing it could affect public and officer safety.

V roce 1989 se sovětsko-ruské impérium začalo rudému caru Gorbačovovi hroutit pod rukama. Oslabená Moskva uvolnila sevření a zejména středoevropské gubernie to pochopily jako signál k emancipaci. A tak 9. listopadu 1989 padla i zlopověstná Berlínská zeď. V Československu, v němž za podpory sovětských okupačních vojsk vládl jako gubernátor Husák se svým gangem, se začal ruský (komunistický) imperiálně-koloniální režim rozpadat až po 17. listopadu, v reakci na brutálně potlačenou studentskou demonstraci. Moskva tehdy vzkázala, že místní geronty nepodpoří a její vojska zůstanou v kasárnách. Tak začala sametová revoluce, onen nádherný československý happening svobody, který vedl k obnovení demokracie. Jenže málokdo si uvědomoval, že Listopad skončil až 30. června 1991, kdy byl podepsán závěrečný protokol o odchodu sovětských okupačních vojsk. Teprve tehdy byla obnovena i suverenita naší země, skončila její geopolitická sovětizace a mentální rusifikace. Říše zla se záhy rozpadla, což byl největší geopolitický zázrak 20. století. Česko se vrátilo domů, do Evropy a lůna západní civilizace. Jsme členem NATO & EU. Pokud se někomu stýská po kuratele Moskvy a podporuje Rusko v jeho dobyvačné válce proti Ukrajině a Evropě, pak jde o odpůrce svobody a vlastizrádce. BlackBuck Q2 FY27 Concall Summary:

Another strong quarter: revenue growth sped up, led by record telematics device sales and fast-growing loads. Margins dipped a little as the company invests in growth.

Key numbers:
• Revenue from operations +56% YoY, +15% QoQ
• Total income ₹253 cr, +51%
• Net revenue ₹183 cr, +35%; contribution margin above 90%
• EBITDA ₹51 cr, +39%; adj. EBITDA ₹55 cr, +29%
• PAT ₹41.4 cr, +42%
• Core business +31% YoY; growth businesses (loads, vehicle finance) +166% YoY (~2.7x)
• Transacting users ~9 lakh, +13%; power users ~4.8 lakh, +20%
• Tolling GTV ₹7,070 cr, +17%
• Total expenses +36% YoY (historically in the teens)

Guidance:
• Vehicle finance on track for EBITDA break-even this year
• Q3/Q4 are seasonally stronger for tolling; October is "business as usual"
• Super loads investment to keep increasing as the playbook firms up
• No capex or depreciation guidance

Key positives:
• Record new telematics device sales for the second straight quarter, driven by state AIS mandates; deferred revenue +56% YoY means revenue still to be recognised
• Own FASTag issuance (BlackBuck TZF, PPI licence) rising sharply
• Super loads: 14 cities (12 new), working-capital light, AI-led productivity gains
• Management expects near-zero impact from UPI MDR (over 50% of transactions are under ₹2,000, plus the zero-PDN route)

Key watchouts:
• Adj. EBITDA (+29%) lagging net revenue (+35%); core operating leverage down to ~50% from 70–100% before
• Tolling GTV roughly flat QoQ (~₹6,800–7,000 cr for 3–4 quarters); transactions -2% QoQ
• Depreciation roughly doubled YoY with telematics hardware
• Some one-off benefits in tolling revenue this quarter
• Possible competition if OEMs cut GPS renewal prices

Final view: Strengthening. Growth is broadening beyond tolling and the core business keeps producing cash, but expect margins to stay under pressure while loads and telematics scale up.

1. IPO Snapshot & Lot Matrix
 * Dates: Nov 19 – Nov 23, 2026

   * Big HNI (Min 7 lots): 4,200 shares (₹10,29,000)
 * Objects of the Issue: ₹98.13 Cr (~82% of proceeds) earmarked directly for purchasing Material Handling Equipment (MHE), Aerial Work Platforms (AWP), and batteries, with the rest for general corporate purposes.

2. Business Overview & Operational Scale
Incorporated in November 2019, Watrana Rentals is a pan-India material and cargo handling equipment rental & trading player serving automotive, tyre, beverage, glass, paper, and logistics clients.
 * Three Revenue Verticals: MHE Rental Solutions (core asset-light leasing for clients), Trading in new/used MHE, and Trading in MHE-compatible batteries.
 * Fleet & Workforce Muscle: Owns 2,646 MHE units (battery/diesel/gas forklifts, electric stackers, pallet trucks, clamps) and 33 AWP units (plus 7 leased units), backed by a 3,883-strong workforce as of June 30, 2026.

3. Financial Growth Trajectory (₹ in Crore)
 * Total Income: ₹130.23 (FY24) ➡️ ₹179.66 (FY25) ➡️ ₹211.69 (FY26) +18% YoY | ₹53.62 (Q1 FY27)
 * EBITDA (Margin): ₹37.98 / 29.2% (FY24) ➡️ ₹51.77 / 28.8% (FY25) ➡️ ₹65.01 / 30.8% (FY26) | ₹18.13 / 33.9% (Q1 FY27)
 * PAT (Margin): ₹18.05 / 13.9% (FY24) ➡️ ₹24.43 / 13.6% (FY25) ➡️ ₹29.16 / 13.8% (FY26) +19% YoY | ₹7.68 / 14.4% (Q1 FY27)
 * Return Ratios (FY26): Strong ROE of 41.08% and RoNW of 29.13%.

4. Why APPLY for Listing Gains? ✅ (Key Drivers)
 * Strong Lead Manager Track Record: Managed by Oneview Corporate Advisors Pvt. Ltd., which boasts an 84% positive listing strike rate (47 out of 56 SME IPOs listed in green)—including a 100% positive listing record across all 4 SME issues managed in 2026 (EverestIMS +48%, Apsis Aerocom +46%, FX Multitech +11%, CKK Retail +5%, averaging ~25.8% listing-day gains).
 * Attractive P/E Valuation Support vs. Peers: Priced at 9.61x pre-IPO and 13.03x post-IPO FY26 earnings (EPS ₹18.80)—offering sharp valuation comfort compared to listed peers like Leap India (~76.8x P/E) and Seemax Resources (~16.1x P/E), as well as recent commercial services SME listings (12.3x–16.0x).
 * Consistent Growth & Pure Capex Issue: Revenue grew 18% YoY and PAT rose 19% YoY in FY26 with expanding margins (~31% EBITDA, ~14% PAT). Being a 100% Fresh Issue, funds directly expand the revenue-generating fleet.
 * Healthy Early Buzz: GMP has ticked up to +₹22 (~9% over cap price) even ahead of opening.

5. Key Factors & Risks to Consider ⚠️
 * Elevated Leverage: Total borrowings stand at ₹164.72 Cr (Debt-to-Equity of 2.91x in FY26) against a Net Worth of ₹93.24 Cr—typical of fleet-heavy rental models, though none of the IPO proceeds are going toward debt reduction.
 * Capital Intensity & Working Capital: Scaling MHE/AWP fleets demands continuous capex and strict utilization rates to protect margins.
 * SME Liquidity & Compliance: Historical delays in certain statutory filings noted in RHP, alongside standard SME post-listing liquidity risks.

Final Verdict: APPLY FOR LISTING GAINS ✅
Consistent ~18–19% top/bottom-line growth, reasonable 13.03x post-IPO P/E, 100% fresh capex deployment, and a strong Lead Manager track record make Watrana Rentals a solid candidate for listing gains. Watch QIB/HNI subscription trends on Day 3 before placing final bids.

Theo Bethke byl voják, kterého potkáte jen výjimečně – měl opravdu silný charakter. Pocházel ze skromných poměrů a už od mládí bylo jasné, že z něj bude vůdce. Jeho jméno je s Großdeutschland tak spojené, že si jednotku bez něj skoro nedovedete představit.

Proto často jezdil na frontu – vojáci ho rádi viděli. Díky své inteligenci a odvaze se vždy pohyboval tam, kde to bylo nejnebezpečnější, a co na frontě viděl, hned prakticky využíval.
Pro mě osobně bude jeho ztráta nenahraditelná. Poprvé jsem se s ním setkal v srpnu 1941 a brzy se z nás stali blízcí přátelé. Věkový rozdíl mezi námi nehrál žádnou roli. Prince William turned into an auto-rickshaw driver to take his wife, Kate Middleton, out for a ride in Mumbai.

But there's something else about the video that caught my attention. Look closely at Prince William. He is visibly bald, and he makes absolutely no attempt to hide it. He has embraced it as a part of his personality.

This is something we Indians could learn from the Brits.

William is extraordinarily wealthy. He could easily afford a hair transplant at one of the world's most expensive medical centres. Yet, he seems perfectly comfortable with his appearance and doesn't feel the need to conceal his baldness.

Can you imagine a prominent Indian celebrity being equally comfortable flaunting a receding hairline or a bald head?

Take Rohit Sharma and Hrithik Roshan, for instance. Both have been widely speculated to use hair systems or patches to maintain a fuller head of hair. Akshaye Khanna, meanwhile, has spoken about how losing his hair affected his confidence.

There is nothing wrong with choosing a hair transplant, wearing a hair patch or doing whatever makes you feel good about yourself.

But why should baldness be something to hide in the first place?

Perhaps the bigger lesson is that confidence comes from being comfortable in your own skin, not from trying to look younger forever.

🚩World Bank's poverty estimate does not pass the thali test

(Thought provoking Article on the recent estimates of Extreme poverty in India.The Article states that the report does not mention the set of goods and their prices that the World Bank used to construct its poverty line for https://t.co/oG3R2hsien 2025, the writers proposed a simple measure of the standard of living in India .Termed as the "thali index", it measures the number of thalis an individual can afford to buy based on the monthly per capita expenditure on food reported in the HCES and adopted Rs 30 as the price of a thali, being the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali as estimated by CRISIL for the year 2023-24.They found that up to 50 per cent of rural Indians and 20 per cent of urban Indians cannot afford two thali meals a day. Imputing the value of the subsidised food, which the WB report refers to as a factor affecting poverty, lowers this percentage to 40 per cent and 10 per cent, respectively. This implies that approximately 30 per cent of the Indian population cannot afford two square meals a day, making it difficult to stomach an estimate of less than 3 per cent for poverty in India.
The latest poverty estimates could create complacency in economic policymaking.Right now, we are experiencing a surge in food price in-flation. Quite unusually, between January and September, it has risen every month, trebling over this period. This means that prices are not just continuously rising but the rise in prices is accelerating. An urgent review of the policies to control food price inflation is warranted. Food price inflation can only be controlled by managing food supply, in particular by producing more food at a steady price. This requires increasing agricultural productivity.)

THE WORLD Bank recently released estimates of poverty in India, pegging "extreme poverty" at 2.6 per cent. If true, that would be good news, as it would imply that high levels of economic deprivation are now a thing of the past. We argue that such a conclusion would be premature.

The WB's poverty estimate is a headcount ratio- the ratio of the number of poor to the population. It estimates the number of poor by applying a poverty line to data reported in the NSS's Household Consumption Expenditure Survey for 2023-24 (HCES). The poverty line translated into goods repre-sents the minimum acceptable level of consumption, below which an individual is deemed poor. The report does not mention the set of goods and their prices that the World Bank used to construct its poverty line for India. The Survey is a rich source of consumption across the population and reveals granular in-formation on the standard of living, which can be used to assess a headcount poverty estimate, as we demonstrate.

In 2025, we proposed a simple measure of the standard of living in India ("The Thali Index', IE, July 1, 2025). Termed the "thali index", it measures the number of thalis an individual can afford to buy based on the monthly per capita expenditure on food reported in the HCES. 

Why did we choose this metric? 

The thali is a metaphor for a complete meal, combining protein, carbohydrates and minerals. It is a unit of food consumption that Indians culturally relate to and is both nutritious and sat-isfying. To measure the standard of living of Indians based on the thali index, we would need to apply a price to the consumption expenditure reported. We have adopted Rs 30 as the price of a thali, being the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali as estimated by CRISIL for the year 2023-24. We chose a home-cooked vegetarian thali as it is the cheapest. Applying the thali index to the data on consumption across expenditure groups, we found that up to 50 per cent of rural Indians and 20 per cent of urban Indians cannot afford two thali meals a day. Imputing the value of the subsidised food, which the WB report refers to as a factor affecting poverty, lowers this percentage to 40 per cent and 10 per cent, respectively. This implies that approxi-mately 30 per cent of the Indian population cannot afford two square meals a day, making it difficult to stomach an estimate of less than 3 per cent for poverty in India.

Note that the Bank's estimate and ours come from the same source, namely, the HCES. The difference is that the Bank ses a poverty line to measure income poverty while we are going by the directly observable data on the food consumptionlovel. If two thali meals per day are considered the minimum acceptable food consumption, our findings imply levels of ext me poverty higher than the Bank's estimate. The implication of our finding is that it must rethink the poverty line that it set for India. 

The point is that even if the income at its currently used poverty line is more than sufficient to enable two thalis a day per person, there are several items of expenditure that must be met by a household to earn a livelihood, maintain good health and educate their young. We can think of rent, medi-cines and school fees. It is likely that these expenses are met first, so as to ensure survival, reducing food to the status of a re-sidual item of consumption. If we accept the criterion of a mini-mum level of food consumption for an individual to be counted as non-poor, then the chosen poverty line must reflect this fea-ture. If 30 per cent of the population does not have access to two square meals a day, surely we cannot hold that less than 3 percent of the population is poor. Our argument has been made with respect to the World Bank's measure of income poverty but carries over to the Multidimensional Poverty Index of the UNDP to the extent that it relies on the Bank's poverty line.

The latest poverty estimates could create complacency in economic policymaking - if extreme poverty is almost non-existent, policies are needed to remedy it. But our finding of a low level of food consumption for a significant section of Indians imparts an urgency to it. The level of food consumption is directly affected by food prices, and controlling the price of food is central to safeguarding the well-being of the popula-tion. Right now, we are experiencing a surge in food price in-flation. Quite unusually, between January and September, it has risen every month, trebling over this period. This means that prices are not just continuously rising but the rise in prices is accelerating. 

An urgent review of the policies to control food price inflation is warranted. Food price inflation can only be controlled by managing food supply, in particular by producing more food at a steady price. This requires increas-ing agricultural productivity.

Balakrishnan is honorary visiting professor, Centre for Development Studies, Thiruvananthapuram, and Raj is a PhD student at Shiv Nadar University, Delhi NCR

PAT is up 57%, but last year carried a ₹93 cr exceptional charge. The cleaner read is pre-tax profit before exceptionals, up 30% to ₹635 cr. Debt is down to ₹941 cr from ₹1,255 cr and interest cost fell 40%.

Now the other side. Q2 was softer than Q1. EBITDA margin slipped from 33.4% to 29.9% and PAT fell 10% QoQ as heavier parts carried more raw material. Inventory days are at 441. Operating cash flow was 55% of EBITDA, against 97% a year ago.

FY27 guidance stays at ₹5,000 cr revenue and ₹850 cr PAT. H2 needs only ₹395 cr of PAT after ₹455 cr in H1, so there is cushion. Management revisits it in January. ⚙️

At CMP of 1197, the stock trades at ~70x that guided profit.

Andrýsek z Rinnu: Historie a kontroverze jednoho kultu

Andrýsek z Rinnu, známý také jako Anderl, se narodil 16. listopadu 1459. Podle legendy byl údajně 12. července 1462 zavražděn v obci Rinn v severním Tyrolsku, když mu byly pouhé tři roky. Příběh tvrdil, že ho rituálně zabili židovští obchodníci na skále v místním lesíku, přičemž způsob vraždy měl připomínat parodii na ukřižování.

Tento příběh vedl k rozvoji kultu blahoslaveného Andrýska, který se začal šířit již v 15. století a stal se velmi populárním poutním místem v Rakousku a Německu. Význam kultu byl dokonce podpořen papežem Benediktem XIV., který v roce 1753 vydal speciální oficiální mešní formulář a officium.

Ve druhé polovině 20. století však začal být Andrýskův kult vnímán jako antisemitský. Roku 1953 byl jeho svátek, připadající na 12. července, vyškrtnut z místního církevního kalendáře. Další rána přišla v roce 1961, kdy papež Jan XXIII. vyřadil Andrýska ze seznamu blahoslavených a celý příběh o rituální vraždě byl prohlášen za podvrh.

Navzdory tomuto církevnímu rozhodnutí přetrvával odpor místních obyvatel. Andrýskovy ostatky byly sice v roce 1985 odstraněny z jeho hrobu, ale kult se nepodařilo zcela potlačit. K jeho násilnému zákazu došlo až v roce 1989, kdy místní biskup Reinhold Stecher nechal zamalovat všechny fresky zobrazující Andrýska v tamním kostele.

Das Europäische Medienfreiheitsgesetz (EMFA) verbietet es den EU-Mitgliedstaaten grundsätzlich, Journalistinnen und Journalisten zu verhaften, um sie zur Preisgabe ihrer Quellen zu zwingen. [1, 2]
Die Verordnung, die seit dem 8. August 2025 in der gesamten EU gilt, soll den Quellenschutz stärken und lässt Zwangsmaßnahmen nur unter extrem strengen Ausnahmebedingungen zu. [1]

Grundsatz: Verbot von Verhaftung und Zwang

Laut Artikel 4 Absatz 3 des Gesetzes dürfen Behörden Medienschaffende sowie deren Mitarbeitende oder Familienangehörige nicht unter Druck setzen, um vertrauliche Informationen oder Informanten offenzulegen. Konkret untersagt das Gesetz folgende Maßnahmen zum Zweck der Quellenausforschung: [1, 2, 3]
Inhaftierung und Festnahme. Journalistinnen und Journalisten dürfen nicht verhaftet werden, weil sie die Aussage über ihre Informanten verweigern. [1, 2]
Sanktionen. Geldstrafen oder andere staatliche Sanktionen wegen verweigerter Quellenangaben sind verboten. [1]
Durchsuchungen und Überwachung. Redaktionsräume und Privatwohnungen dürfen nicht durchsucht und Kommunikationswege nicht abgehört werden, um an Quellen zu gelangen. [1, 2, 3]

Strenge Ausnahmen für Zwangsmaßnahmen

Das Gesetz sieht in Artikel 4 Absatz 4 zwar Ausnahmen vor, knüpft diese aber an hohe rechtliche Hürden. Eine Maßnahme wie eine Verhaftung oder Überwachung ist nur zulässig, wenn alle folgenden Bedingungen gleichzeitig erfüllt sind: [1, 2, 3]
Überwiegendes Allgemeininteresse. Die Maßnahme muss durch ein zwingendes öffentliches Interesse (beispielsweise die Abwehr schwerster Gefahren oder die Aufklärung schwerer Straftaten) im Einzelfall gerechtfertigt sein. [1, 2]
Verhältnismäßigkeit. Es darf kein milderes Mittel geben, um an die benötigten Informationen zu gelangen. [1, 2]
Richterliche Vorab-Genehmigung. Ein unabhängiges Gericht oder eine unabhängige Justizbehörde muss die Maßnahme im Vorfeld ausdrücklich genehmigen. [1]

Einordnung von Debatten und Kritik

Rund um das Inkrafttreten des Gesetzes kursierten online Behauptungen, die EU erlaube nun willkürliche Verhaftungen von Journalisten. Faktenchecks von Organisationen wie AFP und GADMO stellen klar, dass das Gegenteil der Fall ist. Das Gesetz schafft keine neuen Haftgründe, sondern errichtet erstmals EU-weite Mindeststandards gegen staatliche Übergriffe. [1, 2, 3]
Dennoch äußern Presseverbände wie Reporter ohne Grenzen fachliche Kritik an der Formulierung des „überwiegenden Allgemeininteresses“. Sie befürchten, dass einzelne Regierungen diesen unbestimmten Rechtsbegriff im Zweifel zu weit auslegen könnten, um den Quellenschutz zu umgehen. Zudem mahnt die Europäische Journalisten-Föderation (EFJ), dass viele Mitgliedstaaten die Vorgaben in der nationalen Praxis noch zu zögerlich umsetzen. [1, 2]

UNISA’s invite to Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture.
Colleagues, comrades, and family members of the late Dr Neville Alexander have publicly released a formal letter of objection sent to the Vice-Chancellor of the University of South Africa (UNISA). The statement registers our deep dismay over the institution’s decision to invite Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture at the Lagoon Beach Hotel, Milnerton, Cape Town, on Wednesday, 18 November 2026.
A collective letter of objection has been submitted to the Vice-Chancellor of UNISA detailing the profound disquiet of Dr Neville Alexander’s colleagues, comrades, and family members (listed below) regarding the invitation extended to Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver the UNISA Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture on 18 November 2026 in Milnerton, Cape Town.
We submitted this appeal three days ago (as soon as we became aware of the invitation to Mr Manuel) with due respect for the office of the Vice-Chancellor and UNISA’s role in preserving our nation’s intellectual heritage. However, our overriding duty is to safeguard the integrity of Dr Alexander’s political and intellectual legacy - a legacy that stands fundamentally irreconcilable with the policy record of the invited speaker.
Even a cursory engagement with Dr Alexander’s writings, speeches, and lifelong praxis - spanning political economy, racial capitalism, imperialism, internationalism, the national question, national liberation as distinct from nationalism, and language policy - exposes an unbridgeable chasm between his social vision and that of Mr Manuel. These are not minor disagreements over strategy or tactics; they represent diametrically opposed worldviews on the very nature of society and structural transformation. To place Mr Manuel at the podium of a lecture bearing Dr Alexander’s name is to obscure the principled struggles that defined his life.
In our correspondence, we urged: “We trust that you will give this urgent matter your serious consideration, and we would deeply value the opportunity to engage with you further on this issue. Given the immediacy of the event (Wednesday, 18 November 2026), we kindly request a response at your earliest convenience, and no later than the morning of Monday, 16 November.”
We received a response from the Office of the Registrar this afternoon confirming that the event will proceed unchanged. The Registrar cited advanced logistical preparations to justify declining our appeal, offering a pledge of future consultation and a post-lecture meeting. Mindful of UNISA’s refusal to reconsider, we are compelled to place our objection on the public record.
Letter to Professor Puleng LenkaBula, Principal and Vice-Chancellor of the University of South Africa (UNISA).
RE: Our objection to the invitation of former Finance Minister Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver UNISA’s Neville Alexander Memorial lecture at the Lagoon Beach Hotel, Milnerton, Cape Town scheduled for the 18th of November 2026, at 6 pm.
Dear Professor LenkaBula,
We write to you as close colleagues, comrades, and the life partner of the late Dr Neville Alexander to express our profound disquiet about the invitation extended to Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture.
Our objection is informed by our intimate knowledge of Dr Alexander's political convictions, intellectual commitments and lifelong struggle for a society founded on social justice, equality and genuine economic emancipation.
We believe that the invitation raises fundamental questions about the meaning, purpose and integrity of a memorial lecture established in honour of someone whose political and intellectual positions were so sharply at odds with the policies associated with Mr Trevor Manuel.
Dr Alexander's political and intellectual legacy cannot be separated from his opposition to neoliberalism and the socio-economic trajectory adopted by successive post-apartheid governments.
As a former political prisoner on Robben Island, a revolutionary socialist and humanist, an educator and a committed scholar-activist, Alexander dedicated his life to the struggle for a fundamentally different South Africa. His understanding of liberation went beyond the attainment of political democracy in 1994. He believed that genuine freedom required the transformation of the material, social, political and psychological and cultural conditions of the majority of our people, particularly the working class and the poor.
He was among those who warned that political liberation without meaningful socio-economic transformation would leave the structures of inequality largely intact and perpetuate corruption and cronyism. The persistence of mass unemployment, poverty, inequality and the concentration of economic power in post-apartheid South Africa gives continued relevance to the questions he raised.
Our objection to Mr Manuel is not personal. It is rooted in the political and intellectual commitments that Dr Alexander held throughout his life, and which the memorial lecture is meant to honour. Dr Alexander was unambiguous in his opposition to the neoliberal trajectory embarked upon by the post-apartheid establishment in the 1990s. He exposed the links between racism and capitalism and consistently argued that the ANC’s embrace of market fundamentalism betrayed the struggle’s emancipatory promise. He did not shy away from naming the architects of that betrayal.
Mr Manuel is one such architect. As Minister of Finance, he was the political face of the Growth, Employment and Redistribution (GEAR) strategy - a policy framework that Alexander and other anti-capitalist scholar-activists correctly identified as a neoliberal programme prioritising cuts in social and cultural spending, privatisation, and trade liberalisation. Unlike Mr Manuel, Dr Alexander maintained an uncompromising opposition to the precepts of the Washington Consensus.
GEAR was designed to reassure capital and serve the needs of large corporations. GEAR’s ostensible ‘trickle-down’ benefits, such as increased employment failed dismally. Dr Alexander’s critique was never merely abstract; it formed the very bedrock of his intellectual, organisational, and political praxis, serving to forge concrete alternatives to widespread immiseration. He remained until his death - eleven days after the Marikana Massacre - a revolutionary socialist and humanist who rejected the idea that the poor should bear the costs of market fundamentalism.
The contradictions surrounding Mr Manuel's invitation are not confined to his tenure as Minister of Finance.
Mr Manuel also went on to occupy senior leadership positions in the corporate financial sector. The symbolism of Mr Manuel’s later roles in corporations that embody the very neoliberal order Neville fought - makes this invitation even more inappropriate. To have him deliver a lecture in Dr Alexander’s name would be to turn a profound legacy against itself. It would suggest that the radical critique he advanced can be safely ignored, or worse, that the memorial lecture has become a platform for the very forces he spent his life opposing.
We are not suggesting that Mr Manuel should be denied the right to express or defend his economic and political positions. Nor are we opposed to robust intellectual debate. On the contrary, we believe that such debate is essential.
Our concern is that the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture should not become an occasion for the normalisation or uncritical celebration of political and economic positions that Alexander himself spent considerable intellectual energy challenging.
We must ask: What does it mean to honour Dr Alexander by inviting someone whose economic and political policy legacy was fundamentally opposed to the principles and aspirations that informed Dr Alexander's political thought?
Is this an attempt to depoliticise Dr Alexander's legacy and turn him into a ‘respectable’ academic figure, stripped of the radical politics that defined his life's work?
Are we now expected to commemorate Dr Alexander while overlooking the very political and socio-economic struggles that shaped his intellectual contribution to South African society?
We find this deeply troubling.
As people who knew, worked with, and struggled alongside Dr Alexander, we cannot remain silent when his name and legacy are invoked in ways that risk obscuring the political positions he consistently defended.
We recognise that universities must provide spaces for competing ideas and intellectual disagreements. However, there is a difference between hosting a debate about Dr Alexander's ideas and inviting a prominent political and corporate figure to deliver a memorial lecture without adequately accounting for the fundamental contradictions between his policy record and Dr Alexander's political convictions.
Professor LenkaBula, we therefore appeal to you, as Principal and Vice-Chancellor of Unisa, to intervene and reconsider this invitation.
Unisa is a vital public intellectual institution with a responsibility to uphold critical scholarship, intellectual integrity and historical accountability. Its role in preserving and advancing the legacies of South African intellectuals should not be reduced to hollow memorialisation and superficial ceremonial commemoration.
We accordingly call upon you and the relevant university structures to:
Reconsider Trevor Manuel's appointment as the speaker for the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture.
Engage and consult with Dr Alexander's close colleagues and comrades before making decisions concerning the interpretation and public commemoration of his intellectual and political legacy – as the UNISA Western Cape colleagues respectfully did until last year.
Ensure that any memorial lecture bearing Dr Alexander's name reflects the radical intellectual traditions, political commitments and social justice principles that informed his life's work.
Establish an appropriate process through which those closest to Dr Alexander can contribute to safeguarding the integrity of his legacy.
We wish to emphasise that this intervention is not motivated by personal animosity towards Mr Trevor Manuel. It is motivated by our responsibility to protect the intellectual, political and historical integrity of Dr Alexander's legacy.
Dr Alexander was not someone who believed that all political and economic positions were equally compatible with the struggle for emancipation. He held firm convictions and was prepared to challenge those in power, including the leadership of the post-apartheid government, when he believed that their policies betrayed the aspirations of the liberation struggle. Dr. Alexander’s steadfast principles came at a steep personal cost, making him a target of the ruling establishment both during the apartheid era and in the years following 1994.
We cannot celebrate Dr Alexander’s courage and intellectual independence while remaining silent about the contradictions inherent in this invitation.
Dr Alexander's legacy must not be sanitised, depoliticised or appropriated in ways that contradict the very principles for which he struggled.
His memory deserves more than a prestigious lecture bearing his name. It deserves intellectual honesty, political integrity and fidelity to the unfinished struggle for social and economic emancipation.
We are also deeply mindful of Dr Alexander’s association with UNISA. It was through UNISA that he continued his studies while imprisoned on Robben Island, earning a BA Honours in History in 1969, and he became a tutor to other UNISA-enrolled inmates. UNISA later inaugurated the annual Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture in his honour, recognising his contribution to multilingualism and his lifelong commitment to education as a tool of liberation. For UNISA to host a speaker whose political, economic and social orientation to the oppressed and exploited contradicted everything that Neville's life and work represented, would undermine the integrity of that institutional legacy. The university has a responsibility to protect the political and ethical meaning of the memorial it established.
We therefore call on UNISA to withdraw the invitation to Mr Manuel, or on Mr Manuel to decline the invitation in recognition of the contradiction it represents. We ask that the lecture be used instead to reaffirm Dr Alexander’s actual legacy: his opposition to racial capitalism, his insistence that another world is possible, and his unwavering commitment to the poor and marginalised of South Africa. Anything less would be a disservice to his memory and to the struggle to which he gave his life.
We remain committed to defending Dr Alexander’s legacy, and we will continue to speak out whenever it is invoked in ways that contradict the principles he held.
We trust that you will give this matter the serious consideration it deserves and engage with us before proceeding with the proposed lecture.
Yours sincerely,
Close colleagues, comrades, family members and the life partner of the late Neville Alexander
On behalf of many others committed to preserving his intellectual, political and revolutionary legacy.

INDIA'S #AEROSPACEINDUSTRY: GLOBAL ENGINE GIANTS ARE KNOCKING ON INDIA'S DOOR!

Something interesting is happening in India's aerospace industry. Global aircraft engine manufacturers are increasingly looking towards India, not just to sell aircraft engines but also to manufacture critical components here.

One major example is Safran, the French aerospace giant. Today, Safran purchases around €100 million (₹1,040 crore) worth of components annually from Indian suppliers. By 2030, it wants to increase this to €500 million (₹5,200 crore). That's a 5X increase!

THE GLOBAL ENGINE SHORTAGE

Aircraft manufacturers are struggling to increase production because the supply chain cannot deliver components fast enough. Safran and GE Aerospace manufacture LEAP engines through their 50:50 joint venture, CFM International. These engines power Airbus A320neo and Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Safran delivered 1,802 LEAP engines in 2025, up 28%, and is targeting around 2,500 engines annually by 2028. More engines mean greater demand for turbine components, titanium castings, forged parts and precision-machined components. Indian suppliers can benefit from this demand.

WHY INDIA?

India is already a major customer for Safran. CFM engines power approximately 80% of India's narrow-body airline fleet. But there is an imbalance. Safran sells approximately €1 billion worth of products in India while purchasing only €100 million from Indian suppliers. Increasing local sourcing makes commercial and strategic sense.

And this opportunity is not limited to Safran. Airbus, Boeing, GE Aerospace, Rolls-Royce and Pratt & Whitney are also increasing their engagement with Indian suppliers. This makes the opportunity much bigger than one company's expansion plans.

UNDERSTANDING THE SUPPLY CHAIN

An aircraft engine is not manufactured by one company. It requires hundreds of specialised components. The manufacturing chain starts with special materials such as titanium, nickel superalloys and aerospace-grade steel. These materials are converted into components through casting and forging, followed by precision machining to achieve extremely tight tolerances. Individual components are then assembled into systems such as landing gear and wheels before the final engine is assembled and tested.

The interesting part is that value addition generally increases as suppliers move from manufacturing individual components towards delivering complex, ready-to-install assemblies.

THE BIGGEST COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE: QUALIFICATION

Why can't any engineering company simply start manufacturing aircraft engine components?

Because aircraft engines operate under extreme temperatures, pressure and mechanical stress. Even a small defect can have serious consequences. Every component and manufacturing facility must pass strict customer quality checks. This qualification process can take 2–4 years.

But once a supplier is approved and consistently delivers quality products, replacing it becomes difficult. That's the real competitive advantage of aerospace manufacturing.

Slow to enter. Difficult to replace. Potentially decades-long customer relationships.

INDIAN COMPANIES IN THE SUPPLY CHAIN

Several listed Indian companies are already connected to Safran's ecosystem.

#PTCIndustries: Through Aerolloy, it manufactures titanium castings for LEAP engines. Its ability to melt, cast and machine titanium makes it strategically interesting.

#Aequs: Manufactures aerospace components and assemblies, including landing gear and wheels. It works with six Safran entities.

#Raymond (JK Maini): Has supplied Safran for approximately 25 years. Its aerospace order book stands at around ₹5,960 crore over ten years.

#BharatForge: Supplies forged and machined components and has relationships with multiple global engine manufacturers.

#SanseraEngineering: Won its first Safran engine-parts business in Q2 FY27.

#AzadEngineering: Signed an MoU with Safran to develop rotating engine components for defence aircraft.

Other names worth tracking include #HAL, #Titan (through TEAL), #RatnamaniMetals and #INDOMIM.

THE OPPORTUNITY IS BIGGER THAN SAFRAN

This is perhaps the most important development. Aerospace manufacturing is becoming a global sourcing opportunity for India.

When a supplier develops the ability to manufacture complex aerospace components and passes customer qualification, it can potentially serve multiple global manufacturers. The opportunity is not just about one contract with Safran. It is about building capabilities that global aerospace companies need.

MY CONCLUSION

India's aerospace opportunity is gradually moving beyond aircraft assembly towards manufacturing the critical components that go inside aircraft engines and systems.

The real winners could be companies that develop difficult-to-replicate capabilities in titanium, superalloys, precision machining, engine components and complex assemblies.

But a growing industry does not automatically make every company in that industry a good investment.

The companies worth watching are those that can turn global customer relationships into approved products, repeat orders, higher value addition and sustainable cash flows.

That's where the long-term aerospace opportunity lies.

H1 FY27:
Revenue: ₹2,491 Cr (+11.8% YoY)
EBITDA: ₹803 Cr (+38% YoY) | Margin: 32% (+630 bps)
PAT: ₹455 Cr (+57% YoY)

Product-group growth (H1):
Aerospace: +31.5% | Automotive: +19.4% | Consumer: +46.2% | Defence: +19.3% | Medical: +22.7% | ECM: –40.5% (₹268 Cr). Management expects FY27 ECM revenue of ~₹480–500 Cr (in line with budget but below prior-year levels). Defence and medical together ~39% of revenue; automotive remains the largest at ~25%.

Margins:
H1 PBEIT margin 25.3% (vs 21.5% H1 FY26). Reported EBITDA margin 32%. Management’s normal-course framework is 20–25% PBEIT. Elevated H1 levels reflected higher defence/medical contribution and tooling income. Margins depend on component complexity rather than end-market alone; do not extrapolate H1 levels as the new baseline.

Aerospace & IGT:
Portfolio of ~1,200 aerospace components (another 400 targeted). Strong programme activity in civilian aerospace and industrial gas turbines with demand visibility into 2029–30; no cancellations reported. Long qualification cycles mean development wins take time to convert into meaningful production revenue.

Other opportunities:
Medical is currently the highest-margin business and still early-stage. Defence supported by domestic small-arms components and overseas (including NATO-related) demand, subject to customer order conversion. Emerging areas (humanoid robotics, satellite applications, smartphone MIM) followed conservatively—recognised only after confirmed tooling or programme orders. Smartphone MIM programmes increasing but facing customer-side delays; better clarity expected in Q4.

Overseas subsidiaries:
Indo-MIM Inc contributed ₹52.2 Cr to H1 PAT. Triax (–₹18.2 Cr), Phoenix (–₹27.1 Cr) and Conway Marsh/Garrett (–₹0.7 Cr) were loss-making. Management expects Triax to approach breakeven by FY27-end.

Working capital & cash flow:
Inventory days 441 (vs 340); cash conversion cycle 417 days (vs 324). Operating cash flow ₹444 Cr; free cash flow ₹31 Cr; CFO/EBITDA 55.3%. Inventory build attributed to minimum raw-material purchase quantities, casting/machining requirements, customer delivery schedules and higher buffers for aerospace/IGT and machining. Targeting inventory improvement by FY27-end.

Capex & expansion:
Primary MIM/casting capacity adequate; incremental investment directed toward machining and finishing for programme ramps. New iron powder facility has 3,000-tonne annual capacity; meaningful operating leverage expected only at 70–80% utilisation. Evaluating acquisitions in Europe, US and Singapore across gas turbines, vacuum casting and MIM to add technology, customer access and global manufacturing footprint.

Guidance:
FY27 revenue ₹5,000 Cr and bottom line ₹800+ Cr. Management expects to do better and plans an update after Q3.

Key monitorables: Sustainability of margins near the upper end of the 20–25% normalised range as mix evolves; movement of overseas subsidiaries toward profitability; decline in inventory days and improvement in cash conversion without impacting delivery or growth.

Pine Labs: A growing payments platform at an early-profit valuation

1.  What it does to make money 
Pine Labs sells the machines and software merchants use to take payments, then earns more as money flows through them. It also runs prepaid and gift card programmes for brands. Revenue splits into two platforms : 
DITP ₹532 Cr · 66%
IAP ₹275 Cr · 34%

DITP: merchant-side infrastructure (+21% YoY)
        a. POS terminals (22.3 lakh digital checkout points) earn subscription plus a take rate. Subscription is now 27% of total revenue.
        b. Fintech infrastructure: APIs for bill payments and data, paid per transaction (37 Cr in Q2, +33% YoY).

IAP: issuing and acquiring (+31% YoY)
Processing for prepaid and gift cards (management claims 80–85% of that market), plus distribution of cards for brands, interest on float and breakage income. Distribution carries lower margin (company: IAP contribution margin 52–55% vs 81–83% for DITP) so mix shifts move the blended 72–75%.

2 · Impact of MDR on UPI (Talk of the town)
Today, merchant UPI payments carry zero MDR (merchant discount rate), so Pine Labs earns nothing on roughly 70–77% of the transactions on its terminals. Under NPCI’s proposed framework, payments above ₹2,000 would carry a 0.4% (40 bps) MDR. Management expects about 11 bps to reach the acquirer layer and aims to keep 9–10 bps. The rollout is deferred pending regulatory clarity; the CEO said the ball is “completely in NPCI’s court”.

Annual MDR income is projected as  ~₹140 Cr a year. 

3.  Q2 FY27 results and consistency

Revenue: steady double-digit growth: +18%, +24%, +17%, +20%, +24% in the last five YoY readings. Q3 is seasonally strongest, Q4 dips.
Profit: the turn from losses to profit is real, but lumpy. PAT went ₹59 Cr → ₹20 Cr → ₹39 Cr over the last three quarters, swinging with tax and margin.
Margins: adjusted EBITDA margin has moved 23% → 21% → 17% → 19%. Contribution margin slid from 77% to 73% on distribution mix.
International revenue share dipped to 15% (from 17%) after a large retailer exited Singapore gift-card distribution.

4.  Guidance given
FY27 revenue growth : Higher than the 23–23.5% talked about at the start of the year
FY27 adj. EBITDA margin : “At least” 21%; H2 EBITDA much higher than H1

H1 FY27 revenue was ₹1543 Cr (+22% YoY). 
Reaching +23.5% for the year needs H2 growth of about 25%, against a strong Q3 base (₹744 Cr). 

H1 adj. EBITDA margin was ~18.2%; a 21% full-year result needs roughly 23% in H2, versus ~22% in H2 FY26. So both targets require H2 to beat H1.

What to track : 
Q3 revenue growth against the ~25% needed; whether H2 margin reaches the low 20s; NPCI’s final MDR decision; operating cash flow relative to the 13–15% working-capital band; and the tax rate trending to 30%.
Not a recommendation. DYOR

1. FY27 Management Guidance

✅ Revenue growth: 45%+ YoY

✅ EBITDA growth: 35%+ YoY

✅ PAT growth: 35%+ YoY

✅ Implied FY27 revenue: ₹2,433–2,516 Cr

Management expects a strong H2 recovery as mining activity accelerates after the monsoon.

2. Q2 FY27 Performance

• Revenue: ₹519.45 Cr (+127% YoY)

• Normalised EBITDA: ₹73.20 Cr (+163.5% YoY)

• Normalised EBITDA margin: 16.60%, versus 12.14% last year

• PAT: Loss of ₹7.51 Cr versus loss of ₹14.23 Cr last year

Important: Revenue and EBITDA are growing strongly, but higher depreciation and finance costs are still impacting profitability.

3. Mining Volumes – Strong Execution

H1 FY27:

• Overburden removal: 76.49 million cubic metres (+72%)

• Coal extraction: 2.31 MMT (+41%)

• Railway coal loading: 9.83 MMT (+50%)

Management targets around 60 million cubic metres of overburden removal in EACH of Q3 and Q4.

4. Order Book & Future Opportunities

• Order book: ₹8,634 Cr

• Around 5.1x FY26 revenue

• Operations across 9 sites

• New tender pipeline: ₹11,000 Cr+

Three important projects — Dhoptala-II, Jayant-II and Dudhichua-II — are expected to support the H2 ramp-up.

5. Capex & Balance Sheet

• H1 capex: ₹584.88 Cr

• Fleet expanded to 2,226 units

• Net debt/equity reduced from 1.48x to 0.95x

• CRISIL upgraded long-term rating to A-/Positive

The company is investing aggressively in equipment and capacity to execute its order book.

6. What Concerns Me

Mining is capital-intensive. Fleet expansion increases depreciation, interest costs and working-capital requirements.

Also, ₹184.10 Cr of H1 revenue represents diesel-cost pass-through, which inflates reported revenue without adding EBITDA.

My View:

The growth visibility looks strong, supported by the order book and management guidance.

However, the real test will be whether higher mining volumes translate into better margins, PAT and operating cash flows in H2.

Strong order book + execution + improving profitability = the combination to watch.

INDO-MIM: the value is in the complexity, not just the sector label.

H1 FY27 revenue rose 11.8% to ₹2,491 crore. Underneath that headline, aerospace revenue grew 31.5% to ₹224 crore, while the machining business grew 55.4% to ₹188 crore. These are different views of the business, end market versus manufacturing process, not numbers to add together.

The important point from the call: a larger medical or aerospace mix does not automatically mean higher margins. The complexity, weight and finishing requirements of individual components matter.

As CFO Bala put it: “It depends on the complexity in that particular component.”

That also explains the investment priorities. Management says primary moulding and casting capacity is available; spending is directed towards secondary operations and finishing for developing programs. The opportunity is to do more value-added work on the part, not simply install more primary capacity.

There are two different growth clocks here.

The existing business is already delivering. Aerospace, machining and investment casting are growing. Investment-casting revenue reached ₹477 crore, up 36%. But electronic component manufacturing fell 40.5% to ₹268 crore, so the growth is not uniform.

The newer programs are still being developed. Humanoid and satellite opportunities are active, but management has not quantified their revenue contribution. Customer forecasts are not INDO-MIM orders.

The earnings comparison needs care too. Q2 PAT almost doubled to ₹215 crore, but the prior-year quarter included a ₹93 crore exceptional charge. PBT before exceptional items grew about 28% year on year and declined about 5% sequentially. That is the cleaner comparison.

And execution has a working-capital cost: the presentation reports inventory days of 441 versus 340 a year earlier. Management expects roughly 75 days of reduction by year-end under its current calculation, not an inventory level of 75 days.

Our read: judge the opportunity by programs entering production, the economics of the components shipped, and inventory converting into cash. Sector excitement alone cannot tell us those things.

3. What about margin benefits?

An important clarification from management:
The company is NOT factoring in the potential profitability benefit yet.
Meaningful operating leverage is expected only when utilisation reaches approximately 70–80%.💡

4. Stainless steel powder

Backward integration in stainless steel powder is already in place for captive requirements.

Management also mentioned a large customer seeking additional powder supplies, with facility requirements being evaluated.

Two strategic priorities are emerging:

Moving further up the value chain through machining and finishing.

Securing raw-material supply while creating potential external powder sales opportunities.

The opportunity is not just cost savings. Backward integration could also open new customer applications.

However, the real benefit will depend on capacity utilisation, external orders and the eventual contribution to margins.

Agree. Sometimes we spend so much time looking at the P/E that we forget to ask how people are actually using the product and whether that is changing.

A company can still be making money and paying dividends, but have fewer opportunities to grow than it did earlier. In that case, a lower P/E may be justified. We can’t assume it will go back to its old valuation just because it looks cheap against its own history.

This is also what interests me about businesses like Pine Labs and Paytm. Think about the problems a shopkeeper has beyond accepting a payment. Which customer paid? What was the payment for? Has the money reached the bank? Can the customer buy on EMI? How much time goes into sorting all this out at the end of the day?

Someone made a very good point on my Pine Labs post: a jeweller running a gold savings scheme wants to know which of the day’s UPI credits came from scheme customers. That is a real problem. If you solve it properly, there is a reason for the merchant to pay you and keep using your service.

With Paytm too, I’d be more interested in whether merchants keep paying for its devices and services, and whether the company can earn more from those relationships over time. Just saying “UPI transactions are growing” doesn’t tell us enough about what shareholders will earn.

Of course, you can get the change in behaviour right and still overpay for the stock. And cash businesses may have more life left in them than the market assumes.

But the broader point stands. Before calling something cheap or expensive, it helps to spend some time understanding what customers are doing. The spreadsheet can look very precise even when our assumption about the next ten years is wrong.

The issue is not simply higher inventory; it is how quickly that inventory converts into revenue and cash.

INDO-MIM: Margins 💡

Are H1 margins sustainable?

H1 FY27 profitability looks exceptional, but investors need to understand the normalised margin framework.

• H1 PBEIT margin: 25.3%
• H1 FY26: 21.5%
• H1 FY25: 20.7%

Management's normal-course range: 20–25%.
What drove the H1 improvement?

Management attributed the elevated margin to a higher contribution from defence and medical, including tooling income.

What mgmt said in concall? 

Management explained that margins are determined by the complexity and nature of individual components, not simply the end-market segment.

Even within the same segment, component economics can differ significantly.

Investor takeaway:👉

Don't extrapolate H1 profitability as the new normal.

The 20–25% PBEIT framework is the more prudent reference point. Higher defence and medical contribution can provide upside, but product mix will remain critical.

The key monitor is whether Indo-MIM can sustain margins near the upper end of its normalised range while scaling revenue.

👉Long qualification cycles mean development wins will take time to translate into meaningful production revenue.

5/ Emerging opportunities
Humanoid robotics, satellite applications and smartphone MIM are development opportunities.

Primary MIM/casting capacity is adequate. Investment is increasingly directed towards machining and finishing to support programme ramps.

The new iron powder facility has 3,000-tonne annual capacity. Mgmt expects meaningful operating leverage only when utilisation reaches 70–80%.

10/ Global expansion

Mgmt is evaluating acquisitions in Europe, the US and Singapore across gas turbines, vacuum casting and MIM.

The objective is to acquire technology and capabilities, expand customer access and strengthen the global manufacturing footprint.

• Revenue: 5,000 cr
• Bottom line: 800+ cr
Mgmt expects to do better and plans an update after Q3.💡

Indo-MIM is participating in several attractive growth markets: aerospace, IGT, defence, medical and emerging applications such as humanoid robotics.

The opportunity is encouraging, but the investment case must be assessed on three parameters:

🔹Can margins sustain closer to the normalised range as product mix changes?
🔹Can overseas subsidiaries move towards profitability?
🔹Can inventory days decline and cash conversion improve?

INDO-MIM Limited Q2 FY27 Concall - FY27 targets on track, inventory elevated

📌 Company Overview

• Makes complex precision metal parts using Metal Injection Molding (MIM), which shapes metal powder into tiny, intricate components.

• Also offers investment casting, precision machining, ceramic molding and 3D printing.

• Serves 650+ customers across auto, defence, medical, aerospace and consumer products.

• Has the world's largest installed MIM capacity, with plants in India, the US and the UK.

• About 80% of business is exports. The US contributes about 55% of revenue.

📈 Quarterly Performance

• Q2 revenue at ₹1,271cr, up 4% QoQ and about 14% YoY.

• Q2 PBT before exceptional items at ₹309cr vs ₹325cr in Q1.

• H1 revenue up ₹263cr YoY to ₹2,490cr. H1 EBITDA margin at 32%.

• Gross margin improved on better component mix and operating leverage.

🏭 Core Business

• MIM is 60% of turnover. Casting is 19% and machining 8%.

• H1 growth: aerospace up 31.5%, automotive up 19.4%, consumer up 46.5%.

• Electronic component manufacturing (ECM) down 40% YoY. FY27 target of ₹480–500cr, with ₹268cr done in H1.

🚀 Growth Engines

• Signed a long-term contract with Safran Aircraft Engines. Value not disclosed.

• Demand for industrial gas turbine (IGT) parts is very heavy, helped by data centres.

• Developing parts for humanoid robots and private satellites with multiple customers.

🌍 Strategy, CapEx & Expansion

• Setting up a 3,000 tons/annum iron powder plant for supply security.

• New Vietnam subsidiary for ECM. Revenue expected from FY28.

• Evaluating European acquisitions of USD 20–50 million in MIM and vacuum casting. Greenfield if no deal.

🎯 Guidance & Outlook

• FY27 revenue target of ₹5,000cr is on track.

• FY27 bottom-line target of ₹850cr expected to be met or slightly beaten. Update due after Q3.

• Quarters expected to be more even this year. FY28 guidance due in February.

⚠️ Key Watchpoints

• Inventory days rose to 441 from 340. Target is a ~75-day cut by year-end.

• H2 margins may be lower due to a heavier component mix.

Indo-MIM reported Q2 FY27 revenue of ₹1,271 Cr, up from ₹1,218 Cr in Q1, taking H1 revenue to ₹2,490 Cr. H1 PAT reached ₹455 Cr, up ₹165 Cr YoY, but pre-exceptional PBT slipped to ₹309 Cr from ₹325 Cr, so the half-year profit growth rests on exceptional items. Management credited consumer, aerospace, medical and automotive segments for growth, while electronics fell about 40%. A Safran long-term contract was signed. Gross margin improved on component mix. For FY27, management reaffirmed a target of ₹5,000 Cr revenue and ₹850 Cr PAT and said it expects to beat them. It gave PAT assurance only at the Q3 FY27 update, not now, so the profit target is less firm than the revenue target.

Growth triggers
• PAT assurance and FY27 target update at the Q3 FY27 results
• Meena Solar Power Park acquisition completion targeted by December 31, 2026
• Vietnam subsidiary revenue expected in FY28

Blockers
• Inventory days at 441 against 340, with a cash cycle of 417 days
• Electronics revenue down about 40%, and automotive margins under price pressure

🔹 India's benchmark Nifty 50 constituents delivered a resilient September quarter earnings season, with 28 companies surpassing analyst estimates, 17 performing in line with expectations, and only five missing projections.

🔹 Across Motilal Oswal Financial Services' broader coverage universe, large-cap companies posted 31 percent year-on-year earnings growth, mid-caps grew 22 percent, and small-caps recorded 32 percent growth, prompting upward revisions to Nifty FY27 and FY28 earnings-per-share estimates to Rs 1,243 and Rs 1,427 respectively.

🔹 Adani Enterprises emerged as a key outperformer as ramp-up in its copper business, firmer copper prices, and healthy yields in its airports segment more than offset softness in integrated resource management and mining.

🔹 Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone delivered strong operational growth backed by international ports, marine services, and higher domestic realisations, prompting management to raise its full-year FY27 revenue and EBITDA guidance by Rs 1,000 crore each.

🔹 Reliance Industries posted a record second-quarter performance led by strength in its oil-to-chemicals segment, while JSW Steel benefited from higher sales volumes, steel price recovery, and tighter cost controls.

🔹 Tech Mahindra extended its operating margin expansion streak to 12 consecutive quarters, whereas InterGlobe Aviation recorded its strongest quarterly revenue growth in 11 quarters on the back of higher airfares.

🔹 Key index underperformers included Asian Paints, which faced steep margin compression from elevated raw material costs, and Coal India, where lower e-auction realisations and higher expenses weighed on quarterly earnings.

🔹 Maruti Suzuki experienced profitability pressure from softer margins and lower other income, while Tata Motors reported a quarterly net loss due to one-time restructuring expenses at its Jaguar Land Rover subsidiary.

#Robotics - Understanding the entire Industrial Ecosystem

👉 Robotics is much bigger than manufacturing robots. It is an interconnected ecosystem spanning precision engineering, electronics, semiconductors, software, materials and advanced manufacturing.
👉 A robot is the result of several specialised technologies working together. The ecosystem can be understood through these layers:
 1. Core Components & Sub-systems:
  → Motors, gearboxes, actuators and motion transmission systems.
  → Bearings, joints, couplings, shafts, fasteners and structural frames.
  → Cameras, LiDAR, IMUs and other sensing technologies.
  → Batteries, BMS and power-conversion systems.

 2. Electronics & Computing:
  → CPUs, GPUs, microcontrollers and edge AI accelerators.
  → Sensors, controllers, PCBs, power electronics and connectivity.

 3. Software & Intelligence:
  → AI and machine perception.
  → Motion planning, navigation and control systems.
  → Robot Operating Systems (ROS/ROS 2).
  → Simulation, digital twins and fleet-management software.

 4. Engineering & Manufacturing:
  → Mechanical and electrical design.
  → Embedded systems and firmware.
  → Precision machining, component manufacturing and robot assembly.
  → System integration, testing and certification.

 5. Deployment & Applications:
  → Industrial automation and manufacturing.
  → Logistics, warehousing and material handling.
  → Healthcare, agriculture and commercial services.
  → Defence, space and consumer robotics.

👉 The End-to-End Value Chain: R&D → Design & Prototyping → Component Manufacturing → Robot Assembly → Testing & Certification → Deployment → Operations & Maintenance → Upgrades.

👉 The robotics opportunity extends far beyond companies assembling complete robots.
👉 It creates demand for precision motors, gearboxes, bearings, fasteners, sensors, semiconductors, batteries, power electronics, specialised materials and advanced manufacturing equipment.
👉 India's opportunity lies in developing these underlying capabilities - not merely importing robotic platforms and integrating them.
👉 Platforms may capture the attention, but the depth of the robotics opportunity lies across the industrial supply chain.

Hitachi: Has Optimism Overshot? Shares Surge Over 10% on 64% Revenue Growth and 86% Jump in Orders, but Margin Miss and a 91x FY27 P/E Raise Valuation Concerns

Core Theme 
Hitachi Energy is delivering 64% revenue growth, an 86% jump in orders and a ₹33,300-crore backlog, with exports, services and data centres broadening the story, but a margin miss and a 91x FY27 multiple after a 73% rally leave the stock exposed to any slip in margins or HVDC execution.

Q2 FY27 Results: Strong Top Line
Shares of Hitachi Energy India surged over 10% on Friday, after the company reported another quarter of strong revenue growth and order inflows, with upbeat management commentary on growth outlook

Revenue rose 64% year-on-year to almost ₹3,000 crore in the September quarter, aided by strong execution; this follows 69% revenue growth in Q1

Ebitda, excluding foreign exchange impact, grew at a slower 55% to ₹462 crore, impacted by higher material costs and an adverse product mix

In Q1, Ebitda growth was far higher at 158%, aided by improved operating leverage and a favourable base

Total inflow in Q2 jumped 86% Y-o-Y to ₹4,100 crore, taking the order backlog to ₹33,300 crore, or around 3.2 times trailing twelve months revenue

Growth Outlook
Investors can expect near-term revenue growth to sustain, aided by a ramp-up in execution of high-voltage direct current (HVDC) projects and higher revenue recognition from these orders

Beyond the near term, growth should be supported by continued investments in transmission infrastructure and rising demand from data centres and battery energy storage systems (BESS)

Management indicated on the Q2 earnings call that four to five HVDC projects could be awarded over the next 12-24 months

Amid robust demand, management sees business visibility extending at least to 2035

Rising share of exports and services, along with improved operating leverage, should support profitability

Export orders rose 41% Y-o-Y in Q2, contributing 25-30% of total order inflow; these orders typically fetch 300-400 bps higher margins than domestic orders

The services business order inflow grew 77%, accounting for around 7% of total inflows, while railways, metro and renewables saw some moderation

Hitachi introduced a pre-engineered grid-to-rack solution to shorten data centre execution timelines

It is undertaking capex of ₹4,000 crore, including a ₹2,000 crore greenfield facility for large transformers at Karjan in Gujarat; most projects are expected to be completed by 2028, with a focus on technology localization

Margin Story
Hitachi’s Ebitda margin stood at 16.1% in H1 FY27 and 15.4% in Q2 FY27 (versus 15.4% in FY26 H1 per Mint’s text), with the Q2 margin missing estimates

Higher input costs and HVDC project execution could weigh on gross margins in the near term

Motilal Oswal Financial Services expects operating leverage and a higher share of exports and services to offset lower gross margin in HVDC projects; it is factoring in an Ebitda margin of 16.9%, 18.0% and 18.5% over FY27, FY28 and FY29

Jefferies India: “We believe 30%+ revenue growth continuing should see operating leverage-linked margin expansion of 760 bps over FY26-29 to 23%”; it expects earnings per share to grow at a 54% CAGR over this period

Investors will closely watch how margin recovery pans out

Valuation: Has Optimism Overshot?
Hitachi’s shares have gained 73% so far in 2026, and trade at 91 times estimated FY27 earnings, according to Bloomberg

A rise in competitive intensity due to industry-wide capacity expansion, or a delay in HVDC order execution, could lead to higher costs and margin erosion, acting as a dampener for the stock

Valuation may have entered an overheated zone

Why Is the Street Hammering Solar Manufacturing Companies?

Q2FY27 results clearly indicate significant margin pressure across the solar manufacturing industry!

The biggest concern is the massive capacity expansion happening across the sector!

India already has over 200 GW of approved module manufacturing capacity against annual demand of 50-60 GW

As a result, module prices have corrected sharply, with pure play module manufacturers facing the biggest pressure on profitability

Interestingly, the next challenge could emerge in solar cells!

Several manufacturers are aggressively expanding cell capacities, potentially creating an oversupply situation during FY28 as new plants become operational

This is precisely why the entire solar manufacturing sector has witnessed significant valuation derating!

Waaree Energies : "Any player operating below 10 GW scale, without backward or horizontal integration, may not be well positioned for the future. With the upcoming ingot-wafer policy, capex requirements are significantly higher, and viable capacities are typically 5-10 GW. Very few players will be able to undertake such investments, and we expect the industry to consolidate over the next 2-3 years."

Premier Energies "Pure play module manufacturing is going to be really difficult. Backward integration is required. A player with a 1-2 GW cell line will find it difficult to compete with manufacturers operating at five times that scale. Players with scale, financial strength & the execution capability to establish ingot wafer manufacturing will be the ones that separate the men from the boys!"

Integrated manufacturers such as Waaree, Premier Energies are relatively better positioned than pure play module manufacturers, although they are not immune to margin pressure

This is also why valuing these businesses on peak margins can be extremely misleading!

The impact runs through the whole value chain, from the largest companies to unlisted MSMEs, small factories, suppliers, wholesalers and proprietor-run units in the local economy.

Plans for 2.8 GW were announced in one week, at one state investment summit in Visakhapatnam. India has about 1.8 GW today. Forecasts for 2030 run from 5.6 to 12 GW.

AirTrunk

AirTrunk, backed by Blackstone and CPP Investments (Canada's pension fund), signed an MoU with Andhra Pradesh on 13 Nov for two campuses near Visakhapatnam: 400 MW at Rambilli and 1,400 MW at Tootipala. Its detailed project report puts the cost at about $11B, and the state is still considering it. The 1.8 GW counts toward the 5 GW of new capacity AirTrunk set out in June.

Andhra Pradesh is leading the announcements

IPO Index Gives Stellar Returns This Yr, But Experts Stay Cautious: Nifty IPO Index Up 21.41% Year-to-Date With P/E Expanding to 93.5x; Analysts Warn the Index Tracks Post-Listing Rather Than Issue-Price Gains

Core Theme 
The Nifty IPO index has returned 21% this year on the back of Lenskart, Groww, Meesho and other new-age listings, but a 93x P/E dominated by loss-making, richly valued names, concentrated top weights and listing-price-based tracking lead experts to caution that investors may be better off picking individual IPOs.

The Performance: Recent Listings Lead
It has been a tough year for investors, and even though largecap indices were down, midcaps gave good returns; the real winners have been firms that listed over the last two years, which have managed to give some of the best returns in the market

Most of these issues were at least partly offers for sale (OFS), where private equity investors were looking for exits and in some cases promoters also saw an opportunity to sell some shares

The Nifty IPO index closed at 2,473.30 and the BSE IPO index at 19,618.43 on Friday

The Nifty IPO index gained 21.41% year-to-date this year and 16.85% over a one-year period; it is up 18.40% in six months, 5.50% in three months and 4.13% in a week

Over the long run, ecommerce and asset management company sectors, which dominate the index, are expected to grow the fastest

Heavyweights: Nifty IPO Index View
Lenskart Solutions: LTP ₹727.0; weight 10.22%; market cap ₹1.26 trn; 1-year return 81.7%

Groww: ₹225.0; weight 10.18%; ₹1.41 trn; 63.4%

Meesho: ₹257.1; weight 8.2%; ₹1.19 trn; 51.1%

ICICI Pru Asset Management: ₹3,040.4; weight 6.4%; ₹1.50 trn; 17.6%

INDO-MIM: ₹1,276.4; weight 3.91%; ₹0.63 trn; 72.1%

Lenskart is up 82% with a weight of 10.2% in the index; Groww is up 63% and Meesho up 52%; Shadowfax Technologies has been the best performer among the top weights, with a return of 158%

The index’s top 10 constituents account for about 52.8% of the index, per NSE Indices’ factsheet as of October 30; the four biggest weights together make up about 35.1%

Valuation Concerns
Per NSE Indices’ factsheet, the index’s price-earnings (P/E) ratio was 93.51 and price-to-book (P/B) was 8.84 on October 30, meaning the P/E has risen about 17% in two weeks; as of Friday, it has seen the sharpest expansion in P/E among the indices tracked

The P/E makes the index expensive because some of the initial public offerings (IPOs) trade at very high valuations: Physicswallah is the most expensive, at about 401 times earnings, followed by Lenskart Solutions (about 160 times) and Pine Labs (about 126 times)

Of 127 recently listed stocks with available issue prices, 88 trade above their issue price and 39 below; the median stock is up 24%, and 16 have at least doubled

Of 126 stocks with listing-day closing prices, 74 now trade above those levels; the median gain over the listing-day close is 7.5%

Longer-term returns are more modest, as NSE data showed the index has delivered a five-year price return of 4.46% a year and 8.70% since its January 2017 base date

Expert Views: Caution
Geetanjali Kedia, IPO expert at SPTulsian Investment Advisers: “We would not recommend investors put their money in an IPO index. This is primarily because the index would track the performance of these companies from their listing price rather than their issue price. It means investors would miss out on the listing gains in many of these IPOs”; investors are better off applying for quality companies rather than investing in a broad-based index

Kedia feels that investors can miss potential upsides due to quarterly rebalancing

Abhay Agarwal, founder and fund manager, Piper Serica: “The IPO market performance is directly related to secondary market performance, and that has been recovering. There is always room for good companies to go public and list... Some loss-making companies have dragged up the P/E multiple, particularly the larger-sized new economy IPOs. The IPO index has high weightage on these firms which makes the index look more expensive. But the P/E would be fairer if you take them out of the picture”

Mahindra Finance to Cut Mobility Loan Share, Scale Up Newer Segments by FY31: MD & CEO Raul Rebello Targets 16-18% AUM Growth Annually, RoA of 2.2-2.5% and Mobility Share Down From 80-85% to ~70%; AUM Could Exceed ₹3 Trillion

Core Theme
Mahindra Finance is working to reduce its reliance on mobility loans, from about 80-85% of the book to roughly 70% by FY31, by scaling secured housing and MSME lending, targeting 16-18% annual AUM growth and 2.2-2.5% RoA while avoiding unsecured loans, diversifying funding beyond banks and holding buffers against El Niño and drought risks.

Diversification: Why and Where
Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services (Mahindra Finance) is looking to reduce its dependence on vehicle financing by expanding into affordable housing and secured lending to micro and small enterprises

Raul Rebello, MD and CEO (interview with Aathira Varier, Subrata Panda and Manojit Saha): the franchise has a strong position in rural and semi-urban mobility, and protecting that remains the priority

Operating predominantly in one segment naturally limits long-term growth potential, so diversification has to be value-accretive

Two adjacent segments identified: affordable housing and select prime-mortgage lending, and secured lending to micro and small enterprises, since many mobility customers are entrepreneurs, transporters, single-vehicle operators and small business owners

The strategy is largely focused on secured lending; the company remains committed to a secured model and does not intend to enter unsecured lending

On gold loans: an attractive asset category, but there are concerns around business volatility and competition has intensified with several players entering; the company will evaluate costs and returns before entering

Growth Targets: FY27-FY31
The company has doubled its loan books from around ₹60,000 crore to ₹1.30 trillion under the FY31 plan and improved asset quality, though it fell short of its targeted net interest margin

For FY27-31, it is targeting 16-18% annual compounded AUM growth, credit costs within 1.3-1.7% and RoA of 2.2-2.5%

Medium-term goal: return on equity of 15%, with scope for further improvement through leverage

Between FY27 and FY31, the share of mobility in the portfolio is expected to decline from 80-85% to about 70%, with the balance increasingly contributed by newer segments

Today, more than 80% of business is concentrated in the wheels and mobility segment; as a scaled player, growth in the mobility portfolio will broadly track the underlying industry opportunity, with faster growth from newer businesses, particularly mortgages and MSME lending, which have a longer growth runway

At a 16-18% compounded growth rate, loan books could exceed ₹3 trillion by FY31

Risks: Weak Monsoon and El Niño
Targeted credit-cost range of 1.3-1.7% and the business model have the capacity to withstand even a weak monsoon

The company has built additional provisions of around ₹852 crore as buffer against potential downcycles, including an adverse El Niño outcome

It has also strengthened its liquidity, with a buffer of around ₹17,000 crore, which provides flexibility even if funding conditions tighten

Drought in certain states: no stress seen so far

Funding Strategy
The RBI has been encouraging NBFCs to diversify funding; Mahindra Finance’s objective is to diversify through retail deposits and capital markets while optimising cost of funds

Bank borrowings are around 51% of the funding mix; the company wants to look beyond direct bank loans to instruments such as non-convertible debentures, securitisation and direct assignments

The deposit-taking licence provides another source of funding, and focus on deposits is being stepped up

Banks will remain an important source for structural reasons: the company is the largest tractor financier and a leading used-vehicle financier, giving banks access to a substantial pool of priority-sector lending assets they are eager to hold

Insurance Distribution and IRDAI Paper
On the IRDAI consultation paper: the company participates in the insurance-revenue pool in several capacities and is moving towards insurance manufacturing, having submitted views to the regulator

Its central argument: expanding insurance coverage, ensuring fair policies and improving claim settlements require a broader focus than commissions alone

Distribution involves more than selling a policy; it includes advising customers and helping them choose suitable products

With a significant presence in rural and semi-urban markets, the company understands the cost of serving these customers and has called for appropriate commission rates and a phased implementation; rural and semi-urban markets may require somewhat higher commissions to support the broader objective of “Insurance for All by 2047”
