Oswal Pumps Ltd - Q2 FY27 Results

1. Financial Performance -
- Revenue stood at ₹506.3 Cr, up 6.9% QoQ.
- Operating EBITDA was ₹57.5 Cr, with a margin of 11.3%.
- PAT stood at ₹39.6 Cr, with a margin of 7.7%.
- Margins were impacted by higher prices of aluminium, solar glass, copper, zinc and steel, particularly on older fixed-price contracts. Higher employee costs and EPC-related expenses also affected profitability.

2. Business Updates -
- Executable solar pump order book stands at 9,487 pumps, with an additional pipeline of 10,000 pumps across PM-KUSUM, Magel Tyala and exports.
- PM-KUSUM 2.0 has been delayed. Management expects its announcement within CY2026, but meaningful revenue contribution is expected only from Q1 FY28.
- The company is diversifying into rooftop, utility-scale and C&I solar EPC. Combined order book stands at 143 MW, with an additional pipeline of 168 MW.
- EPC business is expected to generate 12–15% operating EBITDA margins with a payment cycle of 90–120 days, significantly better than government projects.

3. Backward Integration: Major Development
- Company approved a 1.2 GW TOPCon solar cell manufacturing facility with total capex of ₹455.85 Cr.
- Funding: ₹159.85 Cr from unutilised IPO proceeds and ₹296 Cr through debt.
- Commercial operations targeted for April 2028.
- The facility is expected to meet 75–80% of internal solar cell requirements.
- Management expects a 6–7 percentage-point improvement in blended EBITDA margins after the plant becomes operational.

4. Working Capital and Debt
- Net debt stood at ₹531 Cr; net debt/equity at 0.30x.
- Receivable days stood at 229 days and inventory days at 56 days.
- Outstanding receivables were ₹1,300 Cr, entirely from government and government-backed entities.
- ₹208 Cr was collected in early October, entirely from Maharashtra.

5. Management Guidance -
- FY27 revenue guidance maintained at ₹4,000–4,500 Cr despite missing the earlier Q2 growth guidance of 10–15% YoY.
- Management expects business performance to improve progressively in H2 FY27.
- Target is to generate more than 25% of total business from non-government verticals.
- PM-KUSUM 2.0 is expected to contribute meaningfully from Q1 FY28.
- Expected cash conversion cycle under PM-KUSUM 2.0 is 140–150 days.
- Management is very confident about FY28, supported by government orders, EPC diversification and backward integration.

6. Key Risks -
- Delay in PM-KUSUM 2.0 is affecting near-term revenue growth.
- High receivables of ₹1,300 Cr and a 257-day cash conversion cycle remain concerns.
- Raw material inflation and competitive bidding are putting pressure on margins.

Overall View -
The company is transitioning from a government-dependent solar pump business towards a diversified solar platform. The long-term strategy of EPC diversification and backward integration is positive. However, near-term growth, margins and cash flow remain under pressure. The key monitorables are PM-KUSUM 2.0 execution, government collections and EPC growth

Sammaan Capital Ltd – Q2 & H1FY27 | Concall Insights

Financial Performance
•Q2 AUM ₹59,188 Cr (+5.2% QoQ); loan book ₹46,482 Cr
•Q2 disbursements ₹6,278 Cr (+62% QoQ); H1 disbursements ₹10,123 Cr
•Q2 PBT ₹425 Cr (+30% QoQ); PAT ₹312 Cr (+28% QoQ)

•ROA improved to 1.5% from 1.3% QoQ; return on managed assets improved to 1.3% from 1.1%

AUM Growth & Disbursement Guidance
•FY27 AUM target maintained at ₹70,700 Cr versus ₹59,188 Cr in Q2
•FY27 loan book target ₹53,000 Cr versus ₹46,482 Cr currently
•FY27 disbursement guidance ₹30,100 Cr, implying ~₹20,000 Cr disbursements in H2
•Management confident of achieving FY27 disbursement and profitability targets
•Growth strategy transitioning from balance-sheet stabilization to aggressive retail lending expansion
•Mortgage lending expected to remain the primary growth engine over the next two years, supported by new product launches

Cost of Funds & Margin Expansion
•Current cost of funds 9.8%; FY27 target ~9.3%
•Gross lending margin currently ~2.9%, with management targeting ~3.5%
•IHC backing, rating upgrades and access to international lenders expected to progressively reduce borrowing costs
•UAE banking relationship already providing >$150 Mn funding at competitive rates; another similar-sized transaction anticipated
•Company increased lending rates by 25 bps effective November, potentially improving near-term spreads
•Declining funding costs and higher-yielding retail products remain key drivers of NIM expansion and profitability
•Management targeting return on managed assets above 2% over time

Retail Lending & Product Diversification
•~94% of Q2 disbursements were secured loans, reflecting continued focus on asset quality
•Personal loans being expanded from purchased portfolios toward direct origination through branches
•Personal loan target ticket size ~₹2 lakh; indicative yields ~16–17%
•Business installment loans targeting MSMEs with ticket sizes of ₹18–20 lakh and yields of ~14–18%
•Gold loan soft launch planned across ~16 branches in Q3 FY27, followed by ~30 additional branches in Q4
•Gold loans targeting ~₹2 lakh ticket size and ~11–13% yields, with broader expansion planned in FY28
•Loan against securities, micro-LAP, rural housing finance and credit-fund partnerships provide additional AUM growth opportunities
•Higher-yielding products retained on balance sheet, while lower-yield mortgages increasingly originated and assigned to lenders

Distribution & Operating Leverage
•Branch network expanded from 217 to 245; FY27 target ~300 branches
•Expansion focused on Tier 2/3 cities and underserved semi-urban markets
•H1 employee additions ~1,123, largely dedicated to retail sourcing and branch operations
•Mortgage branches typically expected to break even within ~6 months; personal/business loan branches in ~4–6 months
•Gold loan branches expected to take ~12–18 months to break even
•Increasing branch productivity and technology-led processing expected to support operating leverage as disbursements scale

FY27–FY28 Earnings Growth Visibility
•H2 FY27 disbursements targeted at ~₹20,000 Cr versus ₹10,123 Cr in H1, creating significant AUM growth potential
•FY27 PAT target of ₹1,400 Cr implies approximately ₹844 Cr profitability requirement in H2
•Funding cost reduction from 9.8% toward 9.3% and margin expansion from 2.9% toward 3.5% offer key earnings upside
•Gold loans, personal loans and business loans expected to become additional growth engines from FY28
•Branch expansion and higher-yielding portfolio mix expected to improve long-term return ratios
•IHC-backed funding access, capital infusion and governance improvements support the company’s ambition to progress from AA+ toward AAA
•Key monitorables include H2 disbursement acceleration, cost-to-income ratio, new product asset quality and realization of funding-cost benefits

Man Industries (India): Q2 FY27 Results and Key Takeaways from the Concall

The company posted its highest ever quarterly EBITDA, helped by the first full quarter of its Saudi acquisition. India dispatches were hit by shipping disruption in West Asia.

Q2 FY27 (Consolidated)
Revenue: ₹1,216 Cr (+49% YoY)
EBITDA: ₹190 Cr (+87% YoY), margin 15.6% vs 12.5%
PAT: ₹82 Cr (+132% YoY)
Order book: about ₹3,500 Cr
Bid pipeline: about ₹19,000 Cr

1.  Saudi acquisition is paying off-
Man acquired National Pipe Company (NPC) in Saudi Arabia in May. In its first full quarter, NPC did revenue of ₹486 Cr, EBITDA of ₹88 Cr and PAT of ₹77 Cr, with no debt. The plant is only 40-45% utilised and has been upgraded to make the large pipes used for water lines.

2.  About ₹300 Cr of revenue pushed out-
Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz delayed raw materials and finished goods, so about ₹300-320 Cr of revenue moved out of Q2. Management says the contracts are intact and most of it should ship this quarter through other ports. The customer has also confirmed in writing that it will pay back the extra freight cost.

3.  Underlying EBITDA was higher-
A one-time accounting entry of about ₹25 Cr was shown separately. Without it, EBITDA would have been about ₹215 Cr. It came from a cancelled order where the customer's advance was kept and the goods were sold to another buyer.

4.  New US plant approved-
The board approved a 3.5 lakh tonne pipe plant in the US at a cost of about ₹980 Cr ($110 million). US tariffs have kept Indian pipe makers out of that market, so making pipes locally is the only way in. The plant is targeted for December 2027 to January 2028, with revenue potential of ₹4,500-5,000 Cr at 75% utilisation.

5.  More projects starting in April 2027-
The stainless steel pipe plant in Jammu starts in April 2027, with peak revenue potential of ₹1,000-1,200 Cr and 18-22% EBITDA margins. A pipe coating facility in Saudi Arabia also starts then. The Merino Shelters real estate project has launched and should bring in ₹800-900 Cr of cash over 5-6 years.

6.  Debt under control for now-

Mike's interrogation technique is actually very feasible and practical. He confronts Carlo with his treachery and sits next to him instead of across from him, thus creating a more intimate approach. When Carlo doesn't admit his guilt, Mike undermines any confidence Carlo has by telling him that all the guys supporting him are dead. He offers him kindness by having a drink supplied, and reassures him that Mike has an emotional responsibility to him as his child's godfather. It's unthinkable that he would have Carlo killed.

As Carlo is breaking, Mike gives him his false punishment to reassure Carlo that whilst he will be punished, it will simply be a removal from the business and a pseudo exile, far removed from the death he expected. It's easy for Carlo to buy this, because he fully expects to be punished somehow, so it's a relief to find that out. Mike even shows him the plane tickets to make the illusion real.

Where is India's smart money moving?

A study of 576 equity mutual fund schemes by The Hindu BusinessLine reveals some fascinating portfolio shifts between October 2025 and September 2026.

₹5.2 lakh crore in inflows. AUM increased from ₹31 lakh crore to ₹35.4 lakh crore.

But what were fund managers doing with the money?

1/ FRESH ADDITIONS: New-age businesses are attracting institutional attention.

Some notable additions:

• Billionbrains Garage – 129 schemes
• Meesho – 85
• Lenskart – 76
• Ather Energy – 80
• Tenneco Clean Air – 69
• Shadowfax – 45
• Sedemac – 47
• Diamond Power – 38

Other notable additions: Shriram Finance, ICICI Prudential AMC, Torrent Pharma, BHEL, One97 Communications, MCX, PB Fintech, RBL Bank, Navin Fluorine, Aditya Infotech, Ujjivan Small Finance Bank and Honasa Consumer.

2/ PROFIT-BOOKING:

Fund managers trimmed exposure even in stocks that delivered strong returns.
Chennai Petroleum, Welspun Corp, Hitachi Energy India and Sansera Engineering witnessed reductions.
Wipro, HUDCO and P&G Hygiene also saw reductions amid weaker stock performance.

The message: Even institutional investors don't chase every winning stock. Valuation and position sizing matter.

3/ BUYING THE CORRECTION: Swiggy stands out.

Despite a 56.1% stock-price decline:

• Schemes holding Swiggy increased from 80 to 134.
• Aggregate shares held increased from 23.6 crore to 65.4 crore.

PB Fintech and HDFC Life also witnessed increased institutional exposure.

Are fund managers positioning for a recovery?

Worth investigating, but accumulation doesn't guarantee a turnaround.

4/ THE ONGC PUZZLE

Mutual fund shareholding declined 9.3%.

Yet the number of schemes holding ONGC increased from 55 to 85.

Existing large holders may have reduced positions while new schemes entered with smaller allocations.
Ownership breadth and investment conviction are two different things.

5/ WHERE DID FUND MANAGERS MAKE MONEY?

BHEL and Laurus Labs are interesting examples.

• Quant Focused Fund had over 6% allocation to BHEL, one factor behind its 8% positive return.

• Samco Large & Mid Cap Fund held over 8% in Laurus Labs and gained over 7%.

6/ SECTOR ROTATION

The value of mutual fund holdings in aluminium and aluminium products increased nearly 8X – from ₹1,677 crore to ₹13,388 crore.

Medical equipment, trading and fintech also witnessed substantial increases in holding values.

Remember: Higher holding values don't necessarily mean fresh buying. Stock-price appreciation also matters.

MY TAKEAWAY

Three institutional trends deserve attention:

1) Growing interest in new-age and recently listed businesses.

2) Profit-booking in stocks after sharp rallies.

3) Selective accumulation in beaten-down businesses.

Don't blindly replicate mutual fund portfolios.

Track:
• Number of schemes holding a stock.
• Aggregate shares held.
• Portfolio allocation and changes in weights.
• Whether accumulation is supported by improving fundamentals.
• Valuation versus earnings growth.

The real investment edge isn't knowing what mutual funds are buying. It's understanding WHY they are buying – and whether the opportunity still exists at today's valuation.

Source: The Hindu BusinessLine | Study of 576 equity MF schemes.

Indo Farm Equipment Q2 | Is crane business really transforming?

Went through last few  ARs, earlier concalls of Indo Farm. Q2 numbers are not bad, but something still not moving as expected.

First numbers.

Q2 Consolidated
Revenue ₹114.59 Cr, up 10%.
Operating profit ₹13.37 Cr, up only 5%.
PAT ₹5.40 Cr vs ₹4.98 Cr.

Segment wise
Cranes ₹51.11 Cr, up 14%.
Tractors ₹57.85 Cr, up 7%.

Crane business improving, but growth still not matching the expansion plans.

Now last 3 years.
FY24 Revenue ₹375 Cr, PAT ₹15.4 Cr.
FY25 Revenue ₹387 Cr, PAT ₹23.5 Cr.
FY26 Revenue ₹440 Cr, PAT ₹24.7 Cr.

Revenue growing slowly, PAT almost flat in FY26.
But what interested me is transformation happening inside.
Indo Farm trying to move from tractor manufacturer into much larger crane business. New Bhud plant, tower cranes, higher capacity and new products.

If executed well, this can change business economics.

But here problem starts.

Company sold around 1,003 cranes in FY26, while expanded capacity can reach nearly 4,800 units annually.

So capacity can become almost 5 times existing sales. But who will buy these cranes?

Dealer network only around 25, management targeting 60+.

ACE already having much stronger distribution, customer relationships and after sales service. This is something Indo Farm cannot build overnight.

And management timelines also shifting.

Earlier new crane plant expected Q1 FY27, then Q2 and later November.

Even September end ₹38.6 Cr IPO funds allocated for crane project remained unutilised.

So capacity announcement is there, but commercial production and utilisation still to prove.

Now positives also there.

Balance sheet improving. Credit rating upgraded to IVR A/Stable.

H1 operating cash flow ₹12.13 Cr against almost zero last year.

But capex around ₹27 Cr, so free cash flow still negative.

ROCE around 7–8%. This is where I am more concerned.

Company investing heavily, but returns not yet coming.

At around ₹610 Cr market cap and 24 PE, valuation may look reasonable if crane business scales.

But for such low ROCE, not exactly cheap also.

Management earlier guided 20–25% FY27 revenue growth. H1 revenue around ₹225 Cr. H2 now needs quite big acceleration.

Latest H1 concall explanations still awaited.

For me question is not whether Indo Farm can manufacture more cranes.

Can it sell them profitably, build dealer network and compete with ACE?

And how much additional capital required to generate next ₹10 Cr PAT?

I like balance sheet repair and crane opportunity. But next 12 months are very important.

Bhud production, actual tower crane orders, dealer expansion, cash flow and improving ROCE.

If these start moving together, Indo Farm may become interesting transformation story.

Otherwise, just another capital intensive business adding capacity without proportionate returns.

Potential is there, but commercial proof still missing.

Every job comes with its challenges.

My grandfather used to earn ₹70 a month. Both his sons worked hard to lift themselves out of poverty, and they succeeded. I'm sure many others who tried just as hard weren't as fortunate.

My father secured AIR 2 in the Shipping Corporation of India examination. Both brothers joined the Merchant Navy, and their family's fortunes changed.

But that prosperity came at a price.

Life in the Merchant Navy meant spending more than half their lives away from family. My father sometimes sailed for over a year without coming home. For much of my childhood and schooling, he was away at sea.

He decided that his son would never join the Merchant Navy.

So I chose medicine.

It's been almost two decades since I first went to Kota. Becoming a doctor has taken far longer than I ever imagined. I'm finally in a reasonably solid position, yet I know it will take several more years to become successful by the standards I've set for myself.

Life hasn't panned out the way I imagined. Yet time keeps moving.

Despite everything I've been through, I feel pretty good about myself today.

Recently, a radiologist asked me which surgeon had the best hands for cholesteatoma surgery. He wanted someone to operate on his relative.

I could think of only a few names.

And that got me thinking.

Surgical training slots are limited. The learning curve is steep. Getting meaningful hands-on experience is an even scarcer resource. Not everyone who enters the profession will emerge as an exceptional surgeon.

But imagine coming out the other end and becoming one of those few surgeons whose names immediately come to mind when another doctor wants the very best for someone in their family.

Wouldn't that give you immense satisfaction and pride?

My point is simple.

Who the hell am I to deny someone the chance to pursue the best life they could possibly live?

At the end of the day, it's all a gamble. Some people succeed. Some don't. Hard work improves your odds, but guarantees nothing.

Are you willing to take that chance? Put in the years? Do everything you can to excel, knowing that success is never assured?

I've personally decided that I want to become the best surgeon I can possibly be, no matter how long it takes.

And one last thing.

People on the internet are remarkably comfortable dishing out career and relationship advice, often with absolute certainty.

But none of these people will necessarily be there for you five or ten years down the line.

You will.

You'll be the one standing in front of the mirror, living with the consequences of your decisions. Good or bad.

So listen to advice. Understand the risks. Be realistic about your circumstances.

But don't let strangers make the most consequential decisions of your life for you.

Because ultimately, it's your life to live. And your gamble to take.

Sammaan Capital's Q2 FY27 profit came from recoveries, not lending

Sammaan Capital, the lender once called Indiabulls Housing Finance, made a ₹312 crore profit in July to September 2026 (Q2 FY27), its results of 14 November show. so its lending works again? not yet. it earned ₹1,161 crore of interest and paid ₹1,299 crore, ₹138 crore more than it earned.

a lender like this borrows from banks and bond buyers, lends the money on, mostly as home loans, and lives on the gap. a year earlier the gap was ₹163 crore. since then interest earned fell 19.9%, after the company moved a pile of slow loans out of its lending book in March to sell or settle. it still owes ₹49,269 crore, more than the ₹42,348 crore it has out as loans.

so the profit came from elsewhere: ₹648 crore of gains on loans and investments it values at market prices, and ₹217 crore of provisions (money set aside for bad loans) written back as old loans were recovered. together they are 2.0x its profit before tax.

that looks like the March clean-up paying back. that quarter it booked a ₹7,152 crore loss on the loans it set aside. in May its chief executive said it would recover close to ₹7,000 crore of what it had provided for.

profit before tax, ₹425 crore, is the same as a year earlier. then lending paid its way; now recoveries carry it. recoveries stop once the old loans are settled, so the lending gap is what has to turn, through cheaper borrowing or a bigger loan book.

Sammaan Capital: Q2 FY27 Results and Key Takeaways from the Concall

Disbursements rose sharply and asset quality improved further. Management says the company is moving from repairing the business to growing it, with its new promoter IHC (International Holding Company, Abu Dhabi) behind it.

Q2 FY27
AUM: ₹59,188 Cr (vs ₹56,239 Cr in Q1)
Disbursements: ₹6,278 Cr (+62% QoQ)
PAT: ₹312 Cr (+28% QoQ)
Gross NPA: 0.15%, Net NPA: 0.11%
RoA: 1.5%, Capital adequacy: 20%
H1 FY27 PAT: ₹556 Cr

1.  Promoter putting in more capital-
IHC converted its first tranche of warrants early, putting in ₹906 Cr on 30 October and raising its stake from 28.34% to 33.32%. Another ₹2,291 Cr will come by September 2027, which will take its holding to about 43.28%.

2.  Borrowing costs still falling-
Cost of funds (the interest the company pays on its own borrowings) is 9.8%, with a target of 9.3%. Interest rates are rising across the market, but management says the company's own borrowing cost will keep falling because its credit rating has improved. It raised its lending rates by 25 bps from 1 November, so spreads may widen in the near term.

3.  New products beyond home loans-
Personal loans are moving from buying loan pools from other lenders to the company's own lending through 20 branches. Gold loans will start in 16 branches this quarter and 30 more in Q4. Loans to small businesses are being prepared. About 94% of Q2 disbursements were secured loans, and collection efficiency was 99.6%.

4.  Margin is higher than the interest line shows-
Part of the loan book is valued at market price, so some of its income appears under fair value gains instead of interest income. Adding these up, gross margin was ₹517 Cr, or 2.9% of assets, against a target of about 3.5%. Fee income from loans sold to banks fell to ₹33 Cr from ₹59 Cr after banks raised their rates, and management expects it to catch up.

5.  More branches and people-
Branches went from 217 to 245 and should reach about 300 by year-end. The company hired 1,123 people in H1, 87% of them for branches. Management says a new home loan branch takes about 6 months to break even and a gold loan branch 12-18 months.

6.  Road to a AAA rating-
The rating today is AA+. To reach AAA, management says it needs steady growth, more retail loans and a return on managed assets (profit as a share of all loans it handles, including those sold to banks) above 2%. That figure is 1.3% today.

Key Guidance
1. FY27 disbursements of ₹30,100 Cr, including ₹20,000 Cr in H2
2. FY27 PAT of ₹1,400 Cr and AUM of ₹70,700 Cr
3. Margin of about 3.5% and cost of funds of 9.3%

That’s the real logic behind support and resistance:

Price moves because buyers and sellers interact.

Support = an area where buying pressure has previously emerged.

Resistance = an area where selling pressure has previously emerged.

The lines are just a way to visualise that behaviour.

Follow @MotilalOswalLtd for more such interesting and informative threads on the market, industry and economy.

So don’t think:

“₹500 is support because the chart says so.”

Think:

“Was there meaningful buying around ₹500 before?”
Or:
“Did sellers repeatedly appear around this level?”

The chart is showing past price behaviour.

It isn’t predicting the future with certainty.

That’s also why round numbers can sometimes attract attention.

₹100
₹500
₹1,000

Investors may naturally watch these levels.

But a round number alone does not guarantee support or resistance.

Price behaviour matters more than the number itself.

But why do these levels matter so much?

Because markets are made of people.
People remember prices.

They have entry prices.
They have losses they want to recover.
They have profits they want to book.

And they react to what happened at those prices before.

For example:

A stock repeatedly struggles around ₹150.
Eventually, buyers push it above ₹150.

If the price later falls back toward ₹150…
buyers may now see that level as an opportunity.

The old resistance can potentially become support.

This is often called a breakout and retest.

And this is where it gets interesting.

Support and resistance are not walls.

They are zones where buying or selling pressure may become stronger.

Price can move through them.

When it does, the old level can sometimes take on a different role.

Resistance works the other way.

Suppose a stock repeatedly struggles around ₹150.

Why?

There may be investors who bought around that level earlier.

When the price reaches ₹150 again, some may decide:
“I’ll sell here and get my money back.”

More selling can appear around the same zone.

That can create resistance.

Now imagine the stock returns to ₹100 later.

Some investors may think:
“I wanted to buy it at ₹100 last time.”

Others may remember that the stock bounced from there.

More buyers can appear around the same zone.

That can create another reaction

Think about support first.

A stock falls from ₹120 to ₹100.
Buyers step in around ₹100.

Demand increases.

The fall slows down or reverses.

That ₹100 zone may become support.
Not because ₹100 is a magical number.

Because buyers showed up there.

Why does a stock sometimes fall to a certain level…
and suddenly find buyers?

Or rise to a certain level…
and suddenly face selling?

That’s the basic idea behind support and resistance.

But the real logic is more interesting than two lines on a chart. 🧵

India’s Future Tech Builders – Week 5

India is building 10 nuclear reactors and putting humans in space. The components for both come from a company that has been quietly doing this for over 60 years. And the market still treats it like a legacy engineering shop.

Let me tell you about Walchandnagar Industries (NSE: WALCHANNAG).

This is not a startup. This is not a new-age defence play. This is a 117-year-old heavy engineering company that has been inside India’s most strategic programmes since the beginning. Nuclear. Space. Defence. And it is only now starting to look like a business again.

Here is the breakdown.

What they are doing right
They make the hardware that goes into places where failure is not an option.

Nuclear is the deep moat. Walchandnagar has supplied core equipment for India’s Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors for decades. Calandria. End shields. Dump tanks. Fuel magazines. Moderator heat exchangers. And they executed the sodium piping contract for the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam. Very few Indian companies have this qualification. Very few can even bid for this work.

Space is the new leg. In August 2026, they won a ₹30.53 crore order from Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre for HS200 motorcase segments for the Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme. Fabrication, proof pressure testing, and supply. All three segments. The order runs for four years. This is not a one-off. It is a credential.
The turnaround is real. FY26 revenue was ₹296.26 crore. EBITDA turned positive at ₹35.49 crore, a swing from a negative ₹35.61 crore in FY25. Net loss narrowed sharply to ₹14.68 crore from ₹86.03 crore. And Q2 FY27 was the fourth consecutive quarter of positive PBT. Revenue grew 81% year-on-year to ₹93.53 crore, and the company turned net positive at ₹0.47 crore.

The order book stood at ₹871.77 crore as of March 2026. In Q2 FY27 alone, they secured ₹99.46 crore of new orders, including ₹38.13 crore from Aerospace. And the nuclear tender for the End Shield has been released — the first concrete step in the anticipated nuclear order flow.

What is going in their favour
The policy backdrop has never been stronger.

India’s nuclear programme is accelerating. The target is 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047. For every 700 MW PHWR reactor, Walchandnagar is eligible to supply equipment worth around ₹1,000 crore. For smaller 220 MW reactors, the opportunity is around ₹700 crore per plant. They are pre-qualified for Class I nuclear components and have over 40 years of direct partnership with the Department of Atomic Energy, NPCIL, BARC, and BHAVINI.

The SHANTI Act changes the game. The passage of the Shanti Bill in December 2025 is expected to open the nuclear sector to private participation. Notifications and rules are expected soon. Private players are expected to firm up plans and place orders over the next 12 months. Walchandnagar is one of the few qualified manufacturers who can serve them.
Gaganyaan is a multi-year programme. The HS200 order is the first visible piece. As the human spaceflight programme progresses, more hardware will be needed. Walchandnagar is already inside the tent.

The Satara lockout is behind them. The plant was locked out from March 2025 to November 2025. That disruption is resolved. Revenue is recovering, and operating leverage is starting to show.

How they can prove they are the company of the future
A legacy name is a credential. A profitable, scaling business is a company.
They need to convert the nuclear pipeline into orders. The End Shield tender is out. More will follow. If Walchandnagar can win a meaningful share of the 10-reactor pipeline, the nuclear segment becomes the backbone of the business for the next decade.

They need to prove that the Gaganyaan order is the start of a space franchise, not a single contract. Rocket motor casings, naval gearboxes, precision components for launch vehicles. The capability is there. The order flow needs to follow.
They need to bring debt down. Finance costs of ₹9.78 crore in a single quarter consume almost all operating profit. Debt stood at ₹219 crore. Every rupee of interest saved goes straight to the bottom line.

If they pull these off, they are not just a heavy engineering company. They become India’s go-to strategic fabricator for nuclear, space, and defence — the one name that can be trusted with the hardware that cannot fail.

Where they need to be careful
Here is where I get uncomfortable.

Finance costs are eating the business alive. Q2 FY27 PBT was ₹47 lakh. Finance costs were ₹978 lakh. That is not a profitable business yet. It is a business that is covering its operating costs and then handing almost everything to the lenders.
Working capital is stretched. Inventory days and receivable cycles in heavy engineering are long by nature. But with debt at this level, every extra day of working capital costs real money.

Order flow is lumpy. Nuclear and space programmes move on government timelines. A tender can be delayed by a quarter. An order can take years to execute. That is the nature of the business. Investors need the stomach for it.
The NCLT application is a lingering risk. An operational creditor filed a claim of approximately ₹7.95 crore under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. It has not been admitted. But until it is resolved, it is a headline risk.

Who they are actually competing with
This is a narrow field. Very few Indian companies can do what Walchandnagar does.

MTAR Technologies is the closest pure-play comparable. They make nuclear assemblies, space vehicle engines, and clean energy systems. They are a qualified supplier to the nuclear and space programmes. Their scale is smaller, but their margins and balance sheet are cleaner.
Larsen & Toubro is the giant in heavy engineering for nuclear. They have the balance sheet, the project management muscle, and the relationships. But L&T operates at a different scale. For specialised, high-precision nuclear island components, Walchandnagar is a specialist that L&T relies on as part of the supply chain.
Godrej & Boyce has a strong aerospace and defence fabrication business. They make rocket motor casings and precision components. They are a credible competitor for space hardware.
BHEL is the public sector heavy engineering major. They supply nuclear turbines and generators. But their focus is on the balance of plant, not the nuclear island equipment where Walchandnagar specialises.
ISGEC Heavy Engineering and Praj Industries appear in peer lists, but their focus is different. ISGEC is broader engineering and EPC. Praj is ethanol and process engineering. Neither competes directly in nuclear island fabrication.

How they can leave the competition behind
Walchandnagar cannot outspend L&T. It cannot outscale BHEL. So it has to win on qualification and trust.

Own the nuclear island. Calandria, end shields, sodium piping, heat exchangers. These are the components that require decades of qualification and a track record that cannot be bought. Walchandnagar has that track record. Every new reactor should have Walchandnagar content. Make that the default.
Build the space franchise. The Gaganyaan motorcase order is a proof point. Use it to win more ISRO work. Motor casings for other launch vehicles. Precision structures for satellites. The space programme is growing. Walchandnagar needs to grow with it.

Fix the balance sheet before chasing growth. Debt reduction is not optional. Every rupee of interest saved is a rupee of profit. A cleaner balance sheet gives them the freedom to bid for larger orders without straining working capital.
Be the private nuclear sector’s first call. The SHANTI Act is opening the door. Private players will need qualified fabricators. Walchandnagar is already qualified. Being early and visible to private developers is a land grab opportunity.

The path I hope they take: Prove the profit, then scale the order book
I would not say stop chasing growth. I would say sequence the proof.

Make the current order book profitable. Bring finance costs down. Show that the turnaround is not just a revenue story but an earnings story. Then use that credibility to bid for the next wave of nuclear and space orders.
The order book is there. The qualification is there. The profit needs to follow.

Final thought
Walchandnagar is at an inflection point. They proved they can win orders in India’s most demanding programmes. They proved the operating turnaround is real. Now they need to prove that the bottom line can follow.

If nuclear orders scale and the Gaganyaan work becomes a franchise, this becomes a serious strategic manufacturing story. If finance costs keep eating the profit, the turnaround stays fragile.
I am watching the End Shield tender conversion and the debt reduction trajectory very closely. You should too.

Goldman Sachs just raised its 2030 global data center forecast to 273 GW.

That is an $8.5 trillion capex estimate over five years. Up 26% from their previous projection.

On paper, it looks like a straight-line supercycle for anyone selling power equipment.

Then you look at what happened in the US midterm elections last week.

While Washington was pushing to fast-track AI infrastructure, ordinary households saw their monthly power bills jump by double digits in places like Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Texas. Utilities passed the cost of grid and transmission upgrades straight down to local ratepayers.

At the ballot box, voters pushed back hard.

Dozens of municipalities passed local moratoriums and caps on new data center construction. Candidates who campaigned against data center utility hikes won key races, handing Congress to Democrats and putting a hard brake on deregulation.

At the same time, federal regulators at FERC are tightening rules on large tech loads, demanding Big Tech fund their own dedicated transmission instead of leaning on the public grid.

Now Wall Street is running the math again: Up to a third of planned US data center capacity could face local delays or regulatory roadblocks.

Why does this matter to an investor in India?

Over the last two years, Indian equipment makers rode this global shortage to new highs. Stocks like Apar Industries and Shilchar Technologies re-rated from low double-digit multiples to 35 to 50 times earnings on massive US export visibility.

Apar trades near ₹14,500. Shilchar trades near ₹3,580.

A spreadsheet can project 273 GW and $8.5 trillion with ease. A political election, angry ratepayers, and local zoning boards are much harder to model.

This is the core rule of Information Pricing: At 40 to 50 times earnings, the stock has already priced in the $8.5 trillion headline. It has not priced in US projects getting delayed by 18 months because local voters rejected a substation.

Tracking the long-term energy transition is necessary. Ignoring the political backlash around who pays for the power is where investors get hurt.

When a global theme hits political and regulatory resistance, do you hold through the cycle, or do you trim when valuations are already full? 👇

Not investment advice. Just how I think about macro headlines and political reality. Do your own diligence.

Oswal Pumps: Q2 FY27 Results and Key Takeaways from the Concall

Revenue grew quarter on quarter, but margins fell sharply because of higher raw material and operating costs. The launch of PM-KUSUM 2.0 is still delayed.

Q2 FY27
Revenue: ₹506.3 Cr (+6.9% QoQ)
Operating EBITDA: ₹57.5 Cr, margin 11.3% (down 437 bps QoQ)
PAT: ₹39.6 Cr, margin 7.7% (down 343 bps QoQ)
Net debt: ₹531 Cr, net debt to equity 0.30x

1.  Why margins fell-
About 210 bps of the fall came from costlier aluminium frames, glass, copper, zinc and steel, mainly on orders taken at older prices. The other 227 bps came from higher staff costs to build the solar EPC team, project expenses and provisions for receivables. Management says some of these costs are temporary.

2.  Moving beyond government pump schemes-
The solar pump order book is 9,487 pumps, with a near-term pipeline of about 10,000. Because PM-KUSUM 2.0 is delayed, the company is entering rooftop, utility-scale and commercial solar EPC. (In EPC the company designs, buys equipment for and builds the full project.) This order book is 143 MW, with another 168 MW in the pipeline.

3.  New solar cell plant-
The company plans a 1.2 GW TOPCon solar cell plant at Karnal costing ₹455.85 Cr. Of this, ₹159.85 Cr will come from unused IPO money (subject to shareholder approval) and ₹296 Cr from debt. The plant should meet about 75% of the company's own cell needs. Government schemes require DCR (Domestic Content Requirement) modules, and Indian-made cells are currently short and expensive.

4.  Capex plan reshuffled-
To fund the cell plant, 500 MW of planned module capacity is deferred. The EVA encapsulant plant (the layer that protects cells inside a module) is cut from 1,500 MW to 1,200 MW, and the aluminium frame plant is dropped because frames can be bought from outside.

5.  Working capital is the main risk-
The cash conversion cycle rose to 257 days from 244. Receivables are at 229 days, all owed by government bodies. The company received ₹208 Cr from the Maharashtra government in early October. It expects more payments from Maharashtra, Haryana and Karnataka this quarter, and receivable days to come down to about 150-160.

Key Guidance
1. PM-KUSUM 2.0 launch expected within this calendar year
2. Management says its revenue guidance of ₹4,000-4,500 Cr is intact
3. Solar cell plant to start commercial operations in April 2028

It had already been destroyed by fire in 2005 and rebuilt. Cultural loss on a World Heritage island.

El venezolano George Wittels diseña la nueva corona del Miss Universo para su 75.ª edición

La Organización Miss Universo presentó la nueva corona oficial de la 75.ª edición del certamen, titulada «The Radiance of an Eternal Legacy» («El resplandor de un legado eterno»), diseñada por el joyero venezolano George Wittels en colaboración con la casa parisina Maison d'OR, según el anuncio de la organización y crónicas de Philstar y The Inquirer.

La pieza, de oro blanco de 18 quilates y 3.150 diamantes, fue develada el 12 de noviembre en San Juan, Puerto Rico, durante The Miss Universe Experience en Plaza Las Américas. El director ejecutivo de Miss Universo, Ronald Day, la describió como un homenaje a la historia del certamen y a las mujeres que han llevado el título. La final está prevista para el 24 de noviembre en el Coliseo de Puerto Rico.

Wittels, de acuerdo con The Inquirer, también ha diseñado coronas del Miss Grand International y del Miss Supranational.

The central premise is that human history has been shaped by a hidden war between mankind, fallen angels, and powerful organizations seeking to control technology, time, and ultimately humanity’s spiritual destiny.

It begins with John Dee at the court of Elizabeth I, where his attempts to communicate with angels accidentally open a doorway through time. But the beings he contacts aren’t angels sent by God. They’re fallen angels, presenting themselves as divine or advanced intelligences and offering forbidden knowledge.

That knowledge passes through the centuries, influencing Nikola Tesla’s discoveries, Nazi occult experiments, and eventually secret programs operating within intelligence agencies and military black projects. These organizations supposedly communicate with the same entities through séances, occult rituals, sacrifices, and increasingly advanced technology, receiving scientific knowledge in exchange for cooperation.

The Nazis attempt to use this knowledge to develop advanced weapons, portals, and time travel, with the Holy Lance—the spear that pierced Christ at the Crucifixion—playing a central role. Their surviving Antarctic operations are eventually encountered by Admiral Byrd’s expedition. Even the mysterious aerial battle witnessed over Nuremberg in 1561 is explained as a future conflict spilling backward through time.

But the real story isn’t about aliens, Nazis, or time travel. It’s about the spiritual war over humanity.

The entities are actually fallen angels who hate God and hate mankind because we were created in His image. They rejected God and cannot share in the eternal communion with Him that humanity is offered. So their mission is to deceive us into rejecting that destiny ourselves.

They do this by manipulating civilizations, religions, governments, scientific development, and human behavior. They encourage division, hatred, fear, materialism, spiritual confusion, and self-destruction, while disguising their influence as enlightenment, progress, or contact with superior beings.

That’s why Christ and the Crucifixion are at the center of everything. His sacrifice opened the way for humanity’s salvation, and the fallen angels are doing everything they can to turn us away from it.

Their goal isn’t necessarily to destroy humanity physically. It’s to corrupt us spiritually. To make us smaller, more fearful, more divided, and more consumed by hatred and power, instead of expanding in love, consciousness, creativity, and communion with God.

In other words, humanity was created to reflect God’s love and carry that goodness outward into creation, potentially even across the cosmos. The fallen angels want to prevent that by convincing us to destroy ourselves or willingly surrender the very things that make us human.

So the entire conspiracy—from John Dee and Tesla to Nazi occultism, Antarctic mysteries, UAPs, and modern intelligence agencies—is really one long campaign of spiritual deception.

The technology is the bait. Humanity is the target. And our eternal separation from God is the objective.

India's ₹14,500 Crore Battery Storage Push: A ₹97,600 Crore Opportunity

India is stepping up its energy storage plans with a ₹14,500 crore Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme to support 92 GWh of new storage capacity.

The numbers:

- ₹14,500 crore in government funding, spread across FY2026-27 to FY2030-31.
- ₹97,600 crore in estimated total project investment.
- 92 GWh of planned storage: 60 GWh pumped hydro, 30 GWh battery storage (BESS) and 2 GWh emerging technologies.
- 40% minimum domestic content requirement for relevant BESS projects.

India is targeting 411 GWh of storage capacity by FY2031-32. The proposed 92 GWh addition is around 170% of the existing grid-scale storage base.

Potential beneficiaries include Exide Industries, Amara Raja Energy & Mobility, Waaree Energies, Siemens Energy India, Power Grid Corporation, Advait Energy Transitions and Oriana Power.

Sammaan Capital : Right path . Maintain 2x    - **Quarter overview**
  - Disbursements increased **62% QoQ to ₹6,278 crore**.
  - The quarter was focused on governance, capital infusion and product development rather than growth alone.
  - Gross NPA was **0.15%**, net NPA **0.11%**, and collection efficiency **99.6%**.

- **IHC partnership and capital**
  - IHC entity Avenir converted its first warrant tranche early, infusing **₹906 crore** on 30 October 2026.
  - Promoter stake increased from **28.34% to 33.32%**.
  - Remaining warrants worth **₹2,291 crore** can be converted through September 2027.
  - Full conversion would take promoter holding to approximately **43.28%**; book value per share is estimated at **₹153.9**, versus **₹162.6** currently, before retained earnings beyond September 2026.
  - Management expects IHC’s international banking relationships to improve liquidity access and support lower borrowing costs.
  - Management did not commit to increasing the stake beyond 43.28%.

- **New products**
  - **Gold loans:** Policies are approved; a soft launch is planned in about 16 branches in Q3 FY27, followed by 30 more branches in Q4 and wider expansion in FY28.
  - Gold-loan technology and operating infrastructure, including vault controls, are being developed.
  - **Personal loans:** The company is shifting from buying loan pools to own origination through 20 identified branches, supported by assisted and digital channels.
  - **Business installment loans:** Policies are approved; the target is MSME customers with ticket sizes of **₹18–20 lakh** and yields of **14–18%**.
  - H2 FY27 expansion plans include retail and e-commerce lending, micro-LAP, rural home loans and gold loans.
  - Product launches will be phased, with hiring aligned to rollout requirements.

- **Funding costs and margins**
  - Cost of funds was **9.8% on a coupon basis**, excluding amortized one-time fees; management says it has declined each quarter.
  - Management is targeting a cost of funds of **9.3%**.
  - Whole-book lending rates increased **25 bps from November**, while funding costs continue to decline, potentially supporting near-term spread expansion.
  - Gross margin was **₹517 crore**, or **2.9% of assets**; management expects it to move toward **3.5%**.
  - Expected margin drivers include lower funding costs, fair-value book revaluation and loan-book growth.
  - Fee income fell from **₹59 crore to ₹33 crore QoQ** as higher bank rates reduced spreads on sold-down stock; management expects recovery over two to three quarters as its own rate increases flow through.
  - Target funding mix: approximately **60% rupee term loans and bonds**, **20% assignments/PTCs/co-lending**, and **20% dollar bonds and loans**.

- **Next-quarter watch points**
  - Traction in the gold-loan launch and personal-loan own origination.
  - Continued reduction in cost of funds toward the **9.3%** target.
  - Whether lending-rate increases and lower funding costs improve spreads and gross margin.
  - Fee-income recovery.
  - Appointment of a new chairperson.

Ramkrishna Forgings: what happens when the capex ends?

Ramkrishna forges and casts steel parts for trucks, farm machines and railways in India, North America and Europe. 

Over four years it invested ₹3,500+ Cr in new plants. While they were being built, its EBITDA margin fell from 21.7% in FY23 to 13.9% in FY25.

From this year, we can see the plants are beginning to fill. Revenue grew 55% to ₹1,405 Cr and the margin reached 18.2% in Q2 FY27

• Trigger 2, demand at home: Domestic revenue grew 59% to ₹822 Cr, driven by Indian commercial vehicle sales, which management says rose 29% in the quarter, and by casting volumes that more than doubled Y/Y

• Trigger 2, demand abroad: Exports grew 53% to ₹425 Cr, driven entirely by North America, where sales rose from ₹129 Cr to ₹302 Cr in what management called a "V-curve recovery" after a year stalled by US tariffs. Europe fell from ₹147 Cr to ₹121 Cr as capacity went to North American orders.

• Trigger 1, utilisation: Plant use rose from 62% to 72%, driven by castings at 88% and ring rolling at 145% of rated capacity.

• Trigger 5, debt reduction: Debt fell ₹126 Cr in H1, and management still targets a ₹500 Cr cut in FY27.

Management expects the margin to expand "every quarter" until it passes the old peak.

The risk:  The company disclosed a ₹220 Cr inventory overstatement in its FY25 accounts, and 16% of promoter shares are pledged as promoters put their own money to recover the hit (signs of improving governance). We also need to keep a watch on the North America Class 8 Truck Demand which is currently a tailwind driven by Policy changes

INDO-MIM Limited has just released a powerhouse Q2 FY27 financial performance. While the headline net profit jump of nearly 100% instantly grabs market attention, the underlying story is much deeper. It is defined by strategic post-IPO debt restructuring, outstanding cash conversion metrics, and aggressive capital expenditure for future growth. Here is the comprehensive breakdown of their financial health and execution.

▪ CORE FINANCIAL METRICS (Q2 FY27)• Revenue from Operations stood at ₹1,271.84 Crores, reflecting a robust 14.3% YoY growth compared to ₹1,112.65 Crores in the previous year.• EBITDA reached ₹393.68 Crores, representing a 17.4% YoY increase. This strong operational efficiency drove the EBITDA Margin up by 82 basis points, securing a healthy 30.95%.• Net Profit skyrocketed by 99.9% to ₹215.18 Crores, up from ₹107.62 Crores.• Profit Base Effect: It is crucial to note that Q2 FY26 was suppressed by a ₹92.66 Crore one-time exceptional loss. The current quarter is completely normalized. While the 100% jump is aided by this base effect, the operational baseline remains fundamentally solid.
▪ STRATEGIC DEBT REDUCTION & MARGIN EXPANSION• Following their highly successful ₹500 Crore IPO in July 2026, INDO-MIM Limited executed a masterstroke by immediately deploying ₹400 Crores to extinguish existing borrowings.• The financial impact is strictly visible: Finance costs plummeted by 39%, dropping drastically from ₹44.10 Crores to just ₹26.97 Crores. This rapid deleveraging is acting as a direct, structural catalyst for net margin expansion.• Cost Efficiency Initiatives: Management acquired a 6.5% equity stake in Meena Solar Power Park Pvt Ltd. Participating in this Group Captive Scheme will substantially reduce long-term power and fuel input costs, providing a protective moat for future EBITDA margins.• Clean Audit: Statutory Auditors (Suri & Co.) provided an unmodified limited review report with zero negative qualifications or contingent liability red flags.
▪ CASH FLOW MASTERCLASS (H1 FY27)• Operating Cash Flow (OCF) came in remarkably strong at ₹470.37 Crores against a recorded Net Profit of ₹455.30 Crores.• This translates to a phenomenal Cash Conversion Ratio of 103%. INDO-MIM Limited is effectively translating every single rupee of accounting profit into tangible bank liquidity.• Working Capital Management: The company generated ₹246.27 Crores in cash via receivables recovery, which efficiently offset the ₹104.95 Crores deployed into new inventory accumulation.• Reinvestment: INDO-MIM Limited executed a heavy Capex of ₹257.34 Crores for new Property, Plant, and Equipment. Despite this aggressive capacity expansion, Free Cash Flow (FCF) remained heavily positive at ₹213.03 Crores.
▪ SHAREHOLDER RETURNS & MARKET CONTEXT• Massive Dividend Payout: INDO-MIM Limited declared a total interim dividend of ₹6.80 per share for H1 FY27. At a ₹1 face value, this represents a staggering 680% payout, distributing ₹329.22 Crores. Sustaining this post-IPO confirms a highly cash-generative manufacturing operation.• Market Reaction: The stock is currently trading near ₹1,277, roughly 7% below its 52-week high of ₹1,374.40. Despite exceptional numbers, the post-results stock action was mildly negative, indicating early post-IPO profit booking rather than fundamental business weakness.
▪ THE BOTTOM LINE• Utilizing IPO capital to aggressively clear corporate debt has structurally elevated the bottom-line margins for INDO-MIM Limited. Combined with an outstanding 103% cash conversion ratio, the core manufacturing business is demonstrating elite financial health, proving their earnings are backed by cold, hard cash.

Sammaan Capital: Is the market underestimating the earnings potential of this transformation?

A few things from the Q2 concall stood out.

1. Cost of funds

COF is currently 9.8%, with management targeting 9.3%.

More interestingly, Gagan Banga mentioned that even in a hypothetical scenario of a 100 bps rate hike, Sammaan's absolute borrowing coupon could still decline.

IHC's banking relationships are helping here. One UAE bank has already extended over $150 million at competitive rates, with another similar-sized transaction expected.

The company has also increased lending rates by 25 bps from November 

1. Management believes spreads could actually improve in the near term.

2. Earnings guidance

FY27 targets remain intact:

• PAT: ₹1,400 Cr
• AUM: ₹70,700 Cr
• Loan book: ₹53,000 Cr
• Disbursements: ₹30,100 Cr
• Cost of funds: 9.3%

H1 PAT was ₹556 Cr, which means H2 needs to deliver ₹844 Cr.

On FY28 a quarterly PAT run rate of nearly ₹800 Cr. 

3. Return ratios and ratings
Current ROA is 1.5%, return on managed assets is 1.3%, and ROE is around 5.8%.

Management wants return on managed assets to cross 2% as it works towards a AAA rating. Current rating is AA+.

A rating upgrade, along with lower funding costs, could be an important driver of valuation rerating.

4. IHC capital and valuation

IHC has already infused ₹906 Cr through the first warrant conversion, taking its stake to 33.32%.

Another ₹2,291 Cr is expected by September 2027, taking promoter holding to approximately 43.28%.

At around ₹137.5, Sammaan trades at roughly 0.85x its current book value of ₹162.6. After full warrant conversion, pro-forma book value is expected to be ₹153.9, before future retained earnings.

5. Understanding the fair-value book

A portion of the loan book is carried at fair value. Hence, some economic interest income is reflected under fair-value gains rather than the conventional interest income line.

Management's adjusted gross margin, combining interest income, fair-value gains and assignment income, less finance costs, stood at ₹517 Cr or 2.9% of assets in Q2.

The target is around 3.5%.

As the fair-value book gets revalued, the loan book expands and funding costs decline, management expects NII and margins to improve. 

This can support PAT growth, although fair-value gains themselves can fluctuate and should not be treated as recurring cash earnings.

Huge Rerating potential 🔥🔥

Aarti Surfactants' profit jumps nearly eightfold to ₹12.5 Cr; revenue up 62.5%

👉 Aarti Surfactants reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹291.2 Cr for Q2 FY27, up 62.5% from ₹179.2 Cr a year earlier and 6.7% from ₹272.9 Cr in Q1. Net profit rose to ₹12.5 Cr from ₹1.6 Cr in Q2 FY26 and ₹9.0 Cr in Q1. For the first six months, revenue reached ₹564.1 Cr, up 42.8%, while net profit came to ₹21.5 Cr against ₹4.5 Cr a year earlier.

👉 Operating margin, calculated as EBITDA less other income over revenue, widened to 10.22% from 5.23% a year ago and 7.48% in Q1. Cost of materials consumed rose to ₹246.7 Cr, but its share of revenue fell to 84.7% from 97.1% in Q2 FY26, although it was up from 84.0% in Q1. Finance costs rose to ₹3.7 Cr from ₹2.8 Cr, and depreciation reached ₹4.8 Cr.

👉 Profit before exceptional items was ₹21.5 Cr, but a ₹4.3 Cr exceptional provision brought pre-tax profit down to ₹17.2 Cr. The provision covers ₹1.47 Cr of stamp duty tied to the demerger scheme and ₹2.83 Cr of customs duty, interest and penalty under Order-in-Original 146/2026-27. The company is pursuing legal remedies, including appeal, and ₹3.73 Cr paid under protest in earlier years remains recoverable.

👉 Net profit margin reached 4.29% against 0.87% a year earlier. Debt-to-equity fell to 0.43 from 0.49, and interest service coverage rose to 7.94 from 3.34. The company redeemed 10,82,387 preference shares on 5 August for ₹23.23 Cr, and CRISIL assigned A-/Stable to its bank loans in September, replacing CARE's BBB+/Stable rating.

👉 Growth catalyst: Management said the newly incorporated US subsidiary, Precision Ingredients USA Inc., is part of its international expansion strategy and had not yet commenced operations by 30 September 2026.

👉 Road blocker: Management is contesting a customs duty demand: a ₹4.3 Cr exceptional provision was booked this quarter, and a further ₹6.71 Cr duty remains a contingent liability pending adjudication.

Caliber Mining and Logistics: Q2 FY27 Results and Key Takeaways from the Concall

Q2 is the monsoon quarter and usually the weakest for mining contractors. Even so, Caliber more than doubled overburden removal and nearly doubled revenue.

Q2 FY27
Normalised revenue: ₹441 Cr (+92% YoY)
Normalised EBITDA: ₹73.2 Cr, margin 16.6% (12.1% last year)
Net loss: ₹7.5 Cr (₹14.2 Cr loss last year)
Overburden removed: 33 million cubic metres (+109%)

H1 FY27
Normalised revenue: ₹992 Cr (+60% YoY)
Normalised EBITDA: ₹183.6 Cr (+49% YoY)
Overburden removed: 76.5 million cubic metres (+72%)

Overburden is the soil and rock removed to reach the coal underneath. Normalised figures exclude diesel costs that are passed on to customers.

1.  Monsoon quarter, still strong-
Rain damages haul roads and cuts the number of working days, so H1 is always weaker. In FY26, H2 revenue was 1.7x and EBITDA 2.5x that of H1. Since depreciation and interest costs stay the same through the year, the company reported a small loss in Q2.

2.  Diesel is now fully passed on-
Customers now reimburse 100% of diesel costs, which came to ₹184 Cr in H1. Management said crude price swings will no longer affect margins.

3.  Order book and bidding-
The order book is about ₹8,000 Cr across 9 sites, with an average remaining tenure of 2.5 years, and ₹4,000 Cr of it was added in H1. Results are awaited on ₹11,000 Cr+ of bids. One risk to note: the DRHP showed the company lost 32 of 38 tenders before its IPO. Management says the IPO money now lets it bid seriously for more contracts.

4.  Customers want more than contracted-
Coal demand is high, and some customers are asking for 105-110% of contracted volumes. H1 capex of ₹585 Cr was brought forward, and equipment for the current order book is already in place. Caliber is also exploring MDO (Mine Developer and Operator) contracts, where a company runs an entire mine over many years.

5.  Balance sheet stronger after IPO-
Net worth rose 77% to ₹1,148 Cr, and net debt-to-equity came down to 0.95x from 1.48x. ₹371 Cr of the ₹377 Cr IPO proceeds has been used as planned. CRISIL has upgraded the rating to A- with a positive outlook.

6.  AI for fleet uptime-
An in-house platform called PulseOne puts all maintenance data in one place and tracks vehicle breakdowns live for 200+ users. A second phase covering MIS (Management Information System) and HR is in beta. With a large fleet, small gains in uptime directly improve margins, though management did not quantify the benefit.

Key Guidance
- FY27 revenue growth of 45%+, and EBITDA and PAT growth of 35%+ (PAT of about ₹205-210 Cr against ₹157 Cr).
- About 60 million cubic metres of overburden removal in each of Q3 and Q4.
- FY28 guidance to be shared with Q3 results.

📅 DATES
Open: Thu, Nov 19, 2026
Close: Mon, Nov 23, 2026
Anchor bidding: Wed, 18 Nov
Allotment: ~Wed, 25 Nov
Refunds & demat credit: ~Thu, 26 Nov
Listing: ~Fri, 27 Nov, 2026 (NSE & BSE) 
(RHP filed 13 Nov, so cutoff date for buying CIL for shareholder quota was 12 Nov)

💰 PRICE & LOT
Price band: Not officially announced yet (expected shortly before opening; some market estimates/tentative figures around ₹118–125)
Lot size: Not officially announced
FV: ₹2
Shareholder quota: Up to ~6.62 crore shares (~10% of offer) for eligible Coal India shareholders (record date was Nov 13)
Employee reservation: Up to ~3.31 crore shares (discount to be announced)

📦 ISSUE
Size: Pure OFS of up to 66.18 crore shares (10% stake sale by parent Coal India)
Type: Book Built, Offer for Sale only (no fresh issue)
Estimated size (media/reports): ~₹8,000–10,000 Cr range (depending on final price)
FV: ₹2
Reservation (net offer): QIB not more than 50%, NII not less than 15%, Retail not less than 35%
Company receives no proceeds — all proceeds go to selling shareholder (Coal India)
Listing: Mainboard (NSE & BSE)

📊 FINANCIALS
FY26: Revenue ~₹30,550 Cr, PAT ~₹10,678–10,698 Cr
FY25: Revenue ~₹31,353 Cr, PAT ~₹10,825 Cr
FY24: Revenue ~₹31,634 Cr, PAT ~₹11,842 Cr
H1/Q1 FY27: Revenue figures in the ₹8,000–16,000 Cr range across reports; PAT solid but margins slightly softer than prior years
High EBITDA margins (~46–50% range in recent years); very low debt

📈 VALUATION
Post-issue market cap: Depends on final price band (media reports earlier suggested potential valuation up to ~$10 billion / ₹80,000+ Cr range in optimistic scenarios)
EPS (FY26): ~₹16.13
RoNW: ~54% (FY26)
Strong cash generation; low leverage

🎯 USE OF PROCEEDS
None to the company (100% OFS). Proceeds (net of expenses) go to Coal India.

🏢 BUSINESS
Wholly-owned subsidiary of Coal India. Largest coal-producing arm of CIL. Operates mainly in Odisha (Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields). Produced ~218 million tonnes of coal in FY26 (~21% of India’s domestic coal output and ~28% of Coal India’s total). Primarily thermal (non-coking) coal via large-scale opencast mining. Miniratna Category I status. Supplies power utilities and industrial customers.

🤝 Lead managers: SBI Capital Markets, Axis Capital, BOB Capital Markets, IDBI Capital Markets & Securities, IIFL Capital Services | Registrar: KFin Technologies

Mahanadi Coalfields' proposed IPO is up to 66.18 crore equity shares, about a 10% stake in the Coal India arm, and not one rupee of the proceeds reaches MCL: Coal India's filing says the issue is entirely an OFS, with all of it going to the parent as selling shareholder. That is fresh capital for no one at the company whose shares are being sold.

Zee Business reports MCL filed its RHP on November 14, after the September 2026 DRHP.

- Issue: OFS of up to 66,18,36,300 shares held by Coal India, about a 10% stake in MCL
- MCL's share of the proceeds: zero, since the issue is entirely an OFS
- SECL, another Coal India arm, filed its DRHP on November 2 for up to 66.81 crore shares at Rs 2 face value, also an OFS by the parent

Both proposals remain subject to regulatory approvals and prevailing market conditions, so "up to" is still the operative phrase.

Waaree Energies: The difference between a good business and a good entry price.

At its 2024 IPO, Waaree attracted enormous market euphoria and traded at a P/E of 90+.

Investors who bought at those valuations are still waiting for an exit.

But look at the business today:
• EPS has grown over 5x in 3 years and 2x in the last 2 years.
• P/E has compressed to below 19.
• A strong order book and significant capacity expansion provide earnings visibility.
• Multiple backward and forward integrations strengthen its competitive position.

The stock is nearly 40% below its peak, yet the business is earning substantially more.

This is why valuation and margin of safety matter.

Even the best businesses can be poor investments when purchased at excessive valuations.

A temporary slowdown, margin pressure, or delayed execution can trigger sharp corrections when expectations are stretched.

At high valuations, your margin of safety is thin. Risk management becomes essential.

The market doesn't just reward business quality. It rewards the price you pay.

At current levels, we believe Waaree offers an excellent opportunity to participate in its next phase of earnings growth at a much more reasonable valuation.

The Greatness of #PMNehru
Look at his contribution to our country!
Around 50–60 central public sector enterprises (CPSEs/PSUs) by the end of his tenure (plus major dams, river-valley projects, and institutions). Exact counts vary by definition and source.
Under his leadership India adopted a mixed economy with the state occupying the “commanding heights,” formalised in the Industrial Policy Resolutions of 1948 and especially 1956, and pursued through the Five-Year Plans. Public-sector growth was rapid in that period.

### Public sector enterprises (central)
Reliable historical figures from Bureau of Public Enterprises / Public Enterprises Survey data show:
- 1951 (start of First Plan): about 5 CPSEs.
- 1961 (start of Third Plan): about 42–47.
- 1964: roughly 50–61 (sources give 49 in 1963 and 61 in 1964).
- By 1966 (end of Third Plan): about 73; by 1969: 84–85.

One recent analysis by political scientist Devesh Kapur puts the number of new public sector enterprises set up in the broader “Nehruvian era” at around 70. A political claim sometimes circulated is 33 (attributed to a CPI leader); that appears to undercount or use a narrower definition.

Major examples established or expanded under Nehru include steel plants (Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur), Hindustan Machine Tools (HMT), Heavy Engineering Corporation, ONGC, Indian Oil Corporation (and related oil entities), Shipping Corporation of India, Bharat Electronics, Hindustan Aeronautics (lineage), National Mineral Development Corporation, Fertilizer Corporation of India, and many others in heavy industry, mining, engineering, and trading.

### Dams and multipurpose river-valley projects
Nehru famously called large dams the “temples of modern India.” Prominent ones initiated or completed in his time include:
- **Bhakra-Nangal** (Sutlej; construction advanced significantly; major completion 1963).
- **Hirakud** (Mahanadi; inaugurated/operational in the mid-to-late 1950s).
- **Nagarjuna Sagar** (Krishna; foundation work and major construction under him).
- **Damodar Valley Corporation** projects (established 1948; multipurpose dams for flood control, power, irrigation).
- Others such as Tungabhadra and elements of related irrigation/power schemes.

These were public-sector hydroelectric and irrigation projects under the First and Second Plans, aimed at agriculture, power, and flood control.

### Broader public-sector institutions
Beyond commercial PSUs and dams, his tenure saw the creation or major expansion of:
- Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs: Kharagpur 1951, then Bombay, Madras, Kanpur, Delhi).
- All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS).
- Atomic Energy Commission / Department of Atomic Energy and Bhabha Atomic Research Centre.
- Early CSIR laboratories and other scientific institutions.
- Planning Commission (1950), Indian Institute of Public Administration, etc.

In short, the core number for central commercial public-sector organisations is in the 50–60 range by the time of his death (growing from a handful at Independence), alongside a handful of iconic large dams/river projects and foundational educational/scientific institutions. Growth continued under subsequent governments (especially through nationalisations later), so the total public-sector footprint is much larger today. Definitions of “public sector organisation” can vary (central commercial companies vs. all government entities, completed vs. initiated, etc.), which explains differing counts in public discussion.

Krishana Phoschem | Q2 FY27 results

Krishana Phoschem's net profit more than doubles to ₹77.9 Cr; margin rises to 14.7%

👉 Krishana Phoschem reported standalone net profit of ₹77.9 Cr for Q2 FY27, up 134.6% from ₹33.2 Cr a year ago and 65.4% from ₹47.1 Cr in Q1. Revenue from operations rose 15.6% YoY to ₹702.5 Cr and 32% QoQ. Total income was ₹708.2 Cr, and profit before tax reached ₹104.4 Cr. The company reported no exceptional items.

👉 Operating margin widened to 14.7% from 11.3% in Q1 and 9.9% in Q2 FY26, a gain of 483 basis points year on year. Profit before other income rose to ₹98.7 Cr from ₹54.4 Cr in Q1 and ₹57.2 Cr a year ago. Other income of ₹5.7 Cr was a small part of pre-tax profit. Finance cost rose to ₹16.1 Cr from ₹6.9 Cr a year ago as the company raised more debt in H1.

👉 For the half year, revenue was ₹1,234.8 Cr, up 23.1% from ₹1,003.4 Cr, and net profit was ₹125.0 Cr against ₹63.7 Cr. Operating cash flow was negative ₹378.9 Cr, against a positive ₹58.3 Cr a year ago. The cash flow statement shows a ₹666.6 Cr increase in inventories, alongside net short-term borrowings of ₹378.6 Cr.

👉 Management's FY27 revenue guidance is ₹2,900–3,000 Cr, which H1's ₹1,234.8 Cr covers about 41–43%. The H2 requirement of ₹1,665–1,765 Cr implies roughly ₹833–883 Cr a quarter, against ₹702.5 Cr in Q2. CRISIL reaffirmed the ratings on its bank facilities on October 8 and removed them from watch.

👉 Growth catalyst: Management is targeting ₹1,000 Cr of incremental annual revenue at full capacity and a 25% market share in 2–3 years, supported by the Meghnagar NPK/DAP expansion and a 10-year SECI green ammonia deal for 70k MTPA.

👉 Road blocker: Operating cash flow turned negative at ₹378.9 Cr in H1 FY27 as inventories rose ₹666.6 Cr, and the FY27 guidance of ₹2,900–3,000 Cr needs ₹1,665–1,765 Cr of revenue in H2 against ₹702.5 Cr in Q2.

The reversing camera was non-functional from the beginning, and the TPMS sensors have also reportedly not worked properly since the start of ownership. The headlight rims had developed corrosion within six months of purchase and were replaced following my complaint. Unfortunately, corrosion has now appeared in several other areas.
I find it difficult to understand how a vehicle with such low mileage and from a reputed automobile manufacturer can develop so many problems.
On 28 October 2026, at Mahindra's request, I sent the vehicle to your authorised Shiva Mahindra workshop, Sahibabad. It remained there for the entire day, but not a single reported defect was rectified. I was subsequently informed that approval from the head office was awaited.

I have no intention of unnecessarily criticising a brand that I once purchased with considerable trust. I am simply seeking accountability, fair treatment and a satisfactory resolution.

I understand that a large organisation has established systems and processes. However, a customer should not have to spend months chasing multiple departments merely to get genuine product-quality concerns investigated.
Mahindra's reputation has been built over decades, and customer trust is one of its most valuable assets. I sincerely hope that the company's commitment to the Mahindra Rise philosophy will also be reflected in how it handles an individual customer's grievance.
I am not asking for a favour, special treatment or another assurance. I am simply asking Mahindra to stand behind the product it sold and resolve this matter fairly.
I still hope this can be resolved amicably, without having to pursue consumer litigation and other available remedies.

What can we make out of AXISCADES Q2, FY27 results, and what can we expect in 2H, FY27 and FY28? 

🧵👇 Read till the end...

1️⃣ The three operating pillars (Defence, XIDA, Aerospace/Cloud Wave) are already profitable at solid margins:
🛡️ Defence Q2: 17.6% EBITDA margin
💻 XIDA Q2: ~22% EBITDA margin
✈️ Cloud Wave Q2: 20.3% EBITDA margin

2️⃣ The drag is almost entirely at the listed parent (corporate overhead + ESOP + legal costs + residual Add Solutions), which will wear off in H2. 📉

3️⃣ Will Margins Improve Going Forward? Yes — management has given a clear path, and the levers are largely within their control. 🎯

Why and What to Expect – 2H FY27? 🔮
📈 Margin recovery should accelerate. ESOP charge halves, legal/professional costs normalise, and the corporate cost base gets absorbed as retained revenue scales. Management is targeting ~20% EBITDA margins at the division level from Q3 for the core BUs.

⚡ Revenue momentum continues: Defence order execution, full contribution from Cloud Wave, XIDA post-restructuring + new customers, realisation of remaining deferred revenue by Q4, and incremental contributions from further acquisitions in the pipeline.

💰 Phase 2 closing by February 2027 brings the remaining cash proceeds, supporting debt reduction and the next phase of capacity/acquisitions.

🚀 Normalised profitability of the retained business should improve meaningfully versus H1.

And, FY28? 🔭
🧹 Cleaner base with most transition costs behind. Phase 2 proceeds fully in, debt lower, and cost structure better aligned.

🛰️ Space starts contributing revenue from Q2 FY28.
🏭 Aerospace manufacturing scales further (Cloud Wave full year + organic + any additional acquisitions; longer-term path toward higher run-rates as the Center for Advanced Manufacturing comes online around Q4 FY28).

🛡️ Defence continues multi-year execution of the large assured order book (growth rates earlier guided at >75% YoY in the near term remain the aspiration, supported by the order intake).

🤖 XIDA platform fully restructured and scaling with the new customer base and any selective inorganic moves in AI/semiconductors.

🏗️ Capacity (DAC Phase 1 by Q2 FY28, CAM later, Hyderabad MAC, etc.) supports the manufacturing pivot.

📊 Earnings conversion improves as revenue grows on a largely fixed cost base that has already been built. Power 930 remains the long-term north star. ⭐

#AXISCADES

Here I will pick 5 companies.

KSH – Overall utilisation is 76% with specialised winding wire capacity above 80%, contributing 75% of revenue. It has Power Grid approval up to 765 kV and an overseas HVDC trial order.

Azad – All six customer dedicated facilities for major global customers are commissioned, revenue ramp up is expected from Q4 FY27 with potential for an annual run rate above 1,300 crore by end FY28, that is exactly the type of transition where a J-curve can develop.

Happy Forgings – It has secured around 300 crore of annual data centre related orders, contracted through 2033 with the customer also investing in the required machining lines.

Quality Power – Order book is above 2,000 crore, excluding Winwin, the Sangli coil factory and Turkey PCS facility have started manufacturing while Winwin has secured 800 kV HVDC and 765/400 kV AC insulator orders.

Centum Electronics – PCB lead times have increased from 8–12 weeks to 40–50 weeks while Centum's order book is around 2,000 crore, up 38%. The question is how much of this constraint it can capture through revenue and margins.

Now, there is a different way to look at these companies too.

Strongest current financial quality: Quality Power → Happy Forgings → Centum → KSH → Azad

Most interesting upcoming business inflection: Azad → Quality Power → Happy Forgings → KSH → Centum

Best balance of existing economics and future opportunity: Happy Forgings → Quality Power → KSH → Centum → Azad

Happy Forgings is currently the most balanced candidate, Quality Power is the strongest financially but its valuation is demanding, KSH has an attractive growth opportunity but the cash flow concern is too important to ignore.

Azad is the most interesting potential financial J curve but also the most dependent on future execution, Centum has a credible opportunity but the gap between its order book growth and historical sales growth needs to close.

There are other companies worth studying as well such as TARIL, Ramkrishna Forgings and Piramal Pharma. I am not saying these or other companies do not fit. I just tried to narrow the list to 5 companies where I see interesting opportunities to study further.

Just my view. Not a recommendation.

SAMMAAN CAPITAL: From Balance-Sheet Repair to Business Expansion. 🚀

Q2 FY27 investor presentation reveals an interesting transformation underway.

The positives: 
▪️ Disbursements surged 62% QoQ to ₹6,278 Cr
▪️ AUM reached ₹59,188 Cr
▪️ GNPA at 0.15%; NNPA at 0.11%

▪️ IHC-backed capital support strengthening the growth runway
▪️ New businesses: Personal Loans, Gold Loans & MSME lending

But the real story is bigger than these numbers.
Sammaan is investing in people, technology, distribution and new products to build a diversified lending franchise.

However, execution is the key.

H1 PAT stands at ₹556 Cr against a FY27 target of ₹1,400 Cr. Achieving this requires a significant acceleration in H2.

Also, reported profitability still needs to demonstrate a stronger contribution from sustainable core lending operations.

My takeaway:
The legacy clean-up was Phase 1.
Business rebuilding is Phase 2.
Sustainable earnings growth will be Phase 3.

Sammaan appears to be progressing through Phase 2.

Now, the market will watch how successfully it delivers Phase 3.

A turnaround is not complete when losses disappear. It is complete when a business starts generating consistent, quality earnings.

5️⃣ Why earnings weakened ⚠️

⚠️ No firm quarterly timeline for achieving that margin improvement was provided.

🎙️ Sammaan Capital (SAMMAANCAP) earnings call, decoded ⬇️

Sammaan Capital reported Q2FY27 profit after tax of ₹312 Cr, up 28% QoQ but flat against ₹308 Cr a year ago. Disbursals were the standout at ₹6,278 Cr, up 62% QoQ, and H1 disbursals of ₹10,153 Cr beat the ₹10,000 Cr target. AUM grew 5% QoQ to ₹59,188 Cr. Margins were the weak spot: cost of funds reached 9.8% against the 9.6% guided for September, and cost-to-income rose to 61.8% from a promised ~50%. For FY27, management targets AUM of ₹70,700 Cr and PAT of ₹1,400 Cr; H1 PAT of ₹556 Cr is about 40% of that. Gold Loans soft launch is set for Q3FY27. The filing record shows Q2 net profit of ₹243.3 Cr, which conflicts with this figure and needs checking.

Growth triggers
• Gold Loans soft launch in Q3FY27
• FY27-end: cost of funds 9.3%, AUM ₹70,700 Cr, PAT ₹1,400 Cr
• Branches from 245 to ~300, with 91% of the FY27 network in place

Blockers
• Cost-to-income at 61.8%, versus ~50% promised for this year
• Cost of funds at 9.8%, versus 9.6% guided by September, with the repo hike adding pressure
