A Question I Received from an Investor: 
What Exactly Went Wrong with Supriya Lifesciences' LATAM Business, How Much Revenue Was Impacted, and What Should We Watch Going Forward?

Supriya Lifesciences hit a 20% lower circuit following its Q2 FY27 results. The stock subsequently corrected another 7% on Muhurat trading and another 6–7% thereafter...

While the sharp decline in profitability has understandably disappointed investors, I think we need to look beyond the headline numbers and understand what actually happened to the business.

This post will  focus on the LATAM disruption, because it has implications for both revenue growth and the company's historically attractive EBITDA margins.

What exactly happened?
During the Q2 earnings call, management explained that regulatory changes in three LATAM markets – Colombia, Peru and Uruguay – resulted in certain products being reclassified as controlled substances.

Earlier, customers could import these products relatively freely. Following the changes, customers now require additional import authorizations before shipments can resume.

Management indicated that existing customer purchase orders and demand visibility were available, but customers now need to obtain fresh import authorizations. The process could take approximately 4–5 months.

Consequently, some higher-margin regulated-market sales were deferred. Management also indicated that the entire lost LATAM contribution may not return within FY27.

The important distinction is that management describes this as a regulatory and timing disruption rather than a complete loss of underlying demand.

However, purchase orders are not guaranteed future sales. We will need to see actual shipment recovery.

What did we find on the regulatory changes and affected products?
I tried to cross-check the regulatory developments in all three countries against Supriya's published product portfolio.

In Uruguay, Decree 198/025, dated September 2025, updated the country's controlled-substance framework. The updated national register includes substances such as Esketamine, Ketamine and Dexmedetomidine. These are relevant portfolio overlaps because Supriya has products in these categories.

However, the consolidated register does not establish that all these molecules were newly added through this particular decree or that they were responsible for Supriya's lost orders.

In Colombia, Resolution 116 of 2026 updated the national lists of controlled narcotics, psychotropic substances, precursors and controlled medicines. One important point is that newly controlled precursors should not automatically be confused with finished pharmaceutical products. I could not establish a direct link between every newly controlled substance and Supriya's existing commercial sales.

In Peru, the Ministry of Health published Resolution 831-2026/MINSA in September 2026, proposing updates to controlled-substance lists. Ketamine is an important potential overlap with Supriya's portfolio. However, this document was a proposal for consultation, not confirmation that a new import restriction had already become effective.

My interpretation is that there appears to be a broader regulatory tightening and updating of controlled-substance frameworks across these markets.

But we should not assume that every molecule appearing in the updated lists was newly controlled or contributed to Supriya's lost revenue.

The exact product-country mapping has not been disclosed by management. Esketamine and Ketamine are portfolio overlaps worth investigating, not confirmed explanations of the Q2 sales disruption.

How significant was LATAM historically?
This is where the situation becomes interesting.

LATAM had become an increasingly important geographical market for Supriya.

Its contribution to export revenue, as disclosed in historical company commentary, was approximately 11% in FY24, increased to 22% in FY25, remained around 20% in FY26 and Q1 FY27, before falling to approximately 12% in Q2 FY27.

The company had therefore built a meaningful business in these markets over the years.

The fall from approximately 20% to 12% in Q2 is significant, especially because these were higher-realization and higher-margin products.

In other words, the issue is not simply lower sales. It is the loss of a favourable revenue mix.

How much revenue could have been impacted?
Let's do our own indicative calculation.

Q2 FY27 revenue was approximately Rs 206.3 crore, with exports contributing around 80%.

This implies export revenue of approximately Rs 165 crore.

Assuming LATAM represented approximately 20% of exports under normal conditions, compared with the reported 12% contribution in Q2, the estimated quarterly revenue shortfall comes to approximately Rs 13–14 crore.

This is a mix-based estimate, not management-confirmed lost revenue.

Q2 FY26 revenue was approximately Rs 199.8 crore, while Q2 FY27 revenue came in at Rs 206.3 crore. This translates into reported YoY growth of approximately 3.2%.

If we add back the estimated Rs 13–14 crore of deferred LATAM sales, normalised Q2 revenue would have been approximately Rs 219–220 crore.

That would imply YoY growth of approximately 10–11%, rather than the reported 3.2%.

So, our calculation suggests that the LATAM disruption could have reduced reported Q2 revenue growth by approximately 7 percentage points.

This is a meaningful difference when assessing the underlying business momentum.

One important clarification: these sales should not automatically be classified as permanently lost. Management's explanation is that some of the business is deferred pending customer authorizations. The actual recovery will depend on permits being granted and orders converting into shipments.

Also, this calculation assumes that the historical 20% LATAM contribution to exports is a reasonable normalised benchmark. It does not prove that every rupee of the estimated shortfall would have materialised.

What does this mean for the investment thesis?
I see two different aspects here.

First, the underlying business may have been growing faster than the reported Q2 numbers suggest. Our indicative calculation puts normalised Q2 growth closer to 10–11%, rather than 3.2%.

Second, the lost LATAM contribution has a disproportionate impact on profitability because these were higher-margin products.

Management itself attributed approximately 3 percentage points of EBITDA margin pressure to LATAM regulatory changes and product mix.

Therefore, even if revenue is replaced through semi-regulated markets, the same level of profitability may not immediately return.

This is why I would track revenue recovery and margin recovery separately.

What should we watch going forward?

I don't think there is any point in being overly smart at this stage or trying to predict exactly when everything will normalise. The next quarter will be important, and we should focus on actual evidence of recovery rather than management assurances.

The key things to monitor are whether customers in Colombia, Peru and Uruguay receive the required import authorizations, whether deferred LATAM orders convert into actual shipments, and whether the region's contribution starts moving back towards historical levels. I would also like management to provide greater clarity on the exact products affected, country-wise revenue exposure and the status of customer permits.

Alongside this, progress on new product launches, the CMO opportunity and Ambarnath ramp-up will determine the broader growth and margin recovery.

My overall view
There is a plausible regulatory explanation for the LATAM disruption, and historical sales trends suggest that this was an important, growing and higher-margin business for Supriya. However, we should not automatically assume that all deferred sales will return or that historical EBITDA margins will be restored.

For existing investors, the focus should be on whether the original investment thesis remains intact. For prospective investors, the opportunity needs to be evaluated against the uncertainty around revenue recovery, margins and execution.

I would rather wait for Q3 performance and actual evidence of recovery than make overly confident predictions based on management commentary alone.

Ultimately, we need to look at both sides: what was genuinely outside management's control and where communication, planning and execution could have been better. That is how we form an unbiased view of the business.

Note: Regulatory product overlaps mentioned above are based on publicly available lists and Supriya's published portfolio. They are not confirmation of the exact products affected in the company's LATAM orders. Revenue impact is our own indicative calculation, not a company-disclosed figure.

Time Technoplast Q2 FY27: Strong growth, but the earnings story is bigger than the 32% sales headline.

The company supplies industrial drums, containers and pipes, alongside composite cylinders for LPG, CNG and emerging hydrogen applications. Its opportunity is to turn that manufacturing footprint into a more efficient, higher-value business.

The call gives a clearer picture of what is working, what is delayed and where expectations need care.

1) Separate price growth from demand growth

Q2 consolidated numbers:
• Revenue from operations: ₹1,994.19cr, up 32.0% YoY
• Volume growth: 13.8%
• Company-reported EBITDA: ₹265.0cr, up 18.4%
• EBITDA margin: 13.3%, versus 14.8%
• PAT attributable to shareholders: ₹146.13cr, up 26.6%
• EPS: ₹2.96, versus ₹2.54, up 16.5%

Higher polymer prices lifted sales because the company passes input costs to customers. Management described a typical 20–25-day lag.

That mechanism helps protect earnings in rupees. It does not automatically preserve the margin percentage: a larger sales denominator can reduce the percentage even when absolute profit rises.

EBITDA grew faster than volumes, but slower than revenue. And after the increase in share capital, per-share earnings grew less than headline PAT. Those distinctions matter when judging the quarter.

2) Composite growth is uneven, which makes the product mix important

The presentation's composite-cylinder product basket generated ₹430cr in H1, up 28.6%. Within it:
• CNG cascades: ₹273.5cr revenue, up 28.7%; units up 22.1%
• LPG cylinders: ₹117.5cr revenue, up 8.0%; units up 6.9%
• Other composite products: ₹38.9cr, versus ₹13.1cr

CNG and newer products are doing more of the growth work than LPG. This basket is roughly 12% of group sales, so its expansion must become large enough to influence the wider business.

IBCs, the large containers used to transport industrial liquids, are another important driver: H1 revenue rose 30.7% to ₹489cr, while volumes rose 14.1%.

For the sector, gas distribution creates demand for mobile CNG storage where pipelines do not reach. Chemical, pharmaceutical and FMCG production supports packaging demand. These are different demand cycles, which gives Time more than one route to growth.

3) Orders today versus markets that still need to develop

The presentation reports ₹210cr of CNG cascade orders and a separate ₹83cr PSU order announcement. These should not be added together without confirming overlap.

Hydrogen has tangible progress: approval for a 250-litre Type IV cylinder and a ₹2.5cr NTPC trial order. But management said large-scale hydrogen demand still needs to emerge, with a clearer assessment expected around mid-to-late 2027.

That is a demand-assessment timeline, not a promise of meaningful hydrogen revenue by that date.

The 14.2kg LPG variant has also slowed. Management is holding the related development spending for at least 3–4 months amid supply and geopolitical uncertainty. Existing LPG business continues, but the larger-format opportunity should not be treated as immediately available.

4) The margin plan is credible in mechanism, conditional in timing

Automation, fewer production locations, better machinery utilisation and solar power can reduce conversion costs.

Management estimated at least a 1-percentage-point EBITDA-margin benefit from power and manpower efficiencies in FY28, and cautioned that this was a rough estimate. Consolidation is expected to provide further benefits.

An analyst suggested that margins could reach about 15.5%; management agreed, but also referred to FY28–29 in its response. This is not a clean, dated 15.5% FY28 commitment.

The practical milestones are more useful:
• Silvassa IBC capacity is targeted to rise from 150,000 to 300,000 units a year by FY27-end.
• About ₹75cr of automation/product-renewal spending was identified for completion by March 2027.
• Solar savings should increase as partial-year benefits become available for a full year.

5) Cash generation supports investment, but asset-sale timing matters

Statutory H1 operating cash flow was ₹371.81cr. Cash spent on fixed assets was ₹174.08cr, leaving ₹197.73cr before asset-sale proceeds and financing flows.

There is a working-capital qualification: higher trade payables contributed ₹110.51cr of cash, while inventories and receivables absorbed cash. Continued collections and inventory discipline matter alongside profit growth.

Management discussed approximately ₹375cr of capex. Against that, ₹134cr of non-core assets had been identified, ₹18cr sold in H1 and the remaining ₹116cr targeted over 18–24 months.

Those sale proceeds cannot all be assumed to fund this year's spending. The timing of cash receipts and the return earned on new capacity will determine how efficiently the expansion is financed.

6) Keep the operating guide separate from the bigger ambition

Management retained 15% annual consolidated volume growth, supported by:
• Packaging: 11–13%
• Composite products: 25–30%
• PE pipes: 20–25%

H1 consolidated volume growth was 12.9%, so the annual target still requires stronger performance in the second half.

In Q&A, management also discussed composite-product revenue of ₹800–900cr this year, ₹2,500cr in three years and ₹4,000cr in five years.

The three-year aspiration implies roughly 41–46% annual revenue growth from the current-year estimate. That is substantially faster than the 25–30% volume guide. Prices, product mix, additional capacity and demand would have to bridge the difference. Treat the larger numbers as an ambition, not the base-case operating guide.

7) Diversification helps, but it does not remove regional and execution risk

Management said its Middle East business was down 25%, with other overseas regions compensating for the weakness.

PE pipes face a different issue: EPC customers must obtain revised prices and timely government payments before they can absorb higher polymer costs. Management sees improvement, but retained guidance still depends on that recovery.

A separate development after the call: on 7 November, the company announced a ₹35cr exclusive annual industrial-packaging contract with Saudi Arabia's CHEMANOL, through its wholly owned KSA subsidiary. Execution is within one year. It adds order visibility, but does not by itself establish a broader regional recovery.

Kyro Read

Time's strongest case is the combination of established packaging demand, expanding CNG/IBC volumes and lower conversion costs from automation.

The important evidence from here is whether volume growth accelerates, new capacity earns better returns and the margin benefits arrive without stretching working capital. Polymer-led sales growth, hydrogen optionality and long-range revenue ambitions deserve different levels of confidence.

OnEMI Technology Solutions (KISSHT) | A Digital Lending Company I’m Quite Bullish On

A company that was managing ₹4,000 Cr worth of loans in March 2025 has now crossed ₹10,000 Cr!

And its quarterly profit has doubled in just one year🔥🔥🔥

I’ve been going through Kissht’s latest results and management concall. I think this is becoming a very interesting fintech growth story.

What exactly does Kissht do?

You might know Kissht as an instant personal loan app.

But the actual business is much bigger.

Through its NBFC subsidiary and lending partners, Kissht provides personal loans and loans against property.

What impressed me is its technology.

The company uses an AI-based underwriting system analysing more than 7,200 variables to assess borrowers.

It has already served over 1.28 crore customers and works with 45+ lending partners.

And here’s the interesting part.

Around 55% of its loan portfolio was managed through lending partners rather than sitting directly on its own balance sheet in September.

This partnership-led model allows Kissht to expand its lending business without funding every rupee of loans itself.

Now look at the financial numbers.

FY26:

Revenue: ₹2,179 Cr

PAT: ₹281 Cr (+75% YoY)

Q2FY27:

Total Income: ₹740 Cr (+43% YoY)

PAT: ₹125 Cr (+100% YoY)

AUM: ₹9,317 Cr (+68% YoY)

Quarterly Disbursements: ₹4,612 Cr (+56% YoY)

And on 4 November, the company announced that its AUM had already crossed ₹10,000 Cr.

But what caught my attention wasn’t just the growth.

Credit quality is actually improving alongside it.

Gross NPA has reduced to 2.18%.

Net NPA stands at just 0.34%.

Credit cost has declined from 9.3% to 6.2% of average AUM over the past year.

For a digital lending company growing this quickly, these numbers are worth paying attention to.

Management’s Future Outlook

This is where I became more interested.

Management has increased its FY27 AUM growth guidance from 40%+ to 60%+.

It is also targeting:

• More than 15% YoY reduction in credit cost

• Return on Equity above 20%

• Gross NPA below 2.25%

• Further reduction in borrowing costs

The company recently raised another ₹832 Cr through a preferential issue, strengthening its capital base for expansion.

Management believes it can scale substantially further without another equity fundraise.

My Future View

I’m bullish on Kissht’s business growth over the next 2–3 years.

The combination of digital customer acquisition, AI-based underwriting, improving credit costs and lower borrowing expenses could create meaningful earnings growth.

My aggressive FY28 scenario is a loan portfolio of ₹18,000–20,000 Cr with PAT potentially reaching ₹650 Cr.

These are my estimates, not management guidance.

At around ₹354, Kissht commands a market cap of roughly ₹7,200 Cr.

Based on approximately ₹379 Cr trailing annual profit, that works out to around 19× earnings.

For a lender growing this quickly while delivering over 20% ROE, I find that valuation interesting.

The biggest risk is that more than 90% of its loan portfolio is still unsecured. A deterioration in borrower repayments could change the earnings picture quickly.

But my view remains positive.

I believe Kissht has the potential to become a much larger, highly profitable digital lending business if it maintains its underwriting discipline.

The most interesting part isn’t how quickly Kissht can give someone a loan. It’s how quickly it can scale that business without letting bad loans catch up.

That’s the story I’ll be tracking closely.

A reported holding value of approximately ₹121.7 crore makes Caliber Mining & Logistics the largest of the 11 new disclosures.

That is a substantial position.

The interesting aspect is its exposure to the mining services and logistics ecosystem.

Rather than simply betting on commodity prices, the business participates in the operational value chain of mining.
The investment thesis worth investigating:

Can increasing mining activity, operational scale and execution efficiencies translate into sustainable earnings growth and superior capital returns?
This deserves a closer look.

3/ PARAMOUNT COMMUNICATIONS: A BET ON POWER INFRASTRUCTURE?

Reported holding value: approximately ₹75.8 crore.

Paramount Communications operates in cables, including power, railway, telecom and specialised cable segments.

India's growing investments in:
• Power transmission and distribution
• Renewable energy
• Railways
• Industrial infrastructure
• Data and telecom connectivity

create an interesting demand environment.

The bigger opportunity is not simply revenue growth.

It is whether the company can improve margins, increase capacity utilisation and generate better returns on incremental capital.

4/ DHABRIYA POLYWOOD: THE BUILDING PRODUCTS OPPORTUNITY

Reported ownership: 5.6%.

This is the highest ownership percentage among the new additions.

Dhabriya Polywood operates in uPVC/PVC profiles, doors, windows and modular furniture.

The investment theme is interesting.

India's real estate development, premium housing, renovation and replacement markets could create structural demand for organised building products.

The key question: Can organised players capture market share from fragmented and unorganised competitors while maintaining healthy margins?

5/ PRECISION ENGINEERING: ANOTHER RECURRING THEME

Adroit Industries and Poojaa Precision Engineering are two other interesting additions.

Both provide exposure to specialised manufacturing and precision engineering.

These businesses can potentially benefit from:
• Increasing localisation
• Domestic manufacturing growth
• Industrial capex
• Automotive and engineering demand
• Customer qualification and specialised manufacturing capabilities

However, investors must examine customer concentration, order-book quality and cash-flow generation.

A growing order book does not automatically mean a growing shareholder return.

6/ THE PORTFOLIO IS NOT JUST ABOUT MANUFACTURING

Other additions provide exposure to different opportunities.

Glass Wall Systems adds exposure to glass and building systems.

Anawil Wire Engineering adds another industrial wire-related exposure.

Bai Kakaji Polymers provides exposure to polymer products.

QLine Biotech and Credent Connect N Care add healthcare-related exposure.

Maharaja Speedex adds another business to the portfolio's emerging small-company basket.

The common thread appears to be an interest in relatively specialised businesses rather than simply buying popular sectors.

7/ WHERE IS THE EXISTING PORTFOLIO CONCENTRATED?

The portfolio's largest disclosed positions are equally interesting.

Dynamatic Technologies – approximately ₹260 crore.
Jubilant Pharmova – approximately ₹178 crore.
Carysil – approximately ₹145 crore.
Technocraft Industries – approximately ₹141 crore.
IIFL Capital – approximately ₹136 crore.
Caliber Mining & Logistics – approximately ₹122 crore.
Stylam Industries – approximately ₹107 crore.
The Anup Engineering – approximately ₹103 crore.
Ion Exchange – approximately ₹87 crore.
All Time Plastics – approximately ₹81 crore.

The aggregate reported value of the 35 September holdings is approximately ₹2,158 crore.

A few observations stand out.

Dynamatic Technologies is the largest position, accounting for approximately 12.1% of the disclosed portfolio value.

The top five positions account for approximately 40%.

So, despite having 35 disclosed holdings, this is not an equally weighted portfolio.

There is meaningful concentration in selected companies.

8/ A STRONG MANUFACTURING AND INDUSTRIAL CAPEX ORIENTATION

Look at the combination:

Dynamatic Technologies – aerospace, hydraulics and automotive engineering.

Technocraft Industries – industrial manufacturing.

The Anup Engineering – process equipment.

Carysil – specialised kitchen and bath products.

Stylam Industries – decorative laminates.

All Time Plastics – consumer-oriented plastic products.

Paramount Communications – cables.

Adroit Industries – specialised engineering components.

Dhabriya Polywood – building products.

A discernible pattern emerges.

There is substantial exposure to companies that manufacture specialised products and participate in industrial, infrastructure, construction and consumption supply chains.

This is an interesting way of participating in India's manufacturing growth story.

But the quality of each business matters much more than the broad sector narrative.

9/ WHAT IS HE SELLING OR REDUCING?

Portfolio changes are not just about what an investor buys.

What an investor reduces can sometimes be equally revealing.

The most striking change is Rupa & Company.

Its reported holding has declined from 3.4% in June 2026 to 1.6% in September 2026.

That is a reduction of 1.8 percentage points in a single quarter.

The longer-term trend is even more interesting.

The holding was approximately 4.2% in September 2024.

Indogulf Cropsciences has also seen a reduction, from 4% to 3.5%.

Smaller reductions are visible in Technocraft Industries, Stylam Industries and HG Infra Engineering.

The portfolio also no longer shows Mastek, Suven Life Sciences and TTK Healthcare above the 1% disclosure threshold.

Himatsingka Seide, which had a 5.6% holding in March 2026, is also absent from the latest disclosure.

Important: These changes do not establish complete exits or explain the reasons behind the reductions. Falling below 1% simply means the holding is no longer visible under that disclosure threshold.

10/ WHAT DOES THIS PORTFOLIO TELL US?

I see four interesting investment preferences.

First: Niche manufacturing.

Specialised products, customer relationships, technical capabilities and entry barriers appear to be important themes.

Second: Emerging small-cap opportunities.

Several new positions are in relatively smaller listed companies. This could reflect an attempt to identify businesses before they become widely recognised.

Third: India's infrastructure and industrial capex cycle.

Power, cables, mining, engineering, construction products and industrial components feature prominently.

Fourth: Selective diversification.

Pharmaceuticals, financial services, agrochemicals and consumer-oriented manufacturing provide exposure to different economic drivers.

This is more interesting than simply describing the portfolio as a small-cap portfolio.

11/ SHOULD RETAIL INVESTORS FOLLOW THESE STOCKS?

Absolutely worth researching. But blindly copying the portfolio would be a mistake.

There are several questions investors should ask before investing:

• Is revenue growth translating into operating cash flow?

• Are ROCE and ROE improving?

• Is working capital under control?

• Are receivables and inventory growing faster than sales?

• Is the promoter demonstrating sound capital allocation?

• Are valuations reasonable relative to sustainable earnings growth?

• Is there adequate liquidity in the stock?

And perhaps the most important question:

What price did the investor pay, and what is the stock worth today?

A reported holding value tells us the market value of the disclosed shares, not the original investment cost or unrealised return.

Also, a new disclosure does not necessarily mean the entire position was purchased during the latest quarter. It could reflect an existing holding crossing the 1% reporting threshold.

Do your own research. Understand the business. Examine the financials. Check the valuation.

And never confuse a famous investor's ownership with a guaranteed investment opportunity.

Time technoplast 

The auto angle is supplying cylinders fitted inside vehicles to store CNG or hydrogen. Time already supplies CNG cascades for gas transportation; supplying vehicle manufacturers would open another customer base.

Why Morai matters: Previously, available cylinder capacity was prioritised for CNG cascades. In the February 2025 call, management explained that selling a complete cascade earns a margin on the cylinders plus piping and the assembled system. Expanded capacity gives it room to pursue standalone cylinders for vehicle manufacturers too. 

In the November 2025 call, management specifically mentioned approaching Tata, Eicher Motors and Ashok Leyland after expansion, with design and approval work taking time. Those were target customers—not confirmed wins.

The practical attraction is lighter fuel storage, potentially leaving more vehicle capacity for passengers/cargo. But the cylinder must fit the vehicle’s design, meet its requirements and qualify with the manufacturer.

For the thesis: auto is an additional growth opportunity, with revenue still to be proven. The next meaningful announcement would be a named OEM qualification, production nomination or supply order. The international plant visits alone do not establish an automotive win.

Tega Industries – Q2 FY27 Earnings Call Notes 

a few important developments, particularly around Molycop integration, margin improvement, cross-selling opportunities and debt reduction.

1. Legacy Tega business – healthy margin trajectory

H1 EBITDA margin improved to 20.4% from 19.7% YoY.
Gross margin improved to 61% from 59%.
Consumables EBITDA margin expanded to 22.4%, up 190 bps.
Equipment business returned to positive EBITDA in Q2 after reporting losses in Q1.
Management's longer-term margin ambition for the legacy business remains around 22%.

2. Molycop integration – margin improvement opportunity

Molycop delivered approximately 14% EBITDA margin in Q2.
Management is targeting another 100 bps margin improvement over the coming year through cost optimisation, manufacturing efficiencies, SG&A reduction and relocation of certain functions.
Molycop volume growth guidance remains around 5% annually.

3. Cross-selling – an interesting early development

Tega secured an initial 500-tonne trial order of Molycop grinding media from an existing mill-lining customer.
Successful conversion could translate into annualised supplies of 20,000–30,000 tonnes.
Management is exploring similar opportunities across multiple geographies.
Targeted cost synergies are approximately $2 million over 2–2.5 years.

This is an important opportunity to leverage Tega's existing customer relationships to expand Molycop's product reach.

4. Equipment business – guidance revised
FY27 equipment growth guidance reduced from 25% to 15%.
Delayed customer approvals and shipment clearances have impacted execution.
Management expects improvement in Q3 and Q4 as pending approvals come through.
EBITDA margin improved to approximately 2% in Q2 from negative territory in Q1.

5. Chile facility – commissioning timeline

Soft commissioning expected around January 2027.
Commercial production targeted for March 2027.
The facility is being developed to support the next 4–5 years of anticipated growth.
Management expects the new facility to support the broader growth trajectory rather than contribute significantly to FY28 revenue independently.

6. Order book and execution visibility

Consolidated order book, excluding Molycop grinding media, stood at ₹1,397.6 crore.
Approximately ₹1,157.6 crore is executable within the next 12 months.t his provides reasonable execution visibility for the legacy business.

7. Debt and balance sheet – the biggest monitorable

Consolidated gross borrowings: approximately ₹11,492 crore.
Net debt: approximately ₹10,461 crore.
Around 96% of borrowings are long-term.
Management has made deleveraging its top financial priority.
₹100 crore of term debt was repaid in October using preferential issue proceeds.
Non-core asset monetisation is underway, with proceeds expected over the coming 12–18 months.

8. Important Q&A and  concerns

Grasberg and Cobre Panama recovery: Molycop's 5% volume growth guidance remains unchanged. Recovery at these mines could provide additional upside.

Finance costs: Management expects debt reduction through operating cash flows and asset monetisation.

Derivative liability: The ₹710 crore accounting liability relates to Apollo's non-controlling interest and buyout options; it should not be confused with an immediate cash payment.

Acquisition-related expenses: H1 included substantial one-off transaction costs. Management indicated that significant additional one-time expenses are not expected from Q3 onwards.

Adjusted H1 PAT, excluding one-time items, was approximately ₹45.2 crore.

9. Longer-term margin guidance

Management's longer-term consolidated EBITDA margin ambition is 17–18%, with a potential timeline of 2–5 years.

The key drivers would be:

Molycop margin improvement.
Cross-selling synergies.
Operating efficiencies.
Recovery in equipment business.
Better utilisation of the expanded manufacturing footprint.

My Final perspectives after Q2 results : 
Tega is entering an important integration phase following the Molycop acquisition.

The opportunity is no longer just about increasing scale. It is about extracting synergies, improving margins, leveraging the combined global customer base and generating stronger cash flows.

The initial cross-selling opportunity is encouraging, the legacy business continues to demonstrate healthy margins, and Molycop has room for further operational improvement.

However, deleveraging remains the biggest monitorable. Debt reduction, cash-flow generation and successful integration will determine how much value the acquisition ultimately creates.

The next 2–3 quarters will be important to track equipment recovery, Chile commissioning, Molycop margin expansion, cross-selling conversions and progress on debt reduction.

Worth tracking closely. The Molycop integration story is now entering its next phase.

🇸🇮 45,3 %
🇫🇮 42,5 %
🇸🇪 41,1 %
🇩🇰 35,8 %

Če pa merimo vse davčne prihodke glede na BDP, imajo nordijske države res visoke obremenitve — Danska 45,2 %, Finska 42,2 %, Švedska 41,4 %, Slovenija 38,3 % v letu 2024. Toda njihova struktura davkov je drugačna; na Danskem so na primer prihodki iz socialnih prispevkov minimalni. 

Skandinavski model torej ni preprosto: »še bolj obdavčimo plače in bogate«. Delavcu praviloma ostane več od ustvarjene plače, država pa prihodke pobira širše – med drugim z višjo obdavčitvijo potrošnje, ki pa si jo lahko privoscijo, ker jim ostane vec od place. 
Tudi davek od dobička podjetij pri njih ni višji – Slovenija 22 %, Danska in Norveška 22 %, Švedska 20,6 %, Finska 20 %.

Poleg tega se v Sloveniji podjetniški dobiček obdavči dvakrat.

Od 100 € dobička podjetje najprej plača 22 € DDPO. Od preostalih 78 € lastnik ob izplačilu dividende plača še 25 %. Na koncu mu ostane 58,50 €.

Švedska ima za dividende lastnikov manjših podjetij pod določenimi pogoji 20-odstotno stopnjo, Finska pa ima za del dividend nejavnih podjetij lahko efektivno stopnjo le 7,5–8,5 %.

Zato je zelo pomembno kaj in koliko obremenjujemo — posebej visoko produktivno delo, saj visok standard ustvarjajo predvsem produktivnost, konkurenčnost in učinkovita država – ne čim višji davki.

Z Norvesko ne bom izgubljala casa, ker zaradi nafte ni primerljiva.

Lep pozdrav od Polonce!

Vedanta Aluminium Metal Ltd - Q2/H1FY27 | Concall Insights

Performance
•Q2 revenue ₹22,066 cr (+41% YoY, +5% QoQ)
•Aluminium production record 649 kt (+5% YoY, +3% QoQ); alumina 895 kt (+37% YoY, +8% QoQ)
•Value-added production record 432 kt (+31% YoY, +11% QoQ); domestic sales record 338 kt
•NEP improved to $453/t (vs $205/t YoY)
•EBITDA ₹10,192 cr (+83% YoY); PAT ₹6,187 cr (more than doubled YoY)
•Net debt reduced by ~₹3,090 cr to ₹26,442 cr; net debt/EBITDA improved to 0.7x
•ROCE ~60%; cash & equivalents ₹6,318 cr; dividend ₹8/share paid
•Hot metal cost $1,722/t (slightly up QoQ on carbon/fuel inflation)

Volume & Integration Roadmap
•Balco Potline 3: 50% pots in full production; full capacity run-rate by year-end (target 435 ktpa exit)
•Lanjigarh alumina ramp: targeting +10% incremental refinery output in each of Q3 and Q4 to reach designed capacity; captive alumina mix to ~85% by year-end
•Sigimali bauxite: CTO obtained; targeting 1 mt this year and 5 mt in FY28 (EC 9 mt)
•Karnalpat bauxite block: preferred bidder status secured; supports future expansion
•Captive coal: Kudloi shovel on ground; Gogarpali targeted for Q4 start; Jamkhani already contributing ~2.5 mt; captive coal contribution rising
•Target hot metal cost ~$1,550/t and VAP mix >90% post project completion and de-bottlenecking
•RE mix rising (367 MW in H1; targeting >400 MW for full year)

Growth Visibility & Expansion
•Scaling toward 3 mt aluminium and 5 mt alumina capacity
•Next phase of volume growth driven by Balco Potline 3 full ramp + Lanjigarh alumina increase
•Further expansion (up to 3 mt additional aluminium in medium term) at advanced land-acquisition stage for both smelter (~1,450 acres) and refinery (~400 acres); layout configured on 525 kA potlines (replicating Balco execution at ~$2,100/t capital intensity for smelter)
•India aluminium demand expected to grow ~40% between CY25–CY30; company positioned as one of the largest global producers at targeted capacity
•Expect to exit the year at ~$5 bn EBITDA run-rate at current LMEs + planned VAP mix and cost levels
•Cost reduction of ~$100/t expected by year-exit from captive bauxite/coal ramp and operational levers (Q3 costs elevated due to power plant shutdowns)
•Hedged 22% of balance-year volumes at avg $3,274/t
•Capital allocation: cash generation supports deleveraging, growth CapEx and dividends (3–5% yield guidance range); further expansion CapEx to start post land allotment
•Overall, record volumes and strong VAP/domestic mix driving earnings; clear multi-year visibility from Balco/Lanjigarh ramp, captive bauxite & coal integration, and medium-term capacity expansion toward 3 mt aluminium.

@gaze_observer Digi Lenders clocking up to 50% revenue growth with names like Kissht, Moneyview, and Paytm leading the charge shows massive credit demand, though the rising indebtedness definitely warrants some caution. You and @GauravTejwani13 rare the two accounts I most enjoy following.

Digi Lenders Clock 50% Revenue Growth as Credit Demand Surges: Kissht, Moneyview, MobiKwik and Paytm Report 41-49% Revenue Growth in September Quarter; Retail NBFC Lending Up 21.9% as Rising Indebtedness Sparks Caution

Core Theme 
Digital lenders are growing 41-49% as banks’ slower pace in unsecured credit leaves younger and self-employed borrowers to fintechs, with disbursements surging across Kissht, Moneyview and MobiKwik, though the faster rise in retail borrowing across the system is prompting caution about rising indebtedness.

The Growth: Fintech Scorecard
Listed new-age fintech companies reported 40-50% growth in lending and financial services revenue in the September quarter, driven by strong loan disbursements and rising demand for unsecured credit from younger borrowers

Kissht: revenue from operations rose 44.7% YoY to ₹732 crore; Q2 disbursals ₹4,612 crore; AUM ₹9,317 crore

Moneyview: revenue grew 41% to ₹1,120 crore; Q2 disbursals ₹7,701 crore; AUM ₹23,892 crore

MobiKwik: financial services revenue increased 41.8% to ₹87 crore; Q2 disbursals ₹1,083 crore

Paytm: financial services distribution revenue grew 49.3% to ₹912 crore (includes broking and wealth products; revenue metrics not directly comparable across companies)

Loan Disbursements: The Pace
Moneyview facilitated loans worth ₹7,701 crore in the quarter, up 41.3% YoY

Kissht’s disbursements rose 56% to ₹4,612 crore

MobiKwik reported a 34% increase to ₹1,083 crore

The figures include loans originated through lending partners as well as their own NBFC subsidiaries

Moneyview, which primarily serves consumers outside India’s largest cities, said about 75% of its lending capital comes from partner institutions, allowing it to expand without proportionally increasing its own balance sheet

Broader Credit Backdrop
The growth reflects a broader expansion in household and small-business credit, a key indicator of domestic consumption and economic activity

According to the RBI, retail lending by non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) grew 21.9% YoY in September, compared with 16.8% a year earlier

Banks’ personal loan portfolios expanded 17.3% during the same period, against 11.5% last year

Larger Lenders Also Benefiting
Bajaj Finance reported a 26% increase in AUM to ₹5.85 lakh crore, booking 13.45 million new loans, up 11%; quarterly disbursements jumped 47% to ₹35,872 crore

Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company’s AUM grew 25% to ₹2.68 lakh crore

Why Fintechs Are Winning
Jinay Gala, director at India Ratings & Research: the relatively smaller base of digital lenders and their ability to reach borrowers underserved by traditional financial institutions were driving faster growth

“Banks have been slow on personal loans and unsecured lending, allowing fintechs to serve more self-employed and Gen Z borrowers,” he said

ET Insight: by capturing the Gen Z wallet, digital platforms have positioned themselves as the primary gatekeepers of future retail consumption

Secondary Fluid Networks (SFN): The Critical Circulation Infrastructure

👉 As AI rack densities rise, cooling is no longer just about cold plates and CDUs. Secondary Fluid Networks (SFNs) connect CDUs to liquid-cooled IT equipment, enabling reliable coolant circulation.

👉 The ecosystem includes:
  → Stainless steel piping and flow systems
  → Flexible metal hoses
  → Metal bellows and expansion joints
  → Precision fittings and leak-resistant connectors

👉 Every liquid-cooling system needs a dependable circulation network. The opportunity extends beyond cooling equipment to the precision-engineered components that connect the entire system.
👉 Listed Indian companies to track:
  1. Aeroflex Industries - Stainless-steel flexible hoses, SFN skid assemblies, metallic bellows and fluid connections.

Di jalan, kami beli sarapan buat suamiku seharga Rp10 ribu. Tapi di tengah perjalanan, ban belakang motorku bocor. Akhirnya kami tuntun motor. Suamiku menyeberang duluan buat tanya apakah bannya bisa ditambal. Dari kejauhan terlihat tukang tambalnya seorang kakek yang sedang tidur. Setelah bertanya, suamiku kembali dan bilang kalau bannya bisa dikerjakan.

Sebagai informasi, penglihatan si kakek sepertinya sudah agak berkurang. Kenapa aku bilang begitu? Karena setelah suamiku menyeberang kembali ke tempatku, si kakek masih terlihat berbicara sambil mengarahkan motor dan memperagakan sesuatu dengan tangannya. Sepertinya beliau mengira suamiku masih ada di sana, padahal sudah menyeberang. Dari awal aku sebenarnya agak ragu apakah kakek itu masih sanggup mengerjakannya karena penglihatannya sudah berkurang.

Tapi ya sudahlah, karena memang nggak ada pilihan lain, akhirnya aku biarkan si kakek mengerjakan motor kami. Singkat cerita, bannya dibuka. Entah karena ban dalamku memang sudah terlalu banyak tambalan atau karena si kakek sudah nggak kuat menambal, akhirnya beliau menawarkan ban dalam bekas miliknya yang juga sudah pernah ditambal, tapi katanya masih bagus. Dengan sigap, si nenek langsung membantu suaminya mengerjakan ban motor. Berkali-kali aku bilang ke suamiku, "Kamu bantu aja biar cepat, kasihan kakeknya." Suamiku juga beberapa kali menawarkan bantuan, tapi selalu ditolak sama si kakek.

Morning.

Last week in Indian markets was one trade, and it was oil. Brent closed 30 October at $117.64. This morning it is about $97.30. That is a fall of more than 16% in a week, the steepest since the early Covid period, and it happened because Washington and Tehran started talking. Trump said renewed strikes on Iran are "highly unlikely" if a strong deal comes through, with the nuclear programme and the Strait of Hormuz reportedly both on the table.

Everything else here was downstream of that. The Nifty rose about 8.4% on the week to 24,986, the Sensex had its best week since February 2021, the rupee jumped 1.2% to 93.91, its strongest since April, and foreigners bought Rs 48,263 crore of equities. The shape of it matters: this is an FII-led, crude-led rally priced on a deal nobody has signed.

Gold and silver had a good week and a weak Friday. MCX December gold closed at Rs 1,42,224 per 10g and silver at Rs 1,84,095 a kg, both up on the week, both knocked back once strong US payrolls lifted the dollar. Base metals are the soft spot, with copper weak and Chinese credit growth projected to drop sharply this month. For India, cheaper crude reads the familiar way: better for paints, tyres, aviation and the oil marketers, worse for upstream realisations, and quietly helpful for the current account.

Asia is repairing this morning after an ugly Friday, Nikkei up about 3.1% and Kospi 1.3%, having fallen 6% and tripped a circuit breaker respectively in a global AI selloff. GIFT Nifty is around 25,080. The US 10-year sits near 4.87% and the market still prices roughly a 70% chance the Fed hikes in December.

On the names, Tata Steel is the print to look at: consolidated profit up 16% to Rs 3,700 crore, EBITDA of Rs 10,665 crore, margin up 90 basis points to 16.1%, volumes doing the work against softer prices. Divi's Labs put up a big quarter with profit up 64% to Rs 1,127 crore. Tata Chemicals went the other way, a Rs 50 crore loss against a Rs 154 crore profit last year. Nuvama moved Tata Steel, Hindalco and Power Grid to Buy. On the primary side, Hindustan Coca-Cola Holdings filed its DRHP for a pure offer for sale of 99.75 crore shares.

Three things to watch today. One, any headline out of the Iran talks, because that is the hinge under crude, the rupee and the index. Two, the US CPI print tomorrow, which lands while we are shut for Balipratipada, so Wednesday opens on a gap. Three, India's October CPI on Thursday, where consensus sits near 5.93% and some forecasts go to 6.2%, against the RBI's 6% upper tolerance. India VIX closed up 20% at 18.43.

🇮🇳 INDIA MARKETS — BEFORE THE OPEN
Monday, November 9

THE SETUP

Samvat 2083 starts today.
It is the first full trading day after Diwali.

GIFT Nifty points to a higher start.
It was near 25,058 at 8:06 am IST.
That is above Sunday's Nifty close.

Asia is mostly higher this morning.
Japan is up about 2.5%.
Taiwan is also up strongly.
Korea is only slightly higher.

Wall Street ended Friday mixed.
The Nasdaq rose 1.1%.
The S&P 500 rose 0.3%.
The Dow fell 0.5%.
All three still fell for the week.

America added 165,000 jobs in October.
That was far above the 65,000 expected.
The jobless rate fell to 4.1%.
Markets now see a higher chance
of a US rate rise in December.

Oil has eased this morning.
Brent is near $97.5 a barrel.
That is down nearly 1%.
President Trump said fresh attacks on Iran
are highly unlikely while talks progress.
Shipping trouble near Hormuz still keeps risk alive.

The rupee is steady near 93.90 to the dollar.
That is its strongest level in over six months.
It gained 1.1% last week.

Foreign investors have bought
over $4.1 billion of Indian shares in November.
That is already the biggest month
since September 2024.

YESTERDAY IN ONE LINE

Sunday's one-hour Muhurat session ended slightly lower — Sensex 80,999.40, down 0.04%, and Nifty 24,986.40, down 0.18%, after seven straight sessions of gains.

WHAT TO WATCH TODAY

Profit-taking after a sharp run.
The two main indices rose about 10.5%
in seven sessions to Friday.
Volatility rose too.
India VIX jumped 5.5% to 18.43.

Weekend results come into focus.
Divi's Laboratories profit rose 63.6%
to ₹1,127 crore.
Tata Steel profit rose 16.2%
to ₹3,700 crore.
Siemens profit rose about 4%
to ₹504 crore.
Tata Chemicals posted a ₹50 crore loss.

Pharma shares face a new rule today.
A 30% trade-margin cap takes effect
on 137 anti-cancer drugs.
The government expects big price cuts
for patients.

58 companies report results today.
They include MRF,
Cochin Shipyard,
Olectra Greentech,
Whirlpool of India,
and Titagarh Rail Systems.

BHEL has a new Power Grid order
worth ₹600 crore to ₹900 crore.

It is a short week.
Markets are shut tomorrow, Tuesday,
for Diwali-Balipratipada.
US inflation data also lands Tuesday.
That will shape the US rate view.

THE ONE THING THAT MATTERS MOST

Oil, then the rupee, then inflation.

Brent near $97 is still high for India.
India buys most of its oil from abroad.
If oil rises again on Hormuz trouble,
the import bill rises,
the rupee comes under pressure,
and inflation becomes harder to control.

If oil stays lower,
the rupee stays supported,
and foreign inflows have room to continue.

That chain decides the tone today.

A domestic dispute turned fatal in Ahmedabad's Naroda area after a 34-year-old woman allegedly stabbed her 39-year-old husband, Dilip Kharadi, a retired Army serviceman, to death with a kitchen knife.

According to reports, the incident took place late Thursday night, November 5, at the couple's residence in Naroda Smart City-2. 

The couple had reportedly been having frequent arguments for nearly a year over household responsibilities, food preferences and financial matters.

The immediate trigger was reportedly a disagreement over dinner. Dilip allegedly questioned his wife, Nirmala Kharadi, about the vegetable she had prepared. 

What began as a verbal argument reportedly escalated into a heated confrontation, during which Nirmala allegedly picked up a kitchen knife and stabbed him on the left side of his chest.

Following the attack, Nirmala reportedly informed her brother-in-law about the stabbing and took Dilip to Shalby Hospital. 

However, he succumbed to his injuries. His father later noticed the stab wound on his chest, along with other injuries on his body.

Dilip had retired from the Army in 2022 and was subsequently working as a contractual driver with the Gujarat Mineral Development Corporation (GMDC). The couple also had two children.

Following the incident, Naroda Police launched an investigation and arrested Nirmala within hours, reportedly using CCTV footage and intelligence inputs. 

A murder case has been registered against her under Section 103(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), along with relevant provisions of the Gujarat Police Act.

The investigation is underway to establish the exact circumstances leading to the fatal confrontation.

A domestic disagreement has now left two children without their father, while their mother remains in police custody.

1. Strong H1 FY27

Revenue 950 Cr (+29.9%)
EBITDA 294 Cr (+35.5%)
PAT 189 Cr (+35.8%)
EBITDA margin 30.9% (+127 bps)
Volume +24%; realisation +4.8% to 260/kg.

2. Diversification :

CV: 33% / strong domestic growth; exports subdued.
Farm equipment: 31% / growth above 20%.
Industrials: 16% / growth above 50%.
Off-highway: 12% / growth above 50%.
PV: 9% / revenue almost doubled YoY.
Forged & machined products now contribute 90% of sales versus 88% last year, reflecting increasing value addition.

3. Heavy-component opportunity: 650 Cr capex

300 Cr heavy hammer line: 2,000 tonnes/month capacity; components weighing 300 kg–3 tonnes.

200 Cr dedicated machining lines for heavy-engine applications.
150 Cr vertical upsetter for North American high-horsepower tractors and wind.

Order visibility & timeline
~300 Cr annual secured business for a dedicated machining programme, with visibility till 2033.💡

~1,000 Cr additional under discussion.
Mgmt aims to close nearly 500 Cr of orders by FY-end.
Cold trials expected Jan–Feb; hot trials around March.
Sample submissions in FY28; revenue contribution expected from Q3/Q4 FY28.

The heavy hammer line is fungible, catering to data centres, large engines, oil & gas, wind, marine and mining—not just data centres.

4. Another 500 Cr expansion

70% towards machining; 30% towards forging/small press lines.

Land already acquired.
Execution across FY28–FY29.
Focus: PV, industrials and CV exports.
Combined expansion adds 59,000 MT forging and 34,000 MT machining capacity over 2–2.5 years, taking planned capacity to approximately 2.17 lakh MT and 1.16 lakh MT respectively.

5. Existing business triggers

North American PV: 4,000-tonne line commissioned; 80–100 Cr projected revenue. Shipments in transit expected to contribute from Q3.

North American CV: ~80 Cr secured business in trials/testing with a global engine manufacturer.

Industrials: strong opportunities in gensets, gas engines, oil & gas, wind, mining, marine and railways.

Farm equipment: market share increased from 42% to 46%; new programme ramp-up began only 2–3 months ago.

European CV: potential supply-chain opportunity following a customer's acquisition; discussions ongoing, likely a 2–3-year opportunity.

6. Guidance : 
FY27 volume: Mgmt expects to meet its high teen volume growth guidance.

FY27 margins: Expected broadly around FY26 levels, despite stronger H1 margins.
EBITDA/kg: Expects absolute EBITDA/kg to be maintained or improve in H2; gross margin and EBITDA/kg expected to trend upwards, supported by product mix, value addition and efficiencies.

Growth: Mgmt sees strong demand across key verticals and expects recent customer wins/programmes to ramp up.

Long-term ambition: Combined growth initiatives could add revenue equivalent to the current business over 3–4 years. 

Capacity: Heavy-forging capacity should be adequate for 4–5 years; machining is likely to become the next constraint.

7. Margin and cost levers
~80% of cost increases passed through; domestic OEMs have largely compensated the increases.

Export freight costs had nearly doubled in the previous quarter but were softening.
33.5 MW renewable energy project ~90% complete; generation expected in Q4 and meaningful contribution from Q1 next year.
Mgmt estimates ~30 Cr annual power savings.

8. Balance sheet
H1 operating cash flow 124 Cr; capex 78 Cr.

Cash/liquid reserves ~350 Cr.
Net debt/equity 0.08.
Working capital impacted by higher receivables and 35 Cr supplier advances; expects normalisation over the full year.
New 500 Cr capex may involve up to 300 Cr debt; actual utilisation could be lower depending on internal liquidity.

Happy Forgings: What is driving margin expansion?

H1 FY27 EBITDA margin improved 127 bps to 30.9%, from 29.7% last year. Gross margin expanded 161 bps to 60.8%.

Key drivers 👉

Higher value addition: Forged & machined components increased to 90% of H1 sales mix, from 88%. More machining means a greater share of value-added products.

Better realisations: H1 realisation increased 4.8% to 260/kg, supported by raw-material pass-through, conversion-cost-linked price hikes and product mix.

Operational efficiency: Better capacity utilisation, execution and operating leverage supported per-unit profitability.

Diversified product mix: Higher contributions from passenger vehicles, industrials and off-highway segments supported the overall business mix.

Evidence: H1 EBITDA/kg increased 9.3% to 80, while EBITDA grew 35.5% against revenue growth of 29.9%.

Margin improvement is being supported by a shift towards higher value-added machining, better realisations and operating efficiency—not just volume growth.

Q2 EBITDA margin was 30.6%, broadly flat YoY at 30.7%. The 127 bps expansion is for H1 FY27.

Happy Forgings: Moving up the value chain 💡

One important shift in Happy Forgings' business is the increasing contribution of forged & machined components.

Product mix – H1 FY27
• Forged & machined: 90% of revenue, up from 88% in H1 FY26.
• Forged-only products: 10%, down from 12%.

Why does this matter?
Machining involves further processing a forged component to meet precise customer specifications. Happy Forgings is therefore supplying more finished, value-added components rather than just forged parts.💡

Diversification is improving too:
• Passenger vehicles: 9% vs 5%
• Industrials: 16% vs 13%
• Off-highway: 12% vs 10%

Commercial vehicles' share declined to 33% from 37%, while farm equipment stood at 31%.

👉Two structural shifts are underway — higher value addition through machining and a broader end-market mix.
This is an important indicator to track as the company expands its precision machining capabilities and enters more complex applications.

Happy Forgings: Lets Understanding the business.

What does Happy Forgings do?

It converts raw steel into critical, precision-engineered components used in trucks, cars, tractors, industrial engines, power generation, wind and mining equipment.

How does it make money?

Forging: Shapes heated steel using powerful presses.
Machining: Converts forged parts into precision-finished components ready for OEMs.

What makes it special?💡

• High entry barriers: Expensive machinery, strict quality standards and lengthy OEM approval processes.
• Precision engineering: Manufactures safety-critical components with tight tolerances.💡
• Vertical integration: In-house forging, machining, heat treatment, testing and die design.
• Value addition: Machined products now contribute 90% of H1 FY27 revenue.
• Diversification: Growing presence in PV, industrials and off-highway segments.
Key growth triggers:👉
• 650 Cr investment in ultra-heavy component manufacturing.
• Additional 500 Cr capex, primarily towards machining.
• Entry into heavier components for data centres, power generation, wind, marine and mining.
• Rising contribution from passenger vehicles and industrials.
• Increasing machining capacity and higher-value products.

The bigger story: 
Happy Forgings is transitioning from a forging-led manufacturer to a precision-engineered, high-value component supplier.
The opportunity lies in moving up the value chain, entering new applications and deepening relationships with global OEMs.

Execution, capacity utilisation and returns on fresh capex remain key monitorables.

While in Tier-1 cities, you can find dozens of good schools. But once you move to Tier-3/4 towns or villages, you might find only a handful of genuinely good schools.

Millions of families in India belong to the middle-class and below-middle-class segments. Some struggle to make ends meet every month, while others manage to move one step at a time, create opportunities and help their children succeed.

The same applies to listed companies. We have thousands of them, but many will disappear or fail over the next 7–10 years. A handful, however, will go on to become much bigger businesses.

What's the common characteristic here?

Maybe God's divine blessings or a bit of luck. But, more often than not, it comes down to hard work, discipline and managing things better.

One word that captures all these attributes is MANAGEMENT.

The headmaster/headmistress and a handful of dedicated teachers would have made all the difference to those few good schools. Similarly, disciplined, hardworking and financially conscious parents would have made the difference to those families and their children's futures.

We keep looking for good stock ideas. Perhaps we should change the starting point.

Look for good management teams with ethics, hunger, aspiration and a willingness to work hard. These are the businesses that have the potential to create consistent wealth for shareholders.

Laurus Labs, Sansera Engineering, Sona BLW, Innomet Advanced and OBSC Perfection are a few examples.

Listen to their concalls, follow their media interactions and observe their behavior. Look for signs of inconsistency, lack of discipline, excessive storytelling or capital misallocation. Equally importantly, look for evidence that management walks the talk.

When you don't find these red flags and continue to see evidence of execution, you know you have a business worth shortlisting.

Once we shortlist a company, at what valuation to buy and at what valuation to sell is a personal choice, driven by conviction and data.

But perhaps we should change the sequence. Start with management, hunger and aspiration. Don't start with valuations and PAT.

Timepass talk on a Diwali!

1. Between the Lines: Signals from the Concall Room 

Divi's Laboratories: "...with the futuristic capacity, we will be in the top 3 players [in Peptides SPPS]..."

KSH International: "...EBITDA per tonne of approximately ₹85,000 per tonne should be sustainable..."

Azad Engineering: "...All 6 customer-dedicated facilities are now commissioned— 44,800 square meters for 4 global OEMs namely Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, GE, Vanova, Siemens Energy, and Baker Hughes.

Sigma Advanced Systems: "...the fundraise is primarily to fuel our growth coming in from M&A, right, new acquisitions. We've been working on multiple opportunities over the last 6 to 8 months, and I think next quarter, Q4, is when we expect to close these transactions..."

VA Tech Wabag: "...Our order book has surpassed ₹20,000 crores, while our net cash position has surpassed ₹1,000 crores, achieving record levels in both parameters. 

Aditya Infotech: "...In the 12 months to September 2026, our share of the total market including the unorganized segment was about 42%, which at the time of our IPO was 30%...In October, we repaid all our borrowings, and now the company is debt-free..."

Sansera Engineering: "...I'm happy to say we have already won in this quarter our first business from Safran...in the semiconductor business, we are making good progress towards adding the customer number 2..."

2. Timex Group India - Shared on June 7th, see below for the latest update

Financial Year 2025-26 marked a structural turning point for Timex Group, ending as a milestone year that fundamentally transformed the company's scale and profitability profile. Total revenue surged 48% year-on-year to ₹800 crore.

The growth was driven by a decisive shift toward premiumization. The core Timex brand expanded 62%, fashion powerhouse Guess grew 51%, and luxury anchor Versace delivered 48% growth. At the same time, e-commerce and quick commerce channels recorded a phenomenal 90% increase, highlighting the strength of the company's omnichannel strategy.

More importantly, profitability significantly outpaced revenue growth as operating leverage began to play out.

What makes this performance particularly noteworthy is that it was not driven by a single exceptional quarter. Revenue growth remained consistently strong throughout the year, with Q1 growing 55% YoY, Q2 40%, Q3 26%, and Q4 an impressive 74% YoY.

The company's sales strategy appears to be creating a sustainable high-growth trajectory. Historically, Q2 has been the strongest quarter due to festive-season bookings, while the remaining quarters were relatively subdued. This year, however, Q4 revenue reached almost 96% of Q2 levels, indicating a far more balanced and resilient demand profile across the year.

What to Expect in FY27 and FY28?

Management is positioning the company to enter the ₹1,100-1200-crore revenue club, targeting a base-case growth rate of 35-40%. This expansion will be supported by a significant increase in local manufacturing capacity, which is expected to rise from 6 million units to 10 million units annually.

While the company continues to prioritize growth, EBITDA margins are expected to stabilize in the 15–16% range. Additionally, employee expenses and administrative overheads appear to have largely normalized, creating the potential for substantial operating leverage as revenues continue to scale.

Latest update (post Q2FY27):

Posted highest-ever quarterly revenue of ₹359 crores. E-commerce grew 75% in Q2, led by Flipkart, Myntra, Amazon, 3P and quick commerce.

The Baddi plant is operating at 100% capacity (6 million units/year) and ran double shifts to meet demand. Investing $1.2 million to double the Baddi plant's capacity to 12 million units by May of next year.

In the ₹2,000–10,000 segment, the competitive landscape is largely a duopoly between Titan and Timex. While Titan's core brand business is still nearly 4x the size of Timex, management sees significant headroom to capture market share and scale up.

The company sees a potential to reach an EBITDA margin of ~20% in the future through operating leverage.

Last but not least, festive season shopping fell in Q2 last year, whereas this year it has shifted to Q3. Hence, do expect some fireworks in Q3FY27!

3. Navin Fluorine

How they make money:

Navin earns its revenue from three verticals. The business operates across i) High Performance Products (refrigerants and inorganic fluorides) - 51%, ii) Specialty Chemicals (agrochemical and industrial intermediates) - 30%, and iii) CDMO (pharma synthesis) with emerging Advanced Materials - 19%.

HPP (High Performance Products) is the biggest and covers refrigerant gases (HFCs, R32 coming), AHF/HF sold to merchant and high-purity buyers, and the HFO supply contract with Solstice Advanced Materials (the old Honeywell/Orchid business), which is a pass-through-priced, long-tenure contract on a dedicated asset.

Specialty Chemicals is mostly agrochemical and fluorination intermediates made in the multi-purpose plants (MPP-1/MPP-2) at Dahej on a campaign basis. It is running at roughly a ₹350 cr per quarter run rate, and the Nectar/Chemours project is being added.

CDMO is largely Fermion/darolutamide, made in dedicated cGMP plants, with a USD100M target for FY27 and a pipeline of other molecules behind it. Advanced Materials (data centres, semiconductors, defence, the DRDO/TDF project) is being incubated as a fourth vertical, expected to be 10-15% of the pie by 2030.

What’s working well:

Q2 revenue was ₹1,191 cr (+57% YoY), EBITDA ₹407 cr (+66%) at a 34.2% margin, and PAT ₹269 cr (+81%). H1 PAT of ₹513 cr already gives an EPS of ₹100. All three segments grew sequentially.

HPP benefited from better refrigerant gas placement than the market average, the AHF plant ramping, and higher HFO volumes.

Specialty gained from squeezing more campaigns out of existing MPP plants, and CDMO from the Fermion base plus new qualification campaigns. Gross profit held despite input inflation because forex tailwinds, pricing actions, operating leverage and efficiency gains offset sourcing costs. Working capital is at 72 days, capex is funded comfortably (H1 capex was about ₹300 cr), and the Solstice HFO contract was extended from 7 to 11 years (to December 2032) with about USD180M of added revenue potential. This protects the base beyond FY28, though the implied ~USD45M/yr run rate versus the earlier ~USD58M drew few "ouch" comments. Management says the pass-through pricing makes simple averaging misleading and that volumes are guaranteed higher.

What to expect for the rest of FY27 and FY28:

Management guided FY27 margins to stay in the H1 range (~34%), while keeping the long-term 30% EBITDA guidance unchanged. Q3 and Q4 should add several visible steps. The MPP debottlenecking (commissioned end-September) is not yet in the numbers, and R32 should give incremental revenue in Q3 with a full ramp in Q4. The Chemours project is due in Q3 with orders already in hand, and cGMP-4 Phase 2 (~₹125 cr) should start by the end of Q4.

Specialty should reach about 60-65% of Nectar’s peak annual revenue in FY27, with the rest in FY28, and CDMO should reach the USD100M order-book target. FY27 capex is guided at about ₹700 cr, at the low end of the ₹700-1,000 cr annual frame. Management says FY28 growth is “pretty much baked in” from the capex already in place, so expect continued 20-25% type growth, with cGMP-4 (₹900-1,000 cr peak potential, split across Phase 1 and Phase 2) mostly a FY28-FY29 story.

Advanced Materials adoption capacity arrives by Q2 FY28. The main swing factors are geopolitics and input costs (fluorspar, sulphur and gas are all rising), the pace of AHF utilisation, how much of the current refrigerant pricing proves durable, and whether Chemours adoption (a ~15-month read after commissioning) justifies the larger scale-up.

4. Innomet Advanced

How they make money

Innomet is a Hyderabad-based maker of engineered metal products with two divisions.

i) Metal powders (about ₹38 cr in H1, roughly 68% of revenue) are specialty powders sold by weight to parts makers, additive manufacturing and surface-coating customers. Almost 100% of this is water-atomised, and gas-atomised spherical powder has only just started with a 50 kg unit. Realisation rose from ₹959 to ₹1,487/kg.

ii) Tungsten heavy alloys (THA) (₹17.6 cr, about a third of revenue) are dense, high-value parts and fragments for defence (Pinaka, Astra), aerospace (AS9100D-certified) and other niche uses, sold per piece or per kg (₹25,000-35,000/kg indicated), with about 87% exported. Tungsten feedstock is now partly captured through the 57.5% acquisition of Swastik Tungsten, which was consolidated only for the last few days of H1. Exports were 46% of H1 revenue, against 15% a year ago. Management gave segment EBITDA margins of about 12% for powders and about 22% for THA, which blend to the reported ~15%.

What’s working well

H1 revenue more than doubled to ₹55.7 cr (from ₹23.5 cr), already above all of FY26. EBITDA was ₹8.24 cr at a 14.8% margin, up from 4.4% in H2 FY26 when tungsten prices squeezed profits, though still below 18% a year ago. PAT was ₹4.75 cr and EPS ₹3.64. Powder volumes rose 39% with 55% higher realisation, and 18 new customers were added (including Oerlikon and Medicoat). THA grew about sixfold and its mix rose from 14% to a third, which should lift margins as it grows. Exports rose about sevenfold, helped by China-plus-one sourcing, defence restocking and aerospace certification, and powder sales to the US continue despite the 50% tariff. The tungsten supply problem is described as solved by Swastik, with sourcing vendors up from 2-3 to over 60. Pricing discipline has improved (buying only against confirmed orders, shorter quote validity), and the balance sheet looks fine, with debt-to-equity at 0.36x, net worth up to ₹55 cr, and ₹37.5 cr of preferential funding (about ₹14 cr received).

What to expect for the rest of FY27 and FY28

With ₹55.7 cr delivered and ₹36.7 cr of orders in hand, FY27 revenue should clear the ₹100 cr target, and management says H2 will be “much better” than H1 if all goes well. Tungsten prices have stabilised after a sharp rise, so deferred customer orders (Indian defence programmes and Israeli buyers still in test mode) may start flowing.

Powder capacity rises from 620 to 800 tpa this year, then to 1,350 tpa in FY28 and about 1,600 tpa with the DRDO-backed atomiser.

THA’s current output is about 60 tpa (2-2.5 tonnes a month), and the 120 tpa expansion could support about ₹150 cr of revenue at current prices. Management guides FY28 growth of 30-50% (35-50% for the next two to three years) with better margins, and a long-term EBITDA margin of 16-20%. Their view is that existing assets can reach ₹400-500 cr, while the ₹1,000 cr vision depends on a new greenfield project and fresh fundraising that is “not even on the drawing board”. Swastik’s bottom line won’t improve until it moves up to carbide and pure-tungsten products, at least six months away. Tungsten hexafluoride for semiconductors is a “moonshot”, and the spark plasma sintering furnace and the EIGA atomiser for reactive powders (titanium, zirconium) are early-stage.

But if the company has to achieve ₹1,000 Cr in revenue, Tungsten Carbide is perhaps the most realistic growth avenue to get there!

5. Indo Count Industries

How they make money

Indo Count is a bed-linen and home-textile maker that sells to large retailers, mainly in the US. It runs in two segments.

The core business is bed linen made in India (sheets, duvet covers and similar), with a FY27 revenue target of about ₹4,000 cr and EBITDA margins of roughly 15% or better. Core revenue is about 70% US and about 30% non-US.

The new businesses have a FY27 target of about ₹1,500 cr. They are split roughly two-thirds utility bedding and one-third branded. Utility bedding (quilts, comforters, blankets and similar) is made in three US facilities. The branded side is built around Wamsutta, a US brand the company acquired, plus licensed brands such as Tommy Hilfiger. Revenue comes from product sales: volumes in million meters multiplied by realisation, plus the margin from branded and utility products. 

Management said gross margin should be viewed on an annual basis and should stay in a 50–55% range. Cotton is the main input cost. The company holds 4–5 months of inventory as a cushion and passes cost increases on to customers with a lag of one to two quarters. Most sales are on FOB or CIF terms, so freight increases are borne by the customer.

What’s working well

Execution is strong across the business. Q2 total income was ₹1,699 cr (+57% YoY, +39% QoQ), and EBITDA more than doubled to ₹259 cr at a 15.3% margin, against a full-year guidance of 13%. H1 revenue of ₹2,923 cr is about 52% of the full-year target, and H1 EBITDA margin is 14.4%. Management attributed the growth to market-share and wallet-share gains. Core margins are above 15%. The new businesses have reached about 30% of revenue, with Q2 revenue of about ₹502 cr and about 60% of the FY27 target already done. The three US utility plants are running above 65% utilisation. Wamsutta’s move into US retail, beyond direct-to-consumer, is a big driver on the branded side. 

The balance sheet is at its best: net debt is ₹518 cr (0.2x equity, the lowest ever), cash is ₹315 cr, annualised ROCE is 21.4% and ROE is 15.3%. Management also said working-capital days are down by at least three weeks since March, and the pass-through mechanism has protected margins so far.

Two caveats: Q2 gross margin fell, and management put that down to product mix. The new businesses’ EBITDA margin is still only “lower double digit”.

What to expect for rest of FY27 and FY28

For FY27, management said it will exceed the ₹5,500 cr revenue guidance and the 13% EBITDA margin guidance. Volume guidance is 105–110 million meters, with 51 million done in H1. The margin could reach 14–15% for the year, but management said it will not go beyond that. Rough arithmetic from the H1 run-rate suggests revenue of about ₹6,000 cr or more, though management gave no number. The new businesses’ margins should rise from lower double digits toward the core’s 15% over the next two to three quarters as the US plants fill up. The ₹250 cr capex is spread over 12–18 months, with only about ₹40 cr spent in H1. Most of the spinning capex should land in FY27, and the effluent treatment plant will probably spill into FY28. For FY28, the stated goal is ₹8,000 cr of revenue by CY28 (double the FY25 base of ₹4,000 cr), and management said this needs no growth capex. Utility plants should reach full utilisation and the branded business should reach about $100 mn, both by CY28.

The UK FTA took effect in July and the EU deal is still pending, and non-US revenue should grow by more than 20% in FY27. Management will give FY28 guidance next year. Net debt should keep falling as free cash flow comes in.

That's all for this edition. Wishing you a Sunday filled with festive sparkle, glowing diyas and plenty of Diwali cheer!
